SAMSO : "He is not rich, and yet he makes a great deal more money than he spends." Redd 'how can that be!" Samso : "lie works in the Mint." JONES: "I'm quite a near neighbour of yours now, Mrs. Golightly ; I've taken a house on the river." Mrs. G. : "Oh! well, I hope you'll drop in some day." WIFE: What are you sitting by the open window for? Do you want to catch your death of cold?" Husband : " Thu.t. new homeopathic doctor across the way says /!e can cure the worst cold in two days. I bet him five shillings he can't. / am going to win his money" IT takes a girl about foar hours longer to clean the front windows of a house than the back win- dows. A PAPER announced for its columns a forthcom. ing story entitled "The Prettiest Girl in Town." A hundred young ladies have sent post-cards and warned the editor not to use their real names. YOUNG MOTHER: " Don't you think baby very much like his father?" Lady Visitor : "Yes, I do. But don't worry. He may grow out of it." MORE THAN SHE ASKED FOR. —Mrs. Spooney : " Will you love me just as much, darling, when I am old?" Mr. Spooney : "More, Lydia; you Won't be so silly then !" HE : " Ah, if I might linger by your side for ever I sl:ould be another man !" She: "How funny ! It is another man that does linger there." Jr was the newly-fledged bee that, alter ventur- ing out of the hive on a wet day, sang out on his return, "There's no place like comb." SOMEBODY says: "True happiness is found in pursuing something, not in catching i ." The man who pursues the last 'bus at night knows better. HE VY-AS FORGIVEN.—She : "You forget your- self, sir." He: "How could I think of myself in your presence?" 17.timER (wishing to impress the lesson): ''Now, ny SOD, tell me why I punished you!" Son : " That's it—you've pounded the life out of toe, father, an' now you don't know whit you done it

107 !" MYSTERY EXPLAINED. —" Way is Miss B. wear- ing black?" "She is in mourning for her husband." " Why, she never had a husband.' "That is why she mourns. She is grieving over the husband she hasn't got. "Ti no happiness, my son, consists in finding that you have paid two shillings for an article exactly like that for which your friend had to pay half a crown the day before. SOMEONE is always wanting special legislation. Here comes a man advoc sting the passing of a law competing railway restaurant-keepers to date their apple pies and sandwiches. "On, for some new-coined name by which to call him! Oh, for some name no other lips could give !" was the prayer of Violet until she married him. Now she is content to call him Old Beeswax. "Is his lordship at home?" asked a gentleman of a well-powdered flunkey. "Don't know, sir, I'm sure. I will just inquire." He returned with the message, " No, sir. His lordship desires me to say that he has just gone out.' " Ah! thank you very much. Kindly give him my com- pliments, and say I didn't call !' A CRUEL SUGGESTION. —" But you do not love me, mademoiselle; you will never love me ! There is nothing Ida for me to do but to go and put an end to my existence. "In what way, if you please !" "By blowing out My brains." "Then you might oblige me by purchasing your revolver at Durand's. Durand and I are engaged, and I should only be too glad to have an oppostunity of putting 8: mething in his way." "I'm very tired," said the lady at the head of the supper table one Sunday evening. "You should not be," said her minister, who had been asked in to the evening meal; "you haven't preached two sermons to-day." "No," said the lady, absent-mindedly, "but I listened to them." CAUGHT NAPPING.—Uncie : "Dear me, Karl, what a poor memory you have." Nephew: "A poor memory, you say? Why, I can repeat four pages of the names in the directory .after reading them through only once!" Uncle: "Pll bet you a hamper of champagne that Jou can't do it." The nephew sends for a directory, attentively peruses tour pages, and shuts up the book. Uncle: • Well ?" Nephew : " Smith, Smith, Smith," etc., ad infinitum. All the four pages of the direc- tory being taken up with this familiar patronymic, our student won his bet in fine style. OLD GENT (proposing health of happy pair at the wedding breakfast) : "And as for the bride- groom, I can speak with still more confidence of him, for I was present at his christening, I was present at the banquet given in honour of his coming of age, I am present here to-day, and I trust I may be spared to be present at his funeral !" (Ssnsation). Larran ETHEL : "Mamma, Mrs. Nexcloor's childr n are playin' house in their garden. Dlayn't we play house in ours ? " Mamma? "Certainly." Little Ethel : "That'll be lovely. Then we can quarrel over the back fence, just like real neighbours." "What have you aimed your baby, Rastus ? " asked a visitor. "Samuel Pro Tern. Johnson, sah." What is the 'Pro Tern.' for?" "To show dal de name is only temporary, sah. We kind o' thought dat Sam might like to choose his own nat..° when he growed up, sail, so we put 'Pro Tem.' in as a warning to de public." "PLEASE, sir, it was 9.20 when you got here. When were late you always keep us after school," said the smart boy. "Very well," said the school- master ' • "you shall all stay and keep me after school, for an hour." CLERGYMAN: "You say you are going to marry again. You surprise me. This will make the fourth husband, will it not ? " She: " Yes ; and as you performed the ceremony each time, I called to see if I couldn't make some arrangement with you about getting a discount on the marriage fee through taking a quantity." TEN persons at an hotel table ordered " blanc mange' for dessert. No. 1 called for blammange, No. '2 for blue monge, No. 3 for blanc mange, No. 4 for biting mong, No. 5 for bla mong, Na. 6 for bluemong, No. 7 for blanche mange, No. 8 for blammong, No. 9 for blang maunch, and No. 10 for blammonge. A MAN was travelling lately while afflicted with a very bad cough. He annoyed his fellow travellers greatly, till finally one of them remarked, in a tone of displeasure :—" Sir, that is a very bad cough of yours !" "True, sir," replied our friend ; "but you will excuse me, it's the best I've got." "MY dear, look down below," said Mr. Grand- iose, as he stood on the bridge with his wife, and gazed at a tug hauling a long line of barges. Such is life : the tug is like the man, working and toiling, while the barges, like women, are—" "1 know," interrupted Mrs. G., acridly; "the tug does all the blowing, and the barges bear all the burden." THE WAITER'S MISTAKE.—He had made a hearty meal at a restaurant, and, getting up, he said to the waiter : "I declare if I haven't forgotten my purse!" The waiter fired up, and hurled big words at him for fully three minutes before pausing for breath. When a change came the stranger continued, "But I have a five-pound note here in any waistcoat pocket !" The waiter could not smile to save his life. REPORTING PROGRESS.—She is one of those very matter-of-fact girls. "How are you getting on with your music?' asked the young man, who was calling on her. "Well," she answered, "of course it wouldn't be proper for me to compliment myself. But some of the neighbours have told me that they have stayed awake at night for hours listening to my playing." And she smiled in a self-approving way that was sweet to behold. A CERTAIN American, who had a great horror of being called on for an after-dinner speech, described himself, when asked to make one, as being in a worse case than Daniel: for when Daniel saw the lions in the den °peeing their jaws preparatory to the satisfying of their hunger, he said, " Well, if there's ay after dinner speaking to be done on this occasion, it won't be done by !" div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

It is not often that tricks are tried upon the sedate practitioners in the law courts even on the Ist of April. But Monday morning saw one quite as good as the old game of getting the crowd t.o as- semble to see the lions washed at the Tower. A long list of witness actions was on Monday's paper to be heard betore the Lord Chancellor,and of course a considerable array of counsel appeared on the scene. Mr. Justice Romer, who sits in chambers on Monday, referred to the matter with as solemn a face as he ceuld command, and expressed his sor- row at the list having appeared, as none of the cases could possibly be taken before the next day. On his departure there were loud and angry mur- murs, and search is to be made for the gentleman who had so imposed upon the profession.

Lord Rosebery does not act as if he considered his term of office as Prime Minister to be a question of months. Ile is furni4iing No. 10, Downing-street in a most sumptuous style, mostly with his own furniture from Berkeley-square, in preparation for a stay there during the summer. Big as the official residence is, the Office of Works have had great difficulty in finding room for Lord Rosebery s re- tinue. Be brings fifteen servants. Sombre Down- ing-street is now expected to blossom out into great gaity, as Lord Rosebery intends giving several dinner parties there after Easter. The next Cabinet Council is to take place on Thursday next.

There is a growing impression in educational circles that a return of the Conserilative party to power would mean a strenuous attempt to obtain further subsidies from the public purse for Volun- tary schools. Recent speeches by Lord Salisbury and Mr. Balfour are taken to indicate that this is becoming a settled piece of Conservative policy. It is thought by authorities on the question that only a large Conservative majority in the House of Com- mons could carry a scheme of further State aid to Voluntary schools, but it is believed that even a small majority could carry the proposal to relegate the decision to the localities themselves. The pro- posal to extend the benefit of the rates to Volun- tary schools is therefore becoming more significant, and all the more so because a fair number of school boards have already acceded to the request of the Manchester School Board by adopting a resolution in favour of such "rate aid." The friends of a national system of board schools may well be on the alert.

" What," asks the Conservative" Morning,"" has ' Mr. George Peel, a young Treasury clerk, done for the cause of the Union, or what risk has he in- curred, that Mr. Nelson, a man twice his age, who has for ten years been placing Unionist voters on the register at his own expense, should be asked to make way for him? The probable result of this folly will be that a Radical will be returned for Leamington. The electors won't stand having their members chosen for them, even by Mr. Cham- berlain and Mr. Balfour."

Certainly the Russian Government are becoming more liberal. They have lately removed the pro- hibition against Messrs. Moody and Sankey's hymns. which has existed since June 24,1886. The agent of the Bible Society at St. Petersburg never was able to get at the reason of the decree, but it was supposed to be connected with the hymn, " Hold the fort, for I am coming," which the Censor considered capable of being used with a political meaning. •

Thus writes a Tory correspondent :—" The doctrine of the heredity of genius promises to receive a striking exemplification in the career of Lord Robert Cecil. Lord Robert Cecil is the third son of the Marquis of Salisbury. Like all the Cecils, he is not ashamed of earning his own living, and has adopted the profession of a barrister, as did his father before him. " Happening to be in one of the House of Lords Committee Rooms lately I I was struck by the ability of a pale and aristo- cratic young counsel, who seemed more than a match for his opponent, himself one of the ablest of junior counsel at the Parliamentary Bar—Mr. Lewis Coward to wit. I inquired the clever young counsel's name and I as told it was Lord Robert Cecil. Tall, young, and gifted,and with cot a little of his mother's aristocratic beauty, combined with a winning manner and other aids to fortune, Lord Robert C?.cil can hardly fail to get on."

Prince Bismarck celebrates his birthday in illus- trious company. The King of Denmark will be seventy-six on April 8; the-King mf Belgians sixty on April 9; the King of Roumania fifty-sir on April 20; and the Shah sixty-six on April 24. The Sov- ereigns born in April include also several German minor potentates.

Poor Sir Henry Parkes, in Australia, is being chaffed and ridiculed to a painful extent in his old age. Unfortunately, the old politician has been elaborating his family pedigree. He believes that he is a direct descendant of Falconbridge, the left- handed son of Richard Cceur de Lion, and those who know the Blue Mountains will remember that Sir Ilenry's cottage on the way up to Katoomba was called Falconbridge. But the comic papers in Sydney have taken the matter up, and have started writing epitaphs in advance for the ex-Premier. here is a verse from an " olde Englyehe bailude " .

The task of:allocating the Paris fund 13! the Irish Nationalist party is proving a much more protracted business than was at first expected. The number of claims that continus to be made on the fund by solicitors and others for services rendered to the party in Mr. Parnell's time is remarkable, and the ,Jue consideration and settlement of all those will he a work of months The committee appointed for the adjustment af the claims consisted of Mr. Dillon, Mr. Harrington, and Mr. Devitt. As Mr. Devitt is departing for Australia, it has become necessary to appoint someone else in his place, and ltr. Alfred Webb, M.P., has consented to act.

I hear that the Speaker will probably make his farewell speech on Monday night, when he an- nounces his resignation, instead of waiting until Tuesday, when the formal leave-taking takes place. This will shorten the proceedings on Tuesday, which will be practically limited to carrying the usual resolution of thanks. Mr. Peel has no inten- tion of declining the peerage which, according to custom, will be offered him.

A new and a somewhat police virtue has been discovered in the electric light. It was stated at the meeting of the Institute of Electrical En- gineers a day or two ago that at the great goods station at Nine Elms of the Midland Railway, where the light has recently been introduced, the theft of property diminished to such an extent that the saving on this head alone defrayed the cost of the installation. While the old gas lights were in use, shedding their dim rays around, pilfering was carried on upon a great scale. It has now almost reached a vanishing point, and it is expected shortly to disappear altogether. The praises of electricity iu its capacity of policeman deserve to be recorded, as it may .produce equally serviceable results in all places where large quantities of goods are within easy access of the light-fingered tribe.

Folks in " high !ociety " have been watching the movements of poptilar Royal personages for more than a year with a feeling which may be described as speculative curiosity. Latterly all reserve has ! been thrown off by the gossips of the drawing- rooms. Not much notice might,under ordinary cir- cumstances, have been taken of the announcement that the Princess of Wales is to leave for the Con- tinent 80011. But Her Royal Highness happens to leave within a few days after the arrival of her , august husband from his yachting trip in the Medi- terranean. And " Society" recalls that such inci- dents have occurred repeatedly within the past few years. Indeed the Royal couple have scarcely been a fortnight together in England since the end of 1893, and the arrival of one generally synchronises with the departure of the other. So, human nature being as it is,it is not strange that gossips are shak- ing their heads and talking seriously.

Salt put upon the clinkers ha the stove,while they are hot, will loosen them without difficulty. If pure tomato soup is wanted, put in no other veget- able except a scrap of onion. Tomato soup is a distinc- tive variety. When dampening clothes for ironing use water as hot as the hand can bear ; sprinkle the linen, fold smoothly, roll up tight, and they will iron much easier. In the " Westmizaster Budget" is a remarkable inter- view with a fashionable tailor on the subject of men's corsets. " What is the average width of a man's corset- waist ? Fifty, a hundred, or thereabouts ?" asked the writer. " No, not quite that ; though I measured a fat clergyman the other day for a pair of stays who measured fifty inches round the waist. Clergymen are g,ood'customers of mine. A good many officers in the Army and Navy get their corsets from me.

Marchioness Li Hung Chang. Marchioness Li, the wife of Li Hung Chang, of China, is described as a very beautiful and, for China,a learned woman, who looks thirty-five and is fifty-five. Her hus- band's wealth is fabulous, and she spends royally,though she keeps accurate account of every item. In her magni ficent home on the banks of the Pei-ho she lives in great splendour, surrounded by song-birds, peacocks,acquaria, pottery, gems, botanical collections, and a thousand at- tendants and servants. She has two thousand coats,one thousand two hundred pairs of " trouserettes," and five hundred fur robes. Her feet are so small that she is unable to walk more than a few steps. She dresses her hair in fifty ways,her favourite coiffure being ale griffin. She baths twice a day in oil of orange and acacia blooms and takes an airing in a cooli sedan.

Should Wives be Dependent on their Husbands 1' Discussing, the vexed problem of hew women right easily provide against poverty in old age, a writer in the March number of the Windsor Magazine states :—,` The possession of a little money of one's own is never a dis- advantage to a married woman, and the want of it may occasionally be a serious matter. Thus, one of thoyea- sons for the existence of the so-called • New Woman ' in England and America has been stated by a transatlantic writer to be the fact that in these countries dowries for daughters have been the oxception and not the rule. The married women has been, and in most instances is' ab- solutely dependent for every sixpence on her husband. While great mutual affection may make such dependence bearable and even pleasurable, it is not difficult to ima- gine circumstances under which it might be far from agreeable. Men themselves recognise the unpleasant- ness of being entirely dependent on a rich wife, and while the reverse is the more natural pcsition, it is not always more desirable. In view of this, indeed, many settle an annual allowance for pin-money on their wives for they admit that it must be hard to have to ask far every penny one wants even of the best, most loving and tenderest of husbands. In all cases, however gener- ous the husband may be, it is well for a wife to have, even if only for employment in her husband's interest, some small sums of her own, into the disposal of which no one has that right of inquiry which naturally belongs to whoever provides a woman with all she possesses."

WE PARTED AT THE ALTAR;
BY LAURA JEAN !ABBEY,
Author of "A Mad Betrothal," " lone,"" Parted by Fate," " Floribees Lover," etc.., etc.
CHAPEER X. W. A TORTURED II EA RT. FREDERICK was coming home. In a few hours from now she should see him.

—...— The idea seemed almost more than she could grasp. What would he say when he found her there? That question began to assume a terrible form to poor Doris. Would there be a scene? She knelt there, in the red glow of the sunlight, trying in vain to drive the terrible doubts and fears away. Perhaps it was some faint foreshadowing of the sorrow to come that made her tremble as she knelt there—the first thrill of that strange tragedy which was to cross her life. There came a tap at the door. "Mrs. Thornton would be glad to have Miss Carlisle come to her boudoir." And with a slow, hesitating step, Doris went. "I want you to read to me, Miss Carlisle," she said. "I never remembered an afternoon to pass so slowly." Mechanically, Doris picked up the book. The lines on the page seemed to waver before her eyes. The dusk crept up, and the stars came out. Long since one of the maids had entered and lighted the chandelier. Still Doris read on. It was better than talking. Doris felt that she should go mad if Mrs. Thornton were to talk to her about Frederick and Vivian—her favourite subject. Suddenly there was a sound of carriage wheels stopping before the porch, and the next moment voices were heard in the lower hall. "My son has arrived," said Mrs. Thornton. Doris spoke no word. Her face grew pale as marble. She could count the great, gasping heart throbs. She clung with trembling hands to the table lest she should fall, praying, with white lips and shadowed eyes, that she might not die when her eyes fell upon his face. Some minutes passed—how many Doris never knew. Then came the sound of footsteps that Doris knew so well. She pressed her hand on her heart, for its will beating frightened her as each step fell on her ear. She could have cried aloud in agony with the terrible tension of her nerves; but her white lips could form no sound. The next minute he had entered the room. Handsome, laughing Frederick Thornton atood before her. She never understood why the sight did not kill her. Why, when her eyes rested upon him, she did not fall dead. Oh, how kindly he greeted his mother' laughing heartily when she told him the days ha had spent away from her seemed like so many months. How strange it was that he could laugh, Doris thought, when the sin of breaking a heart lay at his door. Doris shrank back among the shadows of the heavy silken curtains, but Mrs. Thornton spoke her name, and Doris rose slowly. "Frederick, my son, this is my companiou, Miss Carlisle," she heard his mother say; what else was uttered Doris never knew. Frederick Thornton looked carelessly in the direction she indicated. He saw a small, slim, dark-faced little creature' who seemed to be trembling with confusion, he thought. His eyes rested on her only an instant. Then with a low bow he turned away. Doris stood rooted to the spot. Silent, motion- less all the tragedy and passion of her love shining in, her face, her arms fell helplessly to her side. She could not have moved to have saved her life. She had expected, despite the change in her, that he would recognise her; that he would cry out either in anger or emotion. But no; he turned away, knowing her not. Oh, the pity of it l—the cruel pity of it She remembered how they had parted in the sunny hotel parlour. "I shall be back within an hour," he had said, as he tossed the well:filled purse into her lap to replenish her warbrobe ; then, with a smile and a nod, without a farewell kiss, he had turned and walked out of the room, leaving her to her fate. She remembered the horrible nights and the days that had followed—how she nearly went mad with watching for him and calling wildly upon him to come back to her. And she remembered the crowning blow of all— when the good old housekeeper had taken her in her arms, attempting to soothe her as though she had been a little child, as she wispered the pitiful words in her ear: "Do not grieve and weep for him, child; in my opinion he is not worth a tear. He will never come back; he has deserted you." Doris lived over again that horrible scene, as, quite unnoticed, she gazed at the handsome face of her faithless husband. Oh ! why had he married her if he had intended to desert her? Of the terrible accident that had occurred, nearly costing Frederick Thornton his life, and the loss of memory as to the late events which had transpired, sweeping away all remembrance of a bride who awaited him, of course Doris knew nothing; and thus fate continued to play at cross- purposes with these two. It was to end in a tragedy so pitiful that the angels would weep for Doris, the helpless child-bride whose young life had all gone wrong. In the evening the ladies assembled in the draw. jag-room, where Frederick and his father awaited them. Doris would have given much to absent herself, but Mrs. Thornton insisted that she should be present. There seemed no loophole of escape for her. Frederick and Vivian were standing by one of the lace-draped windows as she entered; his hand- some face was bent over her, and he was talking to her in so low a tone Doris could not catch the words he uttered. What was he saying to her that brought that lovely flush to Vivian's cheeks and the bright light to her eyes? Was he complimenting her on her beauty? Was he, who was bound to another by every tie that Heaven holds sacred—daring to speak to her of—love? The banker and his wife watched them, and nodded and smiled to each other. Gwendolin and Isabel sat at the piano discussing some pieces of music, and Beatrix at curled up in an arm-chair watching the anguished face of her mother's young companion with much curiosity. "Dear me, what a tragical expression !" thought Trixy, shuddering. "How she watches my brother and Vivian, and—can it be possible I—there are tears in her eyes. Poor girl ! why is she so un- happy? Isivonder if mamma has been scolding her re threatening to discharge her." All unconscious of this intense scrutiny, Doris still sat watching the two, standing by the moonlit window. "How beautiful Vivian is I" thought Doris, sick at heart. "No wonder he regrets that on the impulse of the moment he married me instead of Vivian, the beauty. Ah, who could resist her? Was she not the very queen of love ?" Women have suffered much and will suffer again; they have endured tho pangs of death with a smile: they have listened to words which were their death warrant, and have answered with a bright laugh; they have stood still, firm and undismayed, while the sharpest sword has pierced their hearts; but perhaps no woman ever suffered more than Doris as she sat watching Frederick Thornton and Vivian. • She saw him offer Vivian his arm, and together they stepped from the long French window out on to the porch, and down into the rose garden beyond. How tenderly he had drawn the light scarf over Vivian's shoulders, fearful lest the night wind should blow upon her too roughly. Oh, how Doris longed to follow them I—follow ond confront them in the path, crying out : " He is mine I Do not take him from me! You have every blessing the world holds dear, while I have only him! I am alone in the world but for him Send him from you Do not smile upon him I And Heaven may let his estranged heart drift back to me. I alone have the right to his love." • She rose from her seat with that wild, rash 'intention; then she remembered where she was. "What is the matter, Miss Carlisle?" said Frederick's mother. "There is a look in your eyes which startles me. Are you tired ? " "Yes," replied Doris, faintly. "Then you had better retire to your own room," said Mrs. Thornton. Doris gladly availed herself of this permission. Her window looked out on the rose garden and the fountain. She could watch them unobserved. When she reached her room and stole breathlessly to the window, she found they were not there. They must have passed to some other portion of the grounds. Poor Doris stood by the window, her hands closely locked together, the bitter tears falling from her eyes. She had had her heart's desire. She had looked upon Frederick Thornton's face again. She had heard his voice. For this she had borne the almost intolerable restraint of her disguise, and had !Jared enter hie home. Sue lied believed

DEAREST NELLIE, The new spring out-door wraps have taken my fancy immenSeil. itz; eye,. so much Isrettier than those of last/ year, and the capes particularly are very smart and becoming. They are almost all of one uniform length, viz., reaching just below the elbow (although a few in cloth or serge are rather longer), and fit plainly over the top of the shoulders, but are exceedingly wide round the lower edge, while they are to be seen in an im- mense variety of materials, and are trimmed in a score of different ways. For immediate wear, however, velvet and velveteen are the two most popular fabrics, especially in black. A pretty little cape, for instance, in black velvet is per- forated all over with round holes, about the size of a crown piece, each hole being covered with a star of jet passomentetio, through which the lining of gold•coloured silk is visible. A full ruff of black chiffon finishes the neck, and a couple of bunches of yellow cowslips nestle among the rushing. These clusters of artitichl flowers aro most fashionable in thas situation, but the mode has a suspicion of tawdriness about it whiLh is objectionable.

Just a delighqul little mantle was that I saw worn by a lady I met last week. I) was made in fawn clot h, strapped, the tipp3r cape farming revere. Novelty appears in toe double collar, the shorter one being rolled over in a singularly grace. ful fashion. lho corners of tl.o cape were rvueded, and the neck finished with a gilt chain and hook. Jackets era much shorter in the basque than they have been for some time past, and most of the new models are very neat and jaunty-looking. One of dark Havana brown smooth cloth is quite t7giat- fitting, and has a sort of square cape collar of cream white cloth, covered with fine braiding in brown, the sleeves, which are something of the Garibaldi shape, having little gauntlet cuffs of the braided cream cloth to match the collar. A plainer style of coat Is of dark blue ribbed cloth, close, fitting, and double breasted, with wide revere ornamented with an app!iqu6 of dark blue velvet, the turn-down collar twtLg similarly ornamented. The sleeves of this coat are box-pleated into the armholes in the new way. Loose•fronted double. breasted jackets of covert coating are very suitabli for early spring wear, and, as a rule, they have strapped scams, two rows of large, flat pearl or bone buttons down the front, and turn-down col- lars t.o(1 with velvet. Neither sleeves nor revers in these lailor.m?..de coats are to large as those iv the more fauoif .11 jackets.

Orange green, drab, and grey were blended most artistically in a spring custome I saw the other day at one of the London shops. The cape, which was made with immense revers, had a collar and yoke of light fawn-coloured velvet, and the hat was crowned with those "nodding plumes" we are seeing so much of just now. As I expected, the old " cottage " bonnet is com- ing in; indeed, it was bound to do seeing the foroe of the 183111850 revival. These are quaint, and are not suited to all styles, but at any rate they are generally simple, and often are made of very pretty novel straws. The toque is well to the fore, made entirely of flowers, or of straw draped with chiffon and lace, and trimmed with flowers. The " cart-wheel " hat is to be seen in all materials, but principally in coarse straw, the wide brim being perfectly straight, the crown very low. These are trimmed with wide satin ribbon or with lace mixed with bouquets. A great deal of white

or cream lace is as trimming on black chip or burnt straw hats, the lace being handsome and often worked up with metal. Not so much velvet is to be seen, but broad satin ribbon of rosplendent hues is being largely patronized. pretty hat, made of black open•work straw, has a garniture of black lace encircling the crown, and brightened with sequin wings, jet clusters, black satin ribbon and bunches of osprey, while under the brim at each side the tints of the tea roses give welcome relief. It is a very smart hat. Yours lovingly, JEINNIL

Mr. Asquith, speaking at Nottingham on Wednesday night.aaio that a long time ago their opponents had dug the grave of the Liberal Government, but the latter ex- hibited strong symptoms of persistent vitality. They were urged to dissolve. but they did not intend to do so until they had placed before trA House of Commons mea- sures to which the Liberal party were pledged.He denied that there was no room side by side for political and social legislation, and said that the Government would carry forward large and beneficial reconstruction and social reform. Having dealt at length with the question of disestablishment and disendowment of the Welsh Church, he referred to the lockout in the boot trade,and expressed a hope V- at the two parties would not allow obstinate adherence to even strong and settled convic- tions to prevent their coming to an understanding. He trusted that strikes as a mode of settling disputes would come to be regarded as obsolete as the ordeal of trial by battle of the middle ages.

Ing upon his face just nu,le more would still and calm the lever that Wal'i bm*ning her heart away. She believed after that the ten:lble pain of longing would die away. Instead of that it was redoubled,' it was intensi- fied a thousand times. That first :lance at her husband's handsome, laughing face had roused her love into full and active life again. She had said to herself she would look-, at him just once, and go away. Was she re.ay tn 0, now? Oh, no, no !—a thousand times no! What should she do, then? Live on in this way beneath his mother's roof, a paid companion, or should she go and seek her husband, when the house was still and dark, and beg of him to tell her why he had married her and spoiled her life if he meant to desert her? She would tell him the cruel rumours that they were circulating—that beautiful Vivian was his sweetheart, and that he was soon to marry her— and beg him to refute those stories, for it could never be true while she, his wife lived. He had deserted her, it was true, but for all that she was his wedded wife. No act of man's could ever part the two whom God himself had joined together by the solemn ties of marriage. She would tell him that. The long hours dragged themselves slowly by as she sat at the moonlit window. At length the house was still. Darkness wrapped it in a mantle of gloom. The midnight hour sounded from some far-off belfry. Doris rose to her feet, glided to her chamber door, and softly opened it, stepping out into the corridor. "May Heaven help me !" she moaned. "This action is the turning point of my life." Then she walked swiftly down the dark corridor without once glance behind her.

div.head: CHAPTER XVI.
div.p: CHAPTER XVI.

"ONLY KEEP MY SECRET." Stealthily as a shadow Doris flitted out into the dimly lighted corridor. Her face flushed, her hands burned, her heart beat wildly, her brain seemed on fire. She must know the truth. She could bear sorrow and this cruel despair no longer.

She must know the worst. Her slipperecl feet made nn sound on the thick, velvet carpet as she hurried along. Suddenly a hand was laid on her shoulder, and the voice of Beatrix Thornton exclaimed in astonishment: "Why, Miss Carlisle, what are you doing here so late?" And as she spoke, Trixy threw open the library door before which they stood, and a flood of light streamed out upon Loris's white, startled face. Trixy's question had heen so abrupt it almost took her breath away ; but she recovered something like composure almost the next moment, however. "I was restless ; I could not sleep ; so I came down to the library for a hook,' she faltered. She did not add that she know it was Frederick Thornton's custom to spend long hours here after she family had retired, and she expected to find him here to•night. "That is my case exactly," laughed Trixy. "Come in, and I will help you select a good
book." Trembling with suppressed excitemet, Doris followed her into the library, casting her eyes eagerly about the room as she crossed the thres- hold. She saw that he whom she was in search of

was not there. "You should,not sit up reading and lose your beauty sleep to-night, above all other nights, for to-morrow night is our ball, you know. Some of the handsomest young gentlemen in New York will be present. Take care some of them do not carry away your heart, Miss Carlisle. If I were a hand- some young man, instead of a girl, I should fall straightway in love with you. Why, what are you blushing so for ?" cried Trixy. "Don't you like to talk about love and lovers ?" "No," replied Doris, in a low, disttessed voice, tears filling her deep blue eyes. "If you please, Trixy, I'd rather not talk of such things." "You are certainly an odd girl," laughed Trixy, heartily. ' "Why, do you know, all the handsome young gentlemen hereabouts have fallen deeply in love with you, and have just been besieging both Isabel and Gwendolin for an introduction to you? Every one takes you for a guest of the house, instead of mamma's companion." No laughing rejoinder came from Doris's lips. There was an anxious look in her eyes. Ah ! this, then, accounted for the growing coldness with which the two sisters greeted her. "You do not seem enough interested to even ask who they are," said Trixy, disappointedly. How little she knew that the girl's heart and soul were bound up in her own handsome brother Frederick. Ah, how poor Doris's heart longed for sympathy and consolation. Oh, if she only dared tell Beatrix Thornton the great hidden sorrow that seemed eating her heart away! She felt that she must unburden her heart to someone, or it must surely break. "Trixy," she said, faintly, locking and unlock jug her hands nervously, "I could never love any- one in this world again. I loved once. It was tile sweetest, yet the most bitter experience of my life. The one who vowed always to love me, cruelly cast me from him. Yet, I love him still with all my heart. Do not talk to me of love or lovers, Trixy. I cannot bear it. The world will never hold but one face for me;; and that is the lace of him who is lost to me for ever.'' "Oh, how delightfully romantic I" cried "I said to myself over and over in

Beatrix. said to nip, aged. that there was 801116 mystery in your life. I have seen such strange shadows in your eyes; and your voice often has the sound of tears in it. " I do wish I couhl help you in ~:otne way," said Beatrix, thoughtful " I'd gi vu the world to set the matter straight for you. What's his name and where does he live? " "I cannot tell you,' fait 'red Doris, catching her breath with a little dry sob. "Oh, dear! Then I do not see how I can help you," cried Trixy. "You cannot, secret for me." "I will," answered Beatrix, earnestly. And as they parted Trixy resolved in her own mind to bring this truant lover back to Doris; but the first and most important step was to discover his name. While she stood in the doorway of the library, by a sudden impulse Doris turned and glided back to her side. "Every one is so cold and cruel to me. I think I should die, if I were to lose your friendship, Beatrix," she, said, pantingly. "You will never die, then, if you wait for that event to transpire," laughed Trixy. "When I like person I like them for all time. I never could pretend a friendship Ido not feel. Why, the first moment I saw you I felt strangely attracted toward you, I could not tell why." She wondered why Doris caught her hands in her own and kissed them so passionately, while burning "tears fell from her eyes. Poor Doris! If she had only confided in Beatrix —reckless, impulsive, warm-hearted Bee—it might have been better for her. "Beatrix," she whispered, wistfully, "no matter what you might hear of me in the future—no matter what fate might tempt me to do—promise me, Bee, you of all the world will believe in me; you will not lose your faith in me." Oh, how hollow and unnatural the sweet voice sounded! "There are pitiful secrets in many lives," she went on, "that drive those who are forced to keep them locked in their breasts, to the very verge of madness in their woe. If there is any pity in your heart for me, Beatrix, pray for me. My feet*Are on the edge of a terrible precipice." In after years Beatrix Thornton, in recalling that incident, never forgot the haunted look of despair that crossed poor Doris's face as the words broke from her lips in a piteous cry. "I will see Frederick to-morrow," thought Doris, as she hurried back to her own room. But when the morrow came there was so much going on at the villa she could find no opprtunity. A dozen times or more Frederick Thornton passed the slight girlish figure with the dark face and the haunting blue eyes, with a careless nod, a smile, or a pleasant word. He did not look closely at her, or he would have observed that she looked as though she were abOut to faint. That afternoon there was a long and anxious consultation between Mrs. Thornton and her two daughters as to the propriety of allowing Miss Carlisle—the paid companion—to attend the "She has worked so hard for it," said Mrs. Thornton, "I do not see how we can refuse. She will naturally expect it." "No matter what she expects, mamma,'*returned Gwendolin, flushing angrily. "We are not obliged to consult her wishes. Why, with a face like hers she would be the belle of the ball. It is not once in a lifetime one comes across such a startling face —so rare in style, so perfect in contour." "If mamma cares to see a paid companion out- shine her own daughters, she will allow her to be present; if she studies our interest, she will decline." cut in "There is no denying 1.4
replied Doris.

fact that she would eclipse us if we were foolish over her enough to allow her to appear. All of my gentle men acquaintances are beginning to rave o - already. I wish to the bottom of my heart that girl bad never enteved bilis house. I fear she will bring trouble in the end." A little later Doris entered the boudoir. 'qrs. Thornton turned to her with a forced smile. "You do not know how sorry we are; there will be such a crowd at the ball I find it impossible to IVIi.R "1 did not expect it," saici but quietly ; for the first time she felt like rebelling against her fate—against the lot that condenuma her to obscurity where she should have shone. Her handsome young husband would be there; SO would Vivian. Ah !if she could but have sat in the ball-room and watched them—could have kept them apart by any strategy. Doris was in her room when the carriages corn- menced to roll up to the broad piazza and deposiO their loads of youth and beauty. A ball at Thornton villa was always a success, the room!, were so superb, long and lofty. What would have been a crowd in other places was only a Pleasel number there; and this ball promised to be one o the best given. Doris told herself at first that she would remain in her own room while the grand ball WO, ill progress • then the great curiosity to see ricl Vivian progress; looked, and to see, if possible, she danced with Frederick Thornton, urged her tc' go down. With her heart in a whirl, Doris stole down the broad stairway to the corridor below, where she would have a good view of the ball-room beyond; being herself unseen. How her heart throbbed and her face flushed as she listened to the 11111Sie, as she took up her position behind a marble Cly tie which stood behind a pedestal of blush-red roses. The grand ball room, the reception room, the draw rooms and parlours were thronged with a gay enl ! brilliant assemblage. Ah, what a picture it made , —beautiful faces, flashing jewels, the gleam ci satin and silks, tall men and fair-faced weinen,.l How the light fell on them ! how the warm, Pe'. fumed air stirred gently as they passed ! Suddenly the air seemed to stifle Doris. Passing BO near her that she could have put out her haa and touched them from her place of concealmect" Ow beheld Frederick Thornton and Vivien-- Vivian radiant in white lace and blush-roses, leaning upon his arm. He was escorting her te the ball room. "You will remember, Vivian," she heard hire say, as he bent his dark, 'handsome bead nearer the for beauty, "you are to save most of the waltzes me ; promise me before hand" "That would be unfair," she declared. "It would be just and kind," he answere± eagerly. "I could not endure to see anyone ef:, wartzing with you, dear; I should be tempted '" take you from him." The next instant there was a loud crash. The marble Clytie had fallen from the pedestal to the „d floor ; the crimson roses that had been about it were scattered in all directions, and the debris of roses lay a young girl. " Why, it is Miss Carlisle, your mother's Ore; panion ' cried Vivian, in disruay. "Loo" '- has fainte "Step into the drawing-room while I take Ilef up to mother's apartments," he said to Viviah,.; and without waiting to summon a servant, 'le raised the slight figure in his strong arms and here her rapidly up the broad s airway. ing Then for the first time—in the bright, light light of the chandeliers e looked cur mu: or (lowa into the dark, dimpled face lying against his di:ori —looked—then came to a sudden halt, • perspiration starting out in great beads 03 torenead.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held in the 'town Ball on Tuesday evening. The Mayer (Council- lor4.-Fairclough) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Francotnb, Button, Blackhurst, Wright, Hut- ehinson, Bolton ; Councillors K. T. Fairclough, J. Lyon Whitile Itown clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), Dr. Gornall (medical officer), and Fairhurst (borough treasurer.) THE LAVE MR. SSSEPH DAVIES. The MAYOR said that since they last met the town had sustained a severe loss by the death of Mr. Joseph Davies, J.P. The deceased gentleman had been a mem- ber of that Counoil,and for a great uumber of years had Performed a good deal of valuable work in that capacity. He had been mayor of theborough for two years, and ' there was hardly a public institution in the town with Which Mr. Davies had not something to do. It must have been very gratifying to the widow, her sons, and relatives, to see such a large and respectful gathering at the funeral on the previous Tuesday. Be would say nothing more, but would submit to the Council the fol- lowing resolution of sympathy --" That this Council receives with deep regret the announcement of the death of Joseph Davies, Esq.., a freeman of the borough, •and formerly mayor and an alderman of the borough, and desifes to record the loss that the borough has sustained by his death, and to express its appreciation of the valu- able services rendered by him to the borough during a long period of public service, not only in the Council, ut as a magistrate,and in connection with many institu tions in the town, and that the Town Clerk be requested to convey to Mrs. Davies and her family the sincere EMPathy of the Council with them in their bereave- ' 'tent." Councillor Sims' GREEN said he had a melancholy „..131Easure in seconding the resolution. He had known 'ir• Davies all his life, and he had followed him into an office in which he (Mr. Davies) had spent a good portion of his youth. The deceased gentleman had left his mark ilionn every part of the history of the town during the ast 20 years, and they should in particular always re- member the part he had taken ha acquiring the hall in Which they met. (Hear hear.) Councillor BENNETT and Alderman SUTTON also spoke 411 appreciative terms of the late Mr. Davies' the, latter Stating that he had aitved with Mr. Davies for some 20 2_30 years on vazioi: a ce man ttees ,and he could therefore ,'Peals- with confidenrxi ES to his excellent business abili- He was quite tura that the town had never had ,alayone who had takan a more lively interest in its wel- lire than the late Mr. Davies. The resolution was then put to the Council and carried Unanimously.

div.p: and ask why it was that there was nothing got from the gas works' and that they were not paying this, that and the other. Let them remember the items which hid been mentioned that evening. (Hear, hear.) • Alderman' BOLTON said he saw from the minutes that the average illuminating power of the gas for the past four weeks vias reputed to be equal to 18.89 candles at both works. One night last week, however, the gas in Mersey-street and Latchford was so bad that people had to burn candles to look for the gas. (Laughter.) Courrcillor WOODS said it was an understood thing that the gas should be of a good quality two or three days before the meeting Of the Town Council, but it appeared that the committee had gone off the line this time. ' The illuminating power of the gas was simply disgraceful on Sunday night last. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH explained that the other night there was an accident at the meter in Church-street hut it was put right in a short time. He was at home on the Sunday night in question, and he could see to read. Councillor Woods eyesight must be wrong, he required to use spectacles. (Laughter.) The minutes were then agreed to. Councillor ROBERTS iti moving the confirmation of the minutes. said be was not prepared at that moment to give any information with regard tp the conferences in addition to what appeared on the agenda paper. With regard to the estimate of £lOO, they. could only elk the Council to pass it without asking them too particularly for details. They did not wish to state how the estimate was made up; but if they did spend the money tasy would do so in a mariner which they believed to be in the best interests of Warrington. (Rear, hear.) Alderman BOLTON secunied, and the motion was agreed to.
FINANCE COMMITTEE.-REDUCTION IN THE RATES.,

_ Councillor SHAW GREEN, in moving the coo firmatiou of the minutes, said that it was with much pleasure that he proposed the confirmation of the minutes of the Finance Committee. It was at all times a much more pleasant task to submit figures showing a substantial , decrease in the amount of the rate than it was to bring forward a demand for an increase. For two years a heavy burden had rested upon the ratepayers,and many have been the inquiries, anxious inquiries, as to when a reduction of the rates might be expected. Ttie burden had been onerous, but everybody recognized the cause and generally it had been cheerfully met. He was happy, that night in being able to bring before the Council the 1 , details of the estimated expenditure for the ensuing year, and to announce as the result of their economical preparation that an improvement and sewer rate am o'l nt- ~ ing to 3s. will be sufficient to meet their wants. (Hear, hear.) Going now to the estimates,the borough rate first I claimed their attention. This varied very little from the call of last year, but there was included halt the cost of extending.the,Fark palleade'vhs well as half the cost of providiq the,additional rootcns required at the School of AA,- i&c. eTlin intirpviment rate estimate hoed a very substantial reductlen' amounting to no ten than £3,372. The estimates Included extra items that had already been explained, 'such as the completion of the purchase by the Market Committee of the Queen- *. property,. the cost of making and paving the foot- path in Sankey-st., &c. ;, but notwithstanding those, they estimated last year that after levying a rate of 3s. Bd. they should have a debit balance of £557, and the Gas• Committee, desiring to assist the Cerporatien, very generdusly came to its help and . bad given as a rebate from the charge of street lighting the sum of £656, for which the thanks of the ratepayers were heartily due. Passing to the sewers rate, they estimated the sum of £1,820 to be required, but Considering the demand for a substantial reduc- tion of the rate, the committee had thought it Well to propose the same rate as last year, namely, 2d., and carry forward the belance.• The three estimates, therefore, were—Borbugh rate, £10,564 15s. Bd. ; improvement rate, £21,785 7s. id. ; and sewers rate, £1,820 7s. 9d. ; making the total of £33,970 103 i 63i The estimated rates to produce—Borough rate £10,364. improvement rate at 3s. £21.420, and sewers rate at 2d. £1,200, or altogether E 32,981, leaving a balance against them of £l,OOO. They preferred, however, laying the lower rate of.3s.this year,and thus gives little breathing titne to the ratepayers. They anticipated that with this help they might halve placed a lower estimate before them, but as ttiey*ared the end of the financial year the Borough Treasurer discovered a curious error in the way the accobincd,Of Longford had been made up. He had been antjcipating a surplus of about £l,OOO after the rebate frOm the Gas Committee had been transferred, when to his' Surprise he found that instead 'of a surplus they were in debt no less 'than £1,400. .T d eiror was not at once aoparent. Last year, follossing on the lines of his predecesanr, the Borough Treasurer credited Longford with £5,657, or about £2,400 more than he could possibly receives The estimate in this form had been going on so far as he could find from the beginning, and arose in this way. The amounts owing at the beginning of the year had been calculated, the manure in stock added to it, and then an estimate of the value of the manure to be made during the year had been made and added also, But this manure to be made was not cash until July of the year following its make, and it was clear it was net right to treat it as revenue for the year in which it was made. They therefore struck it out, but the Council would understand the difference it had made in their forecast. Sundry parts of revenue had shown considerable elasticity, notably the improvement rate itself.r ' They had reduced the capital debt during the ye* tty £7,515, but they had taken up the sum of £4,70W ' pay for sewers extension, baths, &c. The, comm4teb looked hopefully to the future, believing that, whateder their obligatipns were they had only to fairly' explain and show the Teasonableness ' and • necessity of their requeets and the Money would .be T'aillingly pro: vided. (Hear, hear.) The Alavon seconded the adoption of the minute. . -Councillor Roams said the whole of the Council,and the town generally would be ready to congratulate the Finance Committee, and the Chairman , upon the yery. satisfactory statement which had been made that night. It seemed that at last they had got the accounts of the town into something of a business-like form. It had ' always been a puzzle to a great many people in years: gone by to understand the Statements of accounts' published by the Corpdration, but now they would be better understood. He believed the town had turned , thp corner in regard to its financial position ; and they Mightlairly expect that with 'the growth of the popula- tion and the rateable value, they would be able to" do greater things in the future than they had done in the past without making an increased burden upon the ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) Councillor WOODS congratulated the Borough Treasurer upon the excellent manner in which he had produced the accounts for the past year. After some remarks by Councillor MoNes,the minutes were agreed to. Councillor SRAM GREEN subsequently formally moved the adoption of the rates. This proposition was seconded and unanimously carried, after which the Council rose.
THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT.

The annual report of Dr. Gornall, the ,Medical Officer of Health for Warrington was issued last week and as usual contains a great deal of inter- esting and important information. In the statisti- cal summary it is stated that the acreage of the borough was 2,004; the population estimated at Mid-summer 1894, 56,054; the number of inhabited houses, 10,411 ; rateable value, £175,927 ; birth-rate during 1894, 396; the death-rate, 17.4. The aver- age death-rate for 10 years 1885-1894, 21.7. The total number of births during the year was 2,222 of whizh 1,171 were males, and 1,051 females. I THE DEATH-ROLL OF THE DIFFERENT WARDS. The death-rates of the various wards was as follows :—Town Hall, 154 ; W hitecross, 171 ; Be,wsey, 13 02 ; Orford, 18.9 ; St. John's 20.1 ; Fair- field, 176 ; Howley, 16.5 ; St. Austin's, 16.1 ; Latch- ford, 20.0. The zymotic death-rate for the whole of borough was 2.6 which is one of the lowest on re- cord. It is interesting to note that during the year small-pox has been introduced three times by tramps but in no case had the disease spread. THE SLAUGHTER-HOUSES. Dr. Gornall reports unfavourably with regard to the slaughter-houses. Twenty-three of the 28 are in close contiguity with dwelling-houses, four are connected with licensed premises. They are governed by certain bye-laws, but the result of an nspection showed that the bye-laws were, toaome extent, disregarded. He was satisfied from histfre- quent visits, that nothing like a systematic daily removal of filth is carried out by the butchers of the town. Dr. Gornall declares that the only effectual way of carrying out the proper slaughtering of animals is by the establishment of a public abattoir, and in future improvements he hopes this will not be lost sight of. The Nuisance Inspector (Mr; R. Norman) in his report,which is attached, also com- ments upon the great difficulty of inspecting the slaughter-houses,and declares that the only way of " simplifying the labour of inspection, end having all carcases of animals slaughtered and intended for human food inspected before being offered for sale, would be accomplished by the erection of a public slaughter-house and abattoir ; and all the existing private slaughter-houses abolished, putting an end Ito the nuisances created by their existence."

MIL EDWIN WOupS' NEW CYCLE SADDLE. It is ksomewhat strahgeahing. that, comparatively speaking', the makers of. tigiycle saddles have.stuck with remarkable, tenacity to the'iindepring and leather saddles without appearing-to consider that it was worth while to attempt any materia4tiange. Improvements are con- tinually being introduked, but up to near, Mr. Edwin Woods' galvanised cifileil-Nvoven saddle is the first corn- Plete metamerphsis f a.ny note. To commence with, ( the saddle itself retains the orthodox shape, but without any vertical or horizontal • spring frame—indeed the centre of the saddle is merely strengthened by a coiled Wire, running from the peak to the back of the saddle. The next feature lathe most noticeable and the one in 'which the genius of the inventor has been allowed to expend itself . with- remarkable success. Instead of leather, the frarlie of, the saddle is covered with finely woven wire, liriked in such a fashion that the most direct pressure rneicly elongtaes the strands from eni to end, and which on being released spring back to their old position in a trice. Together there are 80 wires in the conetructibh of the saddle, each of which is strong ' enOugh to suspetiktwo full-grown men without the pdesibility of breaking. The net-work is very fine and cicfaCnnd capable of'almost unlimited extension. . 10e writer of this article lately made a call on the in- ventor, Mr: Woods, at.the Longford Wire Works, War- rington, for the Purpose of putting to a practical test ;this-new 'saddle, and found the gentleman quite willing to grant our reves% and explain the salient points of his invention. On seeking the naked article produced one was somewhat dublops as to the durability of one's trousers, bat the appearlince of a neat and perforated felt cover- ing, which addild much to the appearance of the saddle, dissipated all 'tlohbts,and the test began. Both level and hp-hill road 'Were tried, and it was found that the "new thing ", was. resilient for the former and firm for the -latter, while'there seemed to be an underlying subJety of motion vihich added rather than detracted from the driving power of the .legs. Satisfied en these points a more crucial test still was tried, namely, a headlong tilt at an uneven quarter-mile of cobble-stones, and it was agreeably surprising to find in Place of a seat-breaking sheck,a gentle switch-back motion which was conclusive evidence that nothing more than clearing a !five barred gate could produce the semblance of a shock when mounted on Woods' patent saddle. Perhaps the idea will have occurred to some that the excessive plia- bility of the texture would initiate vibration, but after a hour's ride on varied road we were unable to detect anything pertaining to that nerve destroying quality. Though the ride did not extend any great distance we were firmly convinced that for a long distance journey the adaptability, coolness, and strength of the saddle make it the cyclists desideratum, and in this opinion we are supported by Mr. Charles Lucas, (record holder),who has adopted the saddle for road work and says "I hardly need say more in its favour, as I consider a satisfactory saddle of such vital importance when riding long dis- tances, that no ricer onght to be content with anything less than the very best Saddle procurable." The fact that the wire is galvanised does away with all possibility of rust, while the particulars stated by Mr. Woods may be vouched for by the success of his wire-woven mat- tresses, from which the principle of the, saddle is derived. In conclusion it may, we think, be affirmed that the future of the cycle saddle is a' good deal dependent ',on the progress of Mr. Woods' inventibo.

Mr. It. B. Matthews presided, and there were also present:— Messrs. J. Corradine, T. Greenwell, B. Grimshaw, W. Jankson, F. Massey, and LL. Tunstall (clerk.)
