div.head: HOUSE COMMITTEE ON TENDERS.
div.p: THE HOUSE COMMITTEE ON TENDERS.

With reference to the minutes of the above committee Mr. A. J. Jolley moved that the name of Messrs. Fletcher and Lee be substituted for that of Messrs. E. T. Evans, and that the name of Messrs. Furness be substituted for that of Messrs. Percival, because those firms had sent in lower tenders than these which were recommended by the House Committee for acceptance. The action of that Board he thought should be guided by economical prin- ciples and net by personal feelings or party principles. He was not prepared to say what motives guided the House Committee in their decision, but he asserted that they had recommended to the Board for acceptance the higher in preference to the lower tenders. The difference in the drapery tenders was £5 all but Id. It did not matter to him what the difference was, but with regard to the grocery tender it was unnecessary for him to go into details,but he pointed out that the tender of Messrs. Furness was in seven items out of 44 slightly higher than that of Messrs. Percival, but in 37 items out of 44 their tender was materially less. He therefore,submitted his amendment.—Mr. BENT said that he was sorry to see that there were only two tenders for the groceries contract, and he thought they should get some from retail grocers. Both Messrs. Fur- ness and Percival were „wholesale grocers. He thought something must have been done wrong in the past that they did not solicit fr3m the retail houses in the town, which could supply them better. That was one reason why he supported Mr.Jolley's amendment. With respect to an assertion that the amount for the six months would lee £so,he said it would be considerably over:ll3e difference between the two groceries tenders was £37 odd. The CHAIRMAN stated that,Messrs. Furness's tender was Z'275 15s. sp., while that of Messrs. Percival was £313 7s. Bd., and thus difference was £37 12s. 111—Mr. S. DAVIES thought the House C3in.nittee would bear him out when he said that it was cot a question of the differ- ence of the money total of each tender.—The CLERK understood that instead of thi, persons who sent a tender coming there to see and be guided by the samples which were kept in accordance wit'i tie advertisement, they sent a letter to say that they would supply any quality of goods and tendered their own specimens. He strongly recommended that in such a case the terms of the adver- tisement be adhered to. (1,1( ar, hear.) Several respect- able tradesmen in Warrington used to tender but by that they had been knocked out and had ceased to send in tenders. He suggested that the best help that Mr. Bent could give would be to se they advertised again that the goods were of pr9per quality.— The Rev. J. H. RIDETTE want( to support Mr. Jolley, but he was in favour of the drapery tender being referred back to the Howie Committee.—Mr. Bora said he felt sure that Mr. Furhess would supply the `goods they had now in the House.—The Rev. G. F. Rois Ears would like to know in which respect the grecery tender did not comply with the advertisement.—The Assistant CLERK said that thst advertisement stated that the goods must be of the quality they had .at, the workhouse,and instead of that Messrs. Fitness had not seen their samples but sent, *lnc fl[,, of their own.— On the amendment beiiat rut to the meeting 10 voted fur Messrs. Fletcher and 1..- •, for Messrs. E. T. Evans 8. Messrs. Fletcher and, Lee were therLore awarded the drapery contract for the coming half-year. For Messrs. Furness having the contract there voted 12, and for Messrs. N. B. Percival 8, which allotted the contract to the former firm. The folle-Ang rider was added to the latter contract': f' Conditionally upon Mr. Furness con- forming to dila terms of the contract." .4. VOTES OF THANKS. This being the last meeting before the election of Chairman and vice-Chairman, Mr. A. J. JOLLEY thought they should record their sense of the able manner in which Mr. Houghtbn had conducted their/business. He therefore moved " That the best thanks of this Board be given to Mr. Houghton and to Messrs. Davies and Pil- ling as vice-Chairmen."—The Rev. J. H. RIDDETTE se- conded, and Mr. Diosula and Mrs. CLAY supported, and the resolution ;was carried. _ _

The Cusiam•N in responding said he never felt he was • fit successor to his eminent predecessors but he had always donetis best for the administration of the Board so far as lie was concerned.—Mr. S. Deviss and Mr. G. Pilling (the vice-Chairman) also responded' in suitable terms. Mr. HoccurraN thought the Ladies Visiting Committee had made a very good start and had proved themselves to be active and determined to give what assistance they could to the , Board. It had been mentioned in that room that they had not beard much from the Ladies' Committee until just recently, but he admired them for the action they had taken in that respect, not to rush anything until they understood the working of the Union' He had great pleasure in proposing a vote of thanks to that Committee.—Mr. CLeux• seconded and the vote was passed unanimously. This was all the business.

div.head: WARRINGTON A.IIXILIARY OF THE BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON A.IIXILIARY OF THE BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY.
ANNUAL MEETING.

On Monday evening there was a good attendance at the Sankey-street Co-operative Hall, Warrington, when the annual meeting of the above society was held. His Worship the Maya (Councillor James Fairclough) occu- pied the chair,and there were also on the platform the Revs. J. Denton Thompson, M.A., and J. E. Symons, of Southport, comprising the deputation, and the Heys. E. C. E. Carleton, J. Davies, P, J. Byrne, J. Kirtlan, and John Yonge. Some excellent music was supplied by the choir and band of St. Anne's Church,under the conduc- torship of Mr. Percy Randall, the evening's programme being commenced with a hymn in which the audience joined with great spirit, and after which the Rev. J. Kirtlan offered up prayer. A letter of apology was received from the Rev. E. T. Reed, and also one from the Rev. B. Percival. A summary of the society's accounts showed that the receipts were £216 15s. 31, less £122 13s. 7d. (the balance at the end of the year), and the expenditure £216 15s. 3d. less £9O 19s. 2d. £55 118. 9d. was paid for thebibles, and a gift to the Parent Society of £3O made a total of £B9 Ils. 91. reducing the balance from £9O 19s. 21 to £4 7s. 51. The accounts up to March 1895 were certified to be correct by Mr. J. L. Punstall, auditor if the auxiliary. The Rev. J. DENTON TILOMPSON said he congratu- lated the people of Warrington in having such kind and able friends to entertain the meeting There were one or two facts upon which he wanted to speak, and he reminded them that this society WaS com- posed of those who believed in the Bible; and secondly, that the object of the society was to circulate the Bible at home as well as abroad.; thirdly, that the revelation contained in the Bible had for its end the redemption of man. The Bible they believed to be the record of a divine revelation which had for its end human redemp- tion. The Bible Society therefore was the society which had brought them together representing various sec- tions of the Christian Church. Unfortunately, there was much diversity if opinion upon some points, but it was no small matter of congratulation to find there was a unity upon the basis of the Bible. (Applause.) It was in the proportion they believed in the Bible that they would circulate it for others to believe in it. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. J. E. SYMONS thought their thanks were heartily due to the last speaker for the way he had advocated the cause of the Bible that night. Their thanks were still more due to those who helped to combine with the power of speech the beauty of music. Their thanks should also be given to Mr. Percy Silcack for securing the services of the band and Mr. Thorepson,and he was rather anxious to emphasise that, as he had an idea that Mr. Silcock's resignation might not be long deferred, the committee should stub- bornly refuse to accept that resignation when it was sent in. The speaker in giving a record of the work cf the society in many lands, said there was no church in the world to-day that was giving greater facilities to their cause than the Church in Russia. In that country they had the enormous circulation of over half-a-million copies of the Word of God. 1., India the bible women were teaching the Bible to 25,000 women every week. On concluding his address to which the audience had listened with great attention, the speaker sald4e honed they would all do what they could to help thociety. fivancially to forward :the Word of God all over the world. I N The figures we give at the commencement were then read by the treasurer Mr. W. Owen, after which, Mr. R. G. RENSHILL moved that the report be adopted. Mr. J. S. GARLAND, in seconding, was pleased to see the chief magistrate presiding over the meeting, and he congratulated him on being chairman ef the largest Bible Society meeting the speaker had seen in the 20 years he had been Warrington. The motion was then carried.

div.head: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.
div.p: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

The Rev. J. DAVIES (St. Anne's Church) proposed that the following be re-elected as officers for the ensu- ing year :—President, Mr. J. C. Parr; vice-president, Mr. John Crosfield ; treasurer, Mr. William Owen ; sec- retaries, the Revs. E. 0. E. Carleton, John Yonge, and Mr. Percy Silcock ; the committee, Messrs. E. J. Guest, John Guest, R. Garnett, R. A. Naylor. John Fairclough, J. R. Buckton, John Hall, J. 8. Garland, Mesdames R. Garnett, Z. Armitage,John Fairclough, E. 'f. Reed,G4ir- nall, Balmford, and the Misses Dutton, Smith, Garner, Harding,and Nellie Bennett. . . . . .

The Rev. P. J. BYRNE seconded the proposition, which on being put to the meeting was carried. The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON asked the audience to award their thanks to the deputation, the choir of St. Anne's Church, and the Rev. J. Davies who, he thought, must have had some influence in obtaining their services,

and also to Mr. Silcock, and to the Mayor for presiding. He thought that the best meeting helremembered in con- nection with the society. With reg 4rd to the committee, from time to time they had been very downhearted,and he could understand Mr. Silcock's desire to resign, and the committee themselves sometimes thought they would resign in a body or discontinue their annual gatherings. After that night he thought they would be encouraged, as the right thing had been hit upon at last. Mr. JOHN FAIRCLOTIGH begged to second the vote of thanks, and felt sure the deputation and choir had con- tributed to the success of the meeting as much as any- thing had done. 'fh3 Rev. JOHN YONGE said that he had been rather alarmed at what had been a revelation to him and that was that a kind of intimation appeared to have been given by Mr. Silcock of his intention to give up his work. Mr. Yonge hoped they would let Mr. Silcock understand that they could not permit that to take place. Mr. Silcock had never served the Auxiliary so well as on the present occasion and he agreed with Mr. Garland that it ' was one of the best meetings held in Warrington. They had every reason to be greatly encouraged to believe that there was work to be done even in apathetic War- rington on behalf of the S)ciety, and he hoped that Mr. Silcock would not let them hear any more about resign- ation as they would have great difficulty in finding a better secretary. The rev, gentleman cordially sup- ported the resolution, which on being put to the meeting was carried with acclamation.

Mr. PERCY SILCOCI said he was much obliged to Mr. Carleton and Mr. Yonge for their expressions. He had been a little disheartened, but after the meeting that night he decided to try it another year. (Applause.) The MAYOR briefly responded to the vote of thanks in which he was included and the meeting terminated.

div.head: HECKLING THE CHLIRII&N.
div.p: HECKLING THE CHLIRII&N.

The Chairman said the first business,as they would see from the notice, was to execute the agreement with the Corporation of Warrington with regard to the inclusion ot Little Sankey in the municipal borough of Warrington.—Mr. Massey said that before they went into that business be should like to ask ,the Chair- man four questions which he had got written down. They referred to the extension of the borough.—The Chairman said he should be glad to answer any ques- tions afterwards, but all the matters with regard to the extension of the borough were now settled.—Mr. Massey said he should like , the question answered before they went any further.—The Chairman: You can ask them if you like; what are they about P—Mr. Massey said they had partly reference to what had been said about the Chairman at the last meeting of the Town Council. Ile Would read the first question :—" Did you, previous to the election of candidates for the Parish Council of Little Sankey have a private interview with the Town Clerk, Mr. Whittle with regard to ' the borough extension and upon what terms.— The Chairman: I cannot answer any question of that sort, as everything is settled.—Mr. Massey: It will very likely come up again for further hearing.—Mr. Corradine : It should have come up at our last meet- ing.—Mr. Massey : I was unakle to attend that parish meeting ; I was ill in bed.—Mr. Corradine : Then it comes to this, that you must for ever hold your peace.— The Chairman: I cannot go into these matters now, it is too late. Ido riot knew what the questions may be, but I iskiilk they had bgter not be brought forward. I shall be grad to answer them privately so that you may let your friends know, but the questions have nothing to do with the business of the Council.—Mr.Massey : Very good then, I will show yc..o them after the Council.. THE AGREEMENT WITH THE CORPORATION. . _

The di—air-1;n then read the mreement with the Cor- poration with regard to the inclusion of the parish in the borough. He said it had not been altered in any shape or way from what he read at the parish meeting.—Tbe agreement was signed by the Chairman,Mr.Jackson,and Mr. Corradine.

div.head: TER CLERK'S SALARY.
div.p: TER CLERK'S SALARY.

The Chairman .aid tiTc-i-n-e-ii" business was to determine the remuneration of the assistant overseer aad clerk to the Council. Be referred to the services Mr. Tunstall had renderepe,thiCqbacil, and said that Mr. Tunstall in his opiniqn had beefiCittremely generous in what he had sugge(tAl. •He, ',II said that he would not r charge anything at ell for what he . had done up •to -the pres t. time, so they could 'not grumble for, work being done for nothing. Mr. Tunstall had-behavedin a very generous manner to the Council and the inhabitants generally. He might men- tion that the township of Warrington, which included Little Sankey, had a rateable value of Z 170,56755. The Proportion of Little Sankey was 2,8,317. The assistant overseer's salary for the total area, including clerks and various expenses, was £3OO, -so that the proportion for Little Sankey was £l4 12g. 7d. in a rateable value of £8,317, £l4 12s. 7d. was Mr. Tunstall's salary for Little Sankey at that moment. They had *power to increase that amount so as,.to remunerate him for his services as clerk to the Council. They had therefore to Consider to what aniount they should increaseJn. . As they would . probably go into the borough shor4o, they would only .he voting the increase for twelve months. Mr. Tunstall had suggested that the £l4 should be increased to £2O, which would represent £7 7s. sd. for his ser- vices to the Ceuncil for,, the ensuing year, and he re- ceived nothing for what he had dqne up to now. He thought the proposed increase was a very moderate one. He had pleasure in moving that the salary of the assis- tant overseer be £2O per annum inclusive of his remu- neration as Llerk of the Council.—Mr. Grimshaw se- conded, and Mr. Jackson supported the motion, which was unanimously passed.

div.head: COLLECTION OF SPECIAL BATES.
div.p: THE COLLECTION OF SPECIAL BATES.

The Chairman moved "that the remuneration of the collector of poor rates for the collection of rates other than poor rates be for the put • year as determined by the overseers, namely, the sum of £lO in respect of the collection of each separate rate upon the rural area of the township of Warrington, subject to apportionment in accordance with the Local Government Act, 1894 and that his future remuneration for the collection of the said rates made upon the township of Little Sankey be £7 10s, in respect of the collection of each separate rate." —Mr, Corradine secondedsand the resolution was passed Mr. Tunstall explaining that the overerseers fixed the amount, but it was necqesary for the council to sanction it. , FUNERALS AT RRINGTON CEMETERY. The Chairman said • adbeen reported to him ths.t hii II the case oi funerals a. , Warrington Cemetery fom Little Sankey twice . was charged in one case as was charge in ano i, he took the particulars and wvtii to tt Town i the subject. In reply, Mr. ial Mittle w te : "In z.to your letter the fees for 1 funerals in the Warrinjto Cemetery vary frem £l.lB. to 53., exclusive of th purchase of the grave and the fees for interments of prsons dying (non-residents) be- yond the municipal boreugh payable to the Council are double. When the new registrar was appointed some months ago, be was given instructions to charge double fees for interments of non-residents." So that be the (Chairman) sent the following :—" In view of Little Sankey being probably soon absorbed into the borough, I consider the raising the cemetery charges for a few months to he irritating and unnecessary. I would venture to recommend a return to the old scale and the refunding of the extra charges which may have occurred during the few months you refer to." The Town Clerk replied as follows :—" I hope I have not misled you in my letter of yesterday's date. The instruction to the Registrar was nothing new. Double fees for the inter- ment ot non-residents were fixed by the regulations in 1880, and it was only by inquiry on the death of the late Registrar that we found in one or two instances he had neglected to charge the full fees. Moreover, the regulations do not apply to Little Sankey alone but to every township beyond the borough." The Chairman added that he had since ascertained that people who had given their address as Liverpool-road had sometinaes escaped the double fees,. the Registrar apparently having taken it for granted that Liverpool- road must be in the borough.—Mr. Corradine said he had been spoken to on the same subject. People had sug- gested that the increase was owing to the Parish Coun- cil. (Laughter.)—The subject then dropped.

div.head: TIM PROPOSED CHILDREN'S PLAYGROUND.
div.p: TIM PROPOSED CHILDREN'S PLAYGROUND.

The Chairman said he had had some correspondence with Lord Lilferd with regard to the provision of a play ground for the children of Little Sankey. He thought something might come out of it, but his Lord- ship was allowing the matter to lie over until the ques- tion af going into the borough was settled, but to show them that he was in sympathy with the proposal he would read the correspondence. The Chairman then read the letter. . In his first letter to Mr. Matthews, Lord Lilford said he was favourably disposed to granting a piece of land for a playground, but he must first consult his agent. In a second letter his lordship said he had been advised to postpone the matter for a time.—The members of the Council ex- pressed their, regret that Lord Lilford had not seen his way to accede to their request, but a hope was ex- pressed that he might still see his way to have a play- ground for the district. The Chairman was Compli- mented upon the way in whict he had taken theimatter up.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT,
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT,
MONDAY.-DIVISION UN WELSH DISESTABLISH- MENT.

In the House of Commons on Monday, a very large number of petitions against the Welsh• Disestablishment Bill were presented ; and it appeared from answers to questions at a later part of the sitting, that the number of petitions presented against the bill up to date was 1,024, containing 204,516 signatures, and that no peti- tions had been presented in favour of the bill, ndt even from Wales. It also appeared that some at least of the signatures to the opposing petitions were these of in- mates of St. Asaph Union .Workhouse.
The Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Bill was read a third time. .

Sir E. GREY. in reply to Colonel Wartime, who put a question on behalf of Mr. CuazoN, said he was glad to say that an agreement between the British and Russian Governments with reference to the Pamirs had now been concluded, and would be laid on the table of the House very soon. In answer to Mr. LABOIICHERE, Sir E. GREY said no papers could be laid up..m the table at present in regard to the discussions with the French Genrnment on the question whether the valley of the Nile between the lakes and the southern frontier of Egypt was within the sphere of British influence. He added that her Majesty's Government could not recognise the Govern- ment of the Mandi or of his successor as in any way ousting or disparaging the rights of Egypt in those territories. The HOME SECRETARY informed Mr. FIELD that on medical grounds he had ordered the release of an Irish political prisoner named O'Callaghan, who had been over twelve years in Portland Prison ; also that he was in communication with the SECRETARY for Scotland respecting the case of Cann, an Irish political prisoner, confined in Portland on sentence of the High Court of Justiciary in 1883. Mr. FIELD pointed out that Cann was an infirm old man, beyond seventy years of age. The debate on the second reading of the Established Church (Wales) Bill was resumed by Sir Joan GORST, who completed the speech against the bill interrupted by the adjournment on March 26. The debate was con- tinued Isy Mr. BRYCE, Mr. GOSCHEN, Mr. AUGUSTINE BIRRELL, Mr. S. SMITH, Sir JOHN MOWERAY, Mr. BRYN- molt JONES, Mr. Bucittant, and Mr. E. J. C. MoaroN,and Mr. BALFoon. Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT having replied, the House divided, and the second reading was carried by 304 votes to 260—majority for the Government, 44.

div.head: TUESDAY. THE IRISH LAND BILL.
div.p: TUESDAY. THE IRISH LAND BILL.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday, on the motion for the consideration of the Great Eastern Railway Bill, Mr. MACDONALD moved the rejection of the bill, on the ground that the Chairman of the Company (Lord C. HAMILTON) at the annual meeting of the shareholders used language which gave eVidence of hostile feeling to- wards the action of the Board of Trade in enforcing the Railway Servants (Hours of Labour) Act. After some discussion, Mr. BRYCH said ha was not surprised thatl Lord C. Hamrizon's remarks had attracted attention.' Such language did net make it easier for those who hat cast upon Om by Parliament the functiod of endetai, veuring to apply the Act, Which was in the interests ndt only of the railway servants but also of the entire travelling public. So far as the present bill was con- cerned, it gave further facilities to the travelling public, and particularly to the working classes, and therefore he hoped the amendment would not be pressed. Mr. MACDONALD withdrew the amendment, and the bill was ordered for third reading. In answer to Mr. DODD, Mr. SIIAW-LEFETHE said he was aware there was not at present a simple or cheap procedure for the trial of disputed elections of parish uncillors. If hldol i nformatien as to whether there had been cases where clear ground existed for upsetting elections, but where no action could be taken because of the expense of the procedure. Mr. Angara, replying to Sir F. Powera., said that in the case of Ireland the question of the, celebration of marriages was dealt with by a measure passed subse- quently to the Irish Church Act, but he would consider whether it was possible and expedient to make any pro- vision with regard to it in the Established Church (Wales) Bill. Sir W. HARCOURT, in reply to Sir M. HICKS-BEACH, stated that the Budget would be intro- duced in the week when the Home met after Easter.

Mr. J. MORLEY, in moving the second reading of the Irish Land Bill, said he was a little disappointed that none of the difficulties of the bill had been cleared up by criticism since the bill was printed. There were signs that the English and Scotch Conservatives, including the leader of the Opposition, were shaking off the thral- dom of their Irish friends. There were some questions which it would be a mockery for a Minister standing there to ask members on the opposite side to approach with a mind free from prepossession, but this ought not to be one of them. Speaking broadly, the intentions of the bill were to restore the great objects of the legislation of 1881, which had been baffled by the course taken in the courts. What the bill directed the valuers to do was to fix a fair rent, and not make the tenant pay on his own improvements. The bill, in effect, provided that in the absence of special circumstances the whole of the increased value due to improvements should go to the tenant who had made them. Mr. CARSON said that though the Unionist party might not divide against the second reading, they intended to fight the proposals contained in the bill line by line and word byword. The debate was adjourned .until Thursday.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

In the House of Commons, on Wednesday, Mr. WILLIAM ALLAN moved the second reading of the Steam Engines (Persons in Charge) Hill, which he explained was now confined to land engines, mines, mills, and factories. Mr. SETON-KAER supported the Bill, and Mr. FORWOOD said he had Come prepared to oppose it, but finding that its operation was to be confined to mines and factories, his feeling had materially changed. Mr. Sawa said the balance of argument was in favour of second reading, and the bill was read a second time and referred to a Select Committee. Mr. HAIM FISHER moved the second reading of the Church Patronage Bill, explaining that the first part was designed to prevent unfit persons being instituted, and the second would facilitate the removal be the bishops of clergymen who had proved themselves unfit for r incap- able to fulfil their high and responsible calling. Colonel SANDYS moved that the bill be read a second time that day six months, but the second reading was carried by a majority of 61. The Merchandise Marks and Court of Criminal Appeal
Bills were read a second time and referred to a Select Committee. On the motion of Mr. STRACHEY, a bill was introduced to amend the Post Office Act, 1891.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY; APRIL 6, 1895.

THE report of the Royal Commis- The Aged Poor. sion on the Aged Poor which has been issued this week can hardly be described as a satisfactory document. It is in fact, not so much a report, but as a series of reports. The o.3minis3ion, which was appointed so far back as January, 1893,appears to have been too numerous, and to have been com- posed of too many discordant elements, with the result that there is nething like unanimity in the conclusion which the Commiseioners have come to. There is, of course, the majority report which will naturally carry most weight, but then on the other hand there are two or three minority reports, and numerous memoranda by different members. When the Commission was originally appointed the PRINCE of WAreis was made a mem- ber of it, but His Royal Highness de- clines to either approve or disapprove of any of its conclusions. His reason for taking this course is, on the whole, a judicious one. " I feel,'l he says, " that as the subject has now to a considerable extent become one of party contro- versy, both inside and outside of Parliament, it has assumed a phase, inconsistent with my posi- tion of political neutrality." The signatories of the main document or majority report are Lords LINGEN, BRASSEY, and PLA MIR, and Messrs. HENLEY,. PELL, HUMPHREY-OWEN, ROUNDE LL, Loon, Amu, and STOCKALL, and their recommen- dations are certainly not of a revolutionary character. They are of opinion " that no funda- mental alterations are needed in the existing system of poor-law relief as it affects the aged, and that it would be undesirable to interfere either by statute or order with the discretion now vested in the guardians as to the manner in which: each relief should be given." At the same time, they urge that when relief is ad- ministered there should be greater discrimina- tion between the respectable aged who become destitute and those whose destitution is distinctly the consequence of their own misconduct. Another suggestion which they make is worth noting and emphasizing. It is that when outdoor relief is given it should be sufficient to meet the extent of the destitution. That, it need hardly be said, is not always the case at the present time, as the amount allowed is often utterly inadequate to properly sustain the person who is "relieved.' On one point the conclusion of the Commission is of some interest. They have, it appears, taken evidence upon the much-debated question as to how far the destitution of the poor is directly due to drunken habits,and they have decided that " as ' regards the great bulk of the working classes, during their working lives they are fairly provid- ent, fairly thrifty, fairly industrious, and fairly temperate." They add that " the statement that pauperism is largely due to think, idleness, impro- vidence, and the like causes has in truth mainly reference to that portion of the aged poor who are in workhouses, and who are there for other reasons than sickness or general infirmity. When it is seen that according to the yearly count under nine per cent. of the aged over sixty- five are in poor-law establishments, and ac;:ording to the one-day count under five per cent., and that this number includes, all sick and inerm persons who cannot be relieved at their own homes, it is apparent that the imputation applies to but a very small proportion of the werking class population." It appears, therefore, that the opinion of the Royal Commission et all events, drink is not the main cause of the "poverty of the poor." The minority reperts have more colour and substance about them tiAu the report of the majority. One of these reports is signed by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, Mr. knemE,Sir H. MAXWELL, Dr. HUNTER and Mr. BOOTH, and the other is the production of Mr. BROADHURST alone. The minority of which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is the leading member, suggests that the schemes for old-age pensions should be at once thoroughly examined in a "judicial spirit" by a body of es-

perts and not of politicians who are already biassed one way or the other. Mr. BROADIVIRST 18 entirely oppo...ed to say further delay,as he is of opinion that" the time has now come for great and fundamental changes in the provisions for the aged poor." He holds that the only adequate way on fi scle e thealin dealing maintenance etnhaen e e e of situationt i s f he a g readn kalys tao rye co e blt charge, to be borne by the whole community. As a whole,however,it is to be feared that the labours of the Commission will carry little weight. The question of old age pensions practically remains where it was before the Cammission reported.

The Warrirgton Township Meeting held the other day was not carried:on with much depressinglformal- ity. Beyond the overseers and officers the only others Present were members of the press, two of whom happened to be ratepayers, and therefore acting in a double capacity. This has been the case for some years now, and the way the business is disposed of is as follows —Pressman No. 1 moves a proposi- tion, No. 2 seconds it, and then they pass it nem. Can. Pressman No. 2 proposes the nest resolution and No.l seconds it and it is duly adopted. It Should be added in all fairness that the business is transacted with unusual promptitude and despatch. What 'would occur at these township meetings if Pressman No. 1 and Pressman No. 2 did not happen to agree it is hard to say. Would the township meeting have to adjourn sine die? Fortunately, there is no reason to anticipate any catastrophe of this kind. Pressmen are a peaceful folk and very harmonious—in spite of appearances.

would be difficult indeed to find a more accept- ed)le chairman than "Joe '' Davies as he was famil- lY called.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

*** NOTICE.—GOOD FRIDAY.—Owing to next Friday being Good 'Friday the " Examiner " will be published on Thursday next. ST. PAUL'S BIBLE CLASS, RUNCORN. At this class on Sunday afternoon, the Bible lesson was given by Mr. B. Kniveton. an interesting address on• "Salvation" was delivered by Mr. Israel Hayes. Mr. B. Crosby contributed a solo, and one entitled " Nazareth " was also sung by Mr. Charles Atherton. The organist, Mr. William Cooke, performed an organ SOIO. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH CHOIR. .

On Wednesday evening a sacred cantata entitled "Song of the Passion" by Dr. W. S. Vinning, was ren- dered by the Parish church choir. There was not a very large attendance. The Vicar delivered a short address. The choir gave a most creditable rendition of the cantata. Mr. James Littler was the conductor, and Mr. Johnson presided at the organ. HOLY TRINITY CRICKET CLUB, RUNCORN. A miscellaneous concert in aid of the above cricket club was held on Monday evening, in Trinity Boys' Schoolroom. Mr. C. A. Timmins occupied the chair, and there was a fair attendance. The programme opened with a pianoforte duet by the Misses Horseiall and Pope. The other instrumental music given, in- cluded, mandoline solo, Mr. Joseph Rawlinson ; violin solo, Mr. A. Hague (Widnes), and clarionet solo, Mr. A. Humphreys. The vocalists were :—Miss Florrie Brad- shaw, Miss Mabel Pope, Miss Johnson, Mrs. Temperlev, Messrs. W. Hague and R. Hague (Widnes), C. Atherton, F. Crowther and Stubbs. Miss and Master Leathwood contributed a duet. The accompanist was Mr. Arthur Savage. DEATH OF MRS. HORSEFIELD.

Mrs. Mary Horsefield, of Canal-street, Runcorn, died on Friday at the advanced age of 88 years. The deceased , lady caine to Runcorn in 1812. She was a member of IHoly Trinity Church, where she had been a regular attendant for rearly half a century, and had identified I herself with every good work in the parish. Her lemains were interred in Runcorn Cemetery on Tuesday. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. Dr. Preston. The mourners were Messrs. Jonathan, George, and Joseph Horsefield (sons), and G. Dunbabin (son-in-law), and Messrs. S. Taylor, T. Taylor, C. Taylor, J. W. Ford, A. R ley, G. Rayner, J. Dunbabin, J. Horsefield, jun., Mrs. Joseph Horsefield, Mrs. G. Horsefieli, Mrs. Jonathan Horsefield, Mrs. G. Dunbabin, Mrs. A. Riley, Misses M. Horsefield, Dunbabin, A. Dunbabin, Mary Jane Horse- field, Loretta Horsefield, and E. H. Horsefield. Rtmonw COUNTY COURT.

Co Tuesday, a sitting of this court was held, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes. The cases for hear- ing were 3 default, 39 original, and 15 judgment sum- monses. One case included a claim for 93. wages due to Alice Elizabeth Hughes, Quarry Bank-terrace,Weston, by George Marshall, Higher Runcorn. The plaintiff btated that she was engaged as domestic servant to the defendant, at 3s. per week. One of the conditions was that she was to be allowed out every alternate Sunday. She was refused permission to go as usual, and her mother asked for an explanation, when she was in- formed that her daughter had been out one night and could not therefore go then. Her mother told her to pack up and go home. Defendant and his wife stated that the girl absented herself without permission, en a date when they lud a clerical visitor. That was the reason why she was kept in on the Sunday afternoon. Plaintiff left of her own accord and had forfeited her right to wages. His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff for the six shillings wages due. THE BISHOP OF CHESTER AT RUNCORN.

There were large congregations in Runcorn Parish Church on Sunday to hear the Bishop of CheSter. At , the morning service he based his discourse on Ist Peter, 12nd c., v. 16. "As free, and not using your liberty for cloke of maliciousness, but as servants of God." In the afternoon, the Bishop conducted the annual confir- mation service. The number of candidates was 173; there being 88 females and 85 males from churches in Runcorn, Halton, Weston and Weston Point. The Bishop delivered the usual address to the candidates. At the evening service he preached from the words con- tained in Matthew xi, 28, 29, and 30 verses. An anthem entitled "Incline thine ear" was sung by the choir, the solo part being taken by Mr. H. Branch. The organist was Mr. Johnson. RUNCORN BOATING CLUB.

Mr. F. Abel presided at the first annual meeting of the bove-mentioned club on Friday evening, and in the course of a short address on boating, explained all the points of rowing. Twelve new members were then balloted for and elected. Sir. R. M Brook, Bart., was re-elected president, and Messrs. J. T. Brunner, M.P., P. Speakman, J.P., J. Brundrit, J.P., E. Imison' J.P., J. F. Hazlehurst, F. J. Norman, J.P., J. W. Lightburn, and J. Atherton, Dr. Steele, and the Rev. Canon Wood were re-elected vice-presidetts. The committee were empowered to add to the list. The election of officers resulted as follows :—Secretary and treasurer, Mr. W. A. Millinger ; captain, Mr. F. Abel (proton.) ; sub-captain, Mr. B. West (pro tern.); committee, Messrs. E. Speak- man, J. A. Smith, jun., E. H. Kniveton, G. Fl. Sherratt and E. Rowlands. A vote of thanks to the Secretary, committee, and Chairman was passed. ANOTHER DROWNING CASE.

At Weston Point on Friday afternoon, Mr. J. E. Wars- ley, corouor, investigated the circumstances connected with the death of John Williams, boatman, aged 45 years, belonging to NorthWicli, whose body was taken out of the Ship Canal at Weston on the previous day, after being missed since December 29th last.—John Wil- kinson, labourer, Weston, identified the body, and said he last saw Williams alive on December 29th, between six and seven o'clock in the evening, at the Weaver Hotel. Ile was sober. His flat was lying in the Ship Canal, close to where he was found.—Peter Coyle, land- lord of the Weaver Hotel, said he had known deceased about twelve months. He had done odd jobs for him. He was first noticed in the house between eight and nine o'clock on the night in question.—Thomas Lydiate, 14, St. John-st., Runcorn, waterman, engaged oh the dred- ger Irk, which picked up the body from the Ship Canal on the previous morning, said it was brought up by one of the buckets and deposited in the well. A rope was fastened tolthe body,and the police were informed of the event.—P.C. Ilammersley spoke to having the body con- veyed to the Weaver Hotel. The state of the clothing was, in his opinion, caused by the dredger. There were no marks of violence. In his pocket was found Id. in money. A verdict of " Found drowned " was returned.

div.head: SPECIAL MEETING OF RUNCORN URBAN COUNCIL.
div.p: SPECIAL MEETING OF RUNCORN URBAN COUNCIL.

Toe Runcorn Urban District Council held a special meeting on wriday evening in the Town Hall. Mr. Imison presided, and there were also present Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C. ; S. Taylor, AP., C.C. ; F. Wis., wall, H. J. Grice, J. Wilson, J. W. Lightburn, .T. Kirk- ham, M. Sweetman, T. Dean, M. Barker (surveyor), E. Marshall (secretary). and F. A. Lake (sataary clerk). The Chairman intimated that the business was to draw on the treasurer for accounts to close the financial year. Mr. Lightburn proposed that the cheques be drawn on the treasurer for the following aggregate demands : General fund, £992 14s. ld. ; district fund, £2 55.; water fund, £1,772 3s. 2d. ; technical institute building fund, £152 Os. 5d.; private street works fund, £155 6d. 4d. ; library fund, £37 4s 93. Total £2,994 83. 7d. —Mr. Speakman seconded,and it was agreed to. Mr. Lightburn also moved that the expenses of the deputa- tion to Manche3ter to interview the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Company re the proposed alteration of agreement of September 15t,1890, amounting to £3 151. 93., be paid.—Mr. Speakman se- conded, and it was agreed to.—This was all the busi- ness.
NARROW ESCAPES FROM DROWNING.

Three youths named W. W. Wiswall, son of Mr. F. Wiswall, ef Higher Runcorn, and Percy and Sydney Buckley, of Wellinattn-st.,ltuncorn,had narrow escapes from drowning whilst rowing on the river Weaver en Saturday afternoon. A couple of extra oars were taken in the boat, and somehow or other one of them slipped into the water. In trying to recover it the boat was up- set, and the occupants were thrown into the water. Wiswall, being a good swimmer, soon got out of the water,but the other two had some difficulty in reaching the banks. They did, however, succeed,and proceeded to an adjoining farmhouse where every assistance was rendered.—Two other youths named Powell, of Duke's Field, and Watson-street, also had a narrow escape from drowning on Sunday afternoon. About 12.30 Mr. Rose, dock master, Runcorn, was proceeding along the line of locks in company with his wife,when he heard cries for help. He saw a lad (Powell) in the water and ran towards the lock, and by getting near to the water, was enabled to reach him with his umbrella. To his sunrise he found that another lad (Watson) was holding fast to Powell's legs. With difficulty he rescued both of them, and it is not too much to say that had it not been for Mr. Rose's promtitude both would have been drowned. They wer,, immediately taken home, and with the exception of a wetting were not much the wore° for the accident. NEW POOR RATH FOR RUNCORN._
Messrs. Thomas and James Handley affixed their signatures to a new poor rate for the township of Run- corn, of one shilling in the £. This is estimated to pro- duce £3,032. BILLIARD MATCH.

At Runcorn Liberal Club on Wednesday evening a match was played between representatives of Runcorn Liberal Club and Crewe Liberal Club. The match re- sulted is an easy victory for the home team by 507 points, they winning ten out of the twelve games. Tea was provided for the visitors at Mr. James Lea's, tem- perance hotel. The following are the individual scores :

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY,_ APRIL 6. 1.895.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY,_ APRIL 6. 1.895.
A MISSING RUNCORN SEAVAN.

Fears are entertained that Herbert George Hedgecock, 21 years of age, of 46, Irwell-lane Runcorn, has been drowned. He was engaged on the flat Tagus, which belongs to the Ship Canal Company. On Saturday the vessel was lying at Garston docks. He proceeded to the station for his food and seems to have returned with it to the vessel, for the food and his hat bays been found on board. Search was made for him but without suc- cess, and it is thought that ho has fallen ovorboard. BRUNSWICK-STREET MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.

At the meeting of this society on Wednesday evening, Mr. William Handley read a paper on "Norton Priory," a summary of which has already appeared in these columns. Mr. Simister occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance. A hearty vote of thanks was tendered Mr. Handley on the motion of Mr. Lawton, seconded by Mr. Jeffreys. Captain Le ConteUr also spoke. A pleasant and profitable time was spent. SAD SUICIDIZ OF SUPT. LAR‘E'S

A tragic suicide was investigated by the coroner at Middlewich on Wednesday, the deceased being Sarah Large, aged 37, wife of Police Superintendent Large. She had suffered from a severe attack of influenza, and became much depressed. On the 26th ult., she cut her throat with a small table knife. Two doctors attended her, and she was making a good recovery until Tuesday when she had a relapse,and died suddenly from syncope. The jury found that deceased had committed suicide while temporarily in3ane after influenza. The informa- tion was received with deep regret at Runcorn. Super- intendent Large was stationed in Runcorn for a number of years, awl had an extensivd circle of friends. MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF SHEEP.

George Farm, Aston, near Warrington, have during the present week lost about 50 sheep under singular circum- stances. It is feared that the death of the animals is the result of a most dangerous disease. The mat- ter has been reported to the authorities who are making a thorough investigation into all the cir- cumstances. Great reticence is manifested as to the nature of the disease until the subject has undergone thorough examination. THE COLLISION WITH A DREDGEI2.--JUD9MENT.

Mr. Justice Bruce delivered judgmentin the Admiralty Court on Friday in an actien brought by the Mersey D,lcks and Harbour Board to recover damages for the loss of their steam sand-pump dredger N 0.7, which was sunk as the result of a collision with the defendants' steamer Greta Holme, of Mary-port, in the Mersey, off New Brighton, on March 6th. The master and crew of the dredger were also suing for the loss of their clothes and effects. The defendants counter-claimed for damage sustained by the Greta Holme.—His bordship,after con- sulting with the Trinity Masters, said the Greta Flolme must be held alone to blame.—Judgment accordingly for the plaintiffs. In connection with this collision it may be stated that the flat Success, belonging to Messrs, Speak- man and Sons, Runcorn, was not far distant when the accident occurred. The noise was heard by Captain Williamson (who resides in Parsonage-road, Widnes), and he put off with the boat to rescue the men. He succeeded in getting seven of them away at onetime, leaving the remaining four wearing life-belts. Having safely landed his first complement of passengers he re- turned to the rapidly sinking dredger, and was success- ful in rescuing the other men who were on board. RUNCORN SHOOTING CLUB. .

On Saturday the first of a series of eight competitions arranged for the present year took place on the Heath. The competition consisted of seven rounds each at dis- tances of 200, 500, and 600 yards. The following were the results :- 200 500 600

The former medal, after being com- peted for during seven years, was finally won by Sergt. W. H. Harvey. U.M. FREE CHURCH MIITTIAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY,

"Impromptu Speaking" was the programme provided for the members of the above-mentioned Society on Friday evening. The leader was Mr. T. Parry, and the subjects introduced included "Socialism ot the Day," " Welsh Disestablishment," "Temperance," " Signs of the Times," and several other topics. The discussions were taken part in by the Rev. J. Stafford, Messrs. T. Parry, E. Jones, W. Fowlds, and others. A pleasant and profitable evening was spent. ST. MICHMIL'S CHURCH, RUNCORN.

On Thursday evening a large Congregation attended the lantern service given in the above-mentioned church. A collection ot suitable slides illustrating scenes in the Passion of Christ were shown by Mr. T. Bowyer, assisted by Mr. J. F. Moulton. The Rev. A. J Jameson, M.A., read the connective portion 9. It intervals the choir, under the conductorship of Mr. Pownall, sang selections from Dr. Stainer's work "The Crucifixion." The solo parts were taken by Mr. Blundell and Mr.Crood- wia. A collection was taken at the close to detray ex- penses. A RUNCORN MAN DROWNED AT EASTEIAM.

Jame; Gregory Marsh, 25 ye,irs of age, son of Mr. James Marsh, Mount Pleasant, Runcorn was drowned at Easthain on Thursday morning. The deceased was a blacksmith's striker and was engaged labouring for carpenters, who ale constructing certain works just out- side the Ship Canal at Eastham. He and a man named J. Bradley, of Runcorn, were sawing a piece of timber, when the deceased over-balanced himself and fell into the water, a depth of about fifteen feet. A boat was immediately put off by his fellow workmen to his rescue, and just as they were within reaching distance, he sank for the last time. Grappling operations were then com- menced. He leaves a wife and three youn. children. INTERESTING ARRIVAL AT THE RUNCORN DOCKS.

There was a rather int« resting arrival at Runcorn Docks on Tuesday, when a fine new steamer named Granuaile came into dock. She has been built to the specification of Mr. Henry West, naval architect and engineer, Liverpool, for the Conjested District Board of Ireland, to assist in developing the fishery industry on the west coast of the island. A good number of Runcorn people turned out to look at the vessel, and a few were privileged to inspect her. She is built of steel, is 150 feet in length, and 24 feet in breadth, and is registered, dead weight, 285 tons. While the vessel has been designed primarily to be useful, she has a small cabin amidships,neatly and comfortably fitted up with three small state rooms. She is lighted by electricity and was built at Troone, Ireland. The vessel is likely to prove useful for the purpose intended. he received a cargo of over 200 tons of fishery salt at Runcorn, and afterwards proceeded on her maiden voyage.

bridge' and his opinion was that the Runcorn entrance would be near to Waterloo Bridge--Mr. Williams spoke in favour of the road commencing from Percival-lane.— The Chairman moved an amendment that the words " from the end of Percival-lane "be omitted. On being put to the vote the amendment was carried.

div.head: LOCAL TOWNSHIP MEETIN(3}S.
div.p: LOCAL TOWNSHIP MEETIN(3}S.
WARRINGTON.

Oa Thursday morning last week the township meeting for Warrington was held in the Yarade Room, Irlam-street, under the presidency of Mr. John Harrison (senior overseer), and there were also pre.,ewt —Messrs. Thomas Birtles and Peter Leigh (overseer), J. L. Tunstall (assistant over- seer), J. Smith (from the assistant overseer's office), and H. Isherwood and James Lawton. The following are the most important of the accounts presented by Mr. Tunstall :—Poor rate account: receipts, balance in hand, £3,968 4a. 10J. ; rates, £18,768 18a. 3d. ; other receipts, £274 Be. 11d. ; total receipts, £23,011 123. Payments : Contributions to the union £7,339 ; contributions to the county rate, £3,128 ; to borough rate, £9,150 183. sd. ; to sanitary general expenses rate, £53 63. Bd. ; other payments, £671 is. 9J. ; leaving a balance in hand, £2,669 ss. 2d. The county rate and special rate accounts were also submitted.—Mr. Lawton moved " That the balance sheets of receipts and payments of the overseers for the half-years ended 25th March and 29th September, 1894, be and are hereby approved."—Mr. Isherwood, seconded and asked if the extension of the borough would make any difference in the colleetion of the special rates.—The Assistant Overseer replied that there would be fewer special rates to collect ; in fact, there would be none if Little Sankey and Latchford Without came into the borough, but it would mean an increase in the other work.—The accounts were then passed.—Mr. Birtles moved—" That the Vestry consents to the remuneration of the Collector in respect of rates other than poor rat's determined by the Overseers, namely, the sum of £lO in• respect of each separate rare collected."—This was seconded by Mr. Leigh, and carried.—A vote of thanks passed to the retiring overseers concluded the business.

div.head: RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL
div.p: RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL

A meeting of this Council was held on Thursday, at the Town Hall, Runcorn. Mr. E. Imison presided, and there were also present: Messrs. F. Wiswall, H.. J. Grine, G. H. Kirkham, S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., R. H. Posnntt, J. W. Lightburn, T. Dean, M. Sweetman, D. Bisbrown, W. Collier, G. Hewitt, J. Wilson, J. Pritchard, J. M. Williams, and Mr. Lake (law clerk), Mr. Marshall (secre- tary), and Mr. Barker (surveyor).

THE MEDICAL OFFICE'R'S REPORT. Dr. M-Dougall (medical officer) reported that the num- ber of deaths registered during the past month amounted Ito 34. Three were inquest cases and of the remaining 31, eight were due to bronchitis, four to convulsions,two to paralysis, two to senile decay, two to mesenteric dis- ease, two to phthisis, two to child birth, two to cancer, and one each to rheumatism, epilepsy, premature birth, kidney disease, diphtheria, pneumonia and ery.ipelas. The 34 deaths showed an average death rate of 21.0.4 of the estimated population for the twelve months, and exclusive of the iuquest cases of 19 05. Twelve were infants one year or under. Sixty births were registered during the month. The number of deaths registered during the corresponding mouth of last year amounted to 28.—Mr. Bisbrown said he was sure the report was very gratifying to the medical officer as well as to the public.

div.head: STANDING ORDERS.
div.p: STANDING ORDERS.

The Chairman moved that the standing orders be adopted. He said they were a re-production of the standing orders adopted by some of the most progressive councils in the country, and appeared to provide for anything that might arise. Due provision had been made for he admission: of the public, and their only regret was that they had net greater accommodation.— Mr. Taylor seconded the adoption ot the orders,and they were approved of.

div.head: LIGHSING OF GAS LAMPS.
div.p: THE LIGHSING OF GAS LAMPS.

The Highways and Buildings Coinmittee recommended , that the street lamps be lighted at the discretion of the manager of the Runcorn Gas Company when the moon is overcast, the lights to be put out at 11 o'clock on such nights. The charge to be at the rate of ss. per hour for all the lamps in addition to the amount already paid. The actual cost in accordance with the above-named rate only to be charged, the company undertaking that the amount shall not exceed £lO for the first year. This resolution to be is force only for one year from the Ist Apri 4:1895. —Ca cried .

NEW BUILDINGS. It was recommended by the Highways and Buildings Committee that the plan of the Runcorn Property and Investment Company for the erection of eleven houses in a new street off York-st., be approved, subject to the undertaking of the Company to substitute a 12 in. for a 9 in. sewer to Oakmere-st. being given under the seal of the company to the satisfaction of the Council. That the amended plan of Mr. Henry Dodd of two houses pro- posed to be built in Weston-road be approved, and that the plan of Mr. Richard Jones for additional scullery and bedroom to each of three houses situate in Ashridge-st., be approved, subject to water carriage and ash-boxes being substituted for the proposed privies and ashpits.— These recommendations were passed.

HEALTH COMHITTEB.—A BATCH 010 NUISANCES. The Inspector had reported to this committee a large number of nuisances, mostly arising from wet ashpits and defective privies, and the committee resolved that notices be served for abatement, and that in the event of non-compliance legal proceedings be taken.—Mr. iswall in moving the adoption of the Health Com- mittee's minutes said that he thought public attention should be called to the great improvement in the health of the town as testified in the Medical Officer's report. Be thought they could con- gratulate themselves and also the medical officer on such an admirable result of the work which had been going on during the last few years with regard to sanitation, and looking after the health of the town. The death- rate, including inquest cases in 1893 was 25.08 ;and dur- ing 1894, the average death-rate was 13.09 per thousand, which was a very remarkably low death rate.—Mr. H. J. Grice seconded the motion, and it was carried.

div.head: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION COEURITTRE.
div.p: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION COEURITTRE.

Recommended by this committee that the salary of the secretary to the Technical Institute be £3O per an- num, and that Mr. E. Marshall be appointed secretary to the Technical Institute.—That the following tenders for the furnishing of the Institute be accepted :—Messrs. W. Farrell and Son, Runcorn,Mr. James Mort,Runcorn, and Messrs. J. Heywood and Son, Manchester.—Mr. Wiswall asked that the Council should go into committer, for the consideration of these minutes. This was agreed to.—When the matter was again brought before the Council,Mr. Wiswall moved in aadition to the above recommendations that the salary of the secretary com- mence from the 4th April, 1895. He said they had given very great attention to the matter,and had endea- voured to recognise Runcorn to the utmost possible ex- tent in deciding the tenders. They hoped that the Tech- nical Institute wonld be a grand success.—Mr. Dean se- conded.—Mr. Wilson expressed regret that Runcorn tradesmen had notbeen able to do all the work in con- nection with the furnishing of the institute.—Mr. Wit- limns said the reason was that no one in Runcorn had ' the facilities for doing this special class of work.—Mr. Grice said he was very :vary that the heaviest contract was being sent out JI town.—The Chairman said he should like to thank Mr. Wiswall for the trouble he had taken to find whether it was possible for the work to be done in Runcorn, It was found that it could not all be done in the town.—Mr. Wiswall said if the contract had been given to a Runcorn firm.three-foarths of the money would have been spent out of the town in getting the materials.—The minutes were then passed. . ,

div.head: NEW LOAN.
div.p: A NEW LOAN.

The Finance Committee recommended that the offer of the Corporation of Bangor to borrow the sum of £1,280 at £3 ss. per cent. interest per annum for seven years, interest to be payaNe half-yearly, be accepted. (Parti- culars of sums invested, General Sinking Fund £578, Water Sinking Fund No. 1 £441, Water Sinking Fund No. 2 £57, Private Street Works Sinking Fund £204).

div.head: LEVYING OV THE GENERAL DISTRICT RATE.
div.p: THE LEVYING OV THE GENERAL DISTRICT RATE.

With respect to the assessment and levying of the general district rate for the year ending 25th March, 1896, the Finance Committee recommended that the owner instead of occupier be rated under the provision of section 211 of the Public Health Act, 1875, where the rateable value of any premises liable to assessment does not exceed the sum of £lO, and that he be assessed on a reduced estimate of threCt-fourths of the net annual value of such property.—Mr. Lightburn, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the Finance Committee said they had suffered from the de- pression of trade, and it had to a very great extent affected the estimates. There was a tallith; off in the market receipts,and then they had a reduction of income to the amount of £4OO arising from empty property for which the Council could not levy rates. They had a deficiency of an overdraft of £BO4 93. 3d., but there was a sum of £3OO which would be paid by owners on pri- vate street works, and also £lB6 of recoverable arrears of the general district rate. This would leave them with a deficiency of £3lB 93. 3d. This sum would have to be provided for in the estimates of the coming year. They declared a district rate of 2s. 9d.in the L. They had had to provide for a loss of something like £400; pay off a debt of £3lB ; and had been able to reduce the rate a penny in the £.—Mr. Taylor seconded.—Mr. Wilson, said he believed every member was anxious to keep the rate at thelowest point, consistent with efficiency. lie thought things might be more efficiently managed in the spending de- partment. With proper management and proper control they ought to have had a balance and not a loss during the year. He complained of work being done twice over. —Mr. Posnett thought the time had come when they should have their drainage put on a thoroughly satisfactory scheme. He thought it was hard on the ratepayers and bad management on the part of the Council when they had to do work twice over. 'The speaker proceeded to speak of a road after being made, having to be taken up in order to lay a drain.—Mr. Wiswall said they had now a complete set of plans show- ing the drains and sewers of the town so that they were in a better position than formerly.—Mr. Lightburn said it was all very well to be wise after a thing was done. What they wanted was something to prevent a recur- rence. They required a detailed statement, not general observations.—The minutes were then passed. SUGGESTED ROAD FROM RUNCORN TO WESTON POINT. In accordance with notice given,Mr. Bisbrown moved that it be an instruction to the Highways and Buildings Committee to open negotiations with the landowners with a view of inducing them to open a road from the end of Percival-lane to Weston Point for vehicular and pedestrian traffic. He said in bringing that resolution forward he recognised that there were numer- ous difficulties in the way. But he ventured to think that those obstacles were not insuperable. He proposed continuing the road from the end of Per- cival-lane, close by the railway embankment, past Swinton's farm, and to finish at. the top end of Weston Point. The owners of the land which would be required were the Bridgewater Trustee, Manchester Ship Canal Co. ,Major Ored and Mr. Bankes. He had no desire to in- crease the rates. His contention was that when a high- way was made, it followed as a !natter of course, that the value of the land was enhanced both for building and other purposes. He did not see any difficulty in dealing with the matter. When they made Victoria-road, Major Ored, in addition to giving the land, gave £l,OOO. ' —Mr. Lighthurn seconded the motion, although he had no confidence of the Council coming to any practical ' conclusion in the matter. Some years ago when a com- mittee was formed one owner objected to giving them the land. The others gave way, but the difficulty was that it would cost two or three thousand pounds to make a good road. They could not spen.i money to en- hance the value of propt.,rty of land owners.—Mr. Tay- lor said it was something like the tenth or twelfth time this question had been brought forward.—Mr. Collier said he had pleasure in supporting the proposition. He was in favour of the proposed road commencing from Percival-lane,and thought they could come to a satisfac- tory arrangement with the owners. They could act in conjunction with the Weston and Weston Point parish councils.—Mr. Hewitt also spoke in support of the motion, and thought their only difficulty would be in ar- ranging with the Salt Union.--Nly. Wilson thought the nearer they could get the road to the Runcorn rally ay station, the better it would be. He thought that the two 'counties would ultimately be connected IT a vehicular

div.head: 1/R. POSNRTT'S PROPOSITIONS.
div.p: 1/R. POSNRTT'S PROPOSITIONS.

Mr. Posnett moved that application be made to the Local Government Board for an order conferring on the council all the following matters, viz. : The appointment of overseers and assistant overseers, the revocation of appointment of assistant overseers, any powers, duties, or liallities of a Parish Council, and applying with the necessary modifications the provisions of this Act with reference thereto ; the appointment of trustees of paroc- hial charities by the Urban District Council.—He said the reason he had brought the first motion forward was that the ratepayers should have an opportunity of choosing their own overseers. He was also anxious that the rate- payers should have the centre' over parochial charities. He had endeavoured to ascertain what he could about the , charities. The committee appointed their own trustees so that the public had no control over the charities. There were four charities, but he could not ascertain the exact amount because it varied. These charities were left, some of them at any rate, for industrial purposes, and he thought the Technical Institute should have the support of these charities.—Mr. Lightburn seconded the motion.—Mr. Wiswall moved that the motion be referred to the General Purposes Committee to be dealt with.— Mr. Taylor seconded, and this was carried.:
UPPER MERSEY NAVICUTION COMMISSION. Mr. Grice gave notice that he would propose that Mr. Taylor be the Council's representative on the Upper Mersey Navigation Commission.
THE ANNUAL MEETING.
It was decided that the annual meeting of thP Council be held on Tuesday, April 23rd, at seven o'clock in the evening.
THE SHIP CANAL AGREEMENT.

Mr. Lightburn asked the Law Clerk whether he had got the agreement I rim the Ship Canal Company.—Mr. Lake said he had received an intimation that the solici- tors were preparing it, but he had riot yet received it.

div.head: TUE WEAVER TRUST.
div.p: TUE WEAVER TRUST.

Mr. Pritchard said he feared the Council was in danger of losing their representation on the Weaver Trust. He thought it was a matter that should be taken into consi- deration and they should make an effort to have their proper representatiot. on the trust.—A Committee was appointed to immediately consider the matter. 'This concluded the business.

div.head: FROD-SHAM.
div.p: FROD-SHAM.

FARM FlRE.—Abodt midnight on Saturday night a fire was discovered in a stack yard which is situated in Ship-st., FrAshatn, and belonging to Mr. William Booth, farmer. A messenger was at once despatched for the Runcorn Fire Brigade, who received information at 2.45 a.m. on Sunday. Deputy Superintendent Wright with a number of men proceeded with the fire engine, and on 1 arrival they found that a large wooden shed had been destroyed, and that two stacks of hay and one of an- threshed oats were on fire. Despite the efforts of the firemen who remained there until two o'clock on Sunday afternoon,the ricks were practically ruined. The damage is estimated. at £3oo,and is covered by insurance. Paßoctuat COMMITTEI3.—A meeting of the Frodsham Committee was held on Friday evening, Mr. Heywood in the chair, Mr. J. M. Williams gave a lengthy report upon the breakages in the water mains, and explained what had beea done to put the mains in working order again, which was considered satisfactory. With refer- ence to Mr. Rothwell's property in Church-street, Mr. W. E. Shore moved that notice be served calling him to put the windows in such property In accordance with the committee's resolution. Therefore Mr. Ringrose moved, and Mr. Barrow seconded, that the windows be allowed tfo remain as they were. Six voted in favour sad five against, Mr. Shore then gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the resolution passed that evening be rescinded.—The minutes were passed at the meeting of the Runcorn Rural Council on Tuesday afternoon. POLICH CASE.—At Frodsham Police Court,on Tuesday, before Mr. A. Thomas,Mary Ann Steadman was charged with being drunk and disorderly on the Ist April in Vicarage-lane, Frodsham Lordship. P.C. Breese proved the case. Defendant was fined 55., or seven days' im- prisonment. She went to prison.

PARISH MHETINGI.-00 Saturday evening the annual parish meeting at Frodsham was held in the Overseer's office at the Town Hall. Mr. Heywood occupied the chair, and expressed surprise that a larger attendance had not been made by the public. He thought it was a desirable thing that the public generally should know something of their doings since the period of their: elec- tion, and he proposed to call upon the Chairmen of the Water,Lighting,ancl Sewerage Committees to give state. ments of the work done.—Mr. T. Earlam, chairman of the Sewerage Coinmittee, said that on account of the severity of the weather the work of cleaning the lower portiou of the main sewer in Marsh Green had been stopped. The work was forced upon them by the fact that the sewers were found on examination, to hi' with- in measurable distance of being silted up.. 9. considerable , quantity of the pipes had been taken up, cleansed, and : replaced with a better fall.—Mr. Shore, chairman of the Lighting Committee, said since the adoption of Urban : powers in Frodsham township, the lighting had been taken over by the existingAnthority,and eight additional lamps had been fixed in Quay and Bridge-lane. This 1 work had been considerably delayed by the recent frost, but it had now been coinpleted to the manifest improve- 1 ment of the roads in question. That work was all that was intended to he done this winter.—Mr. Williams,, chairman of the Water Committee,said the water supply was now accomplished. The quality was stated to be excellent,and the supply abandant, for many ss-ars to come. Two-thirds cf the houses had been connected with the mains,and doubtless within the course of a few months,alinost every house in the district would have a supply. They had also decided to extend their mains to Frodshans Bridge and several other places, and they hoped their water scheme would become almost, if not entirely, self supporting. Mr. Williams stated that t.e engagement of the engineer had proved to be satisfac- tory.—The Chairman in referring to charities said that 1 ,in Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship they had some four Or five bequests at different tinies,and on going over 1 these it was thought that very few of theta ' would come within the care of the coun- cils, they being almost all ecclesiastical. licwever a,small committee was appointed to examine the documents and report thereon.—A number of inter- esting questions of a purely local nature were asked by Mr. Thomas Riley and satisfactorily answered.—Mr. William Jones also called attention to the ploughtng up of a much used footpath across land occupied by Mr. Andrew Hutchinson. This was referred to the parish council. In connection with footpaths it was also stated ! by the chairman that a number of footpaths in the im- mediate neighbourhood had been covered with cinders and ashes and made thoroughly useful. This concluded the business.

div.head: WESTON POINT.
div.p: WESTON POINT.

Panistr MESETING.—The Rev. Canon Wood presided at the annual parish meeting of the Weaver ward on Friday evening. There were also present—The Rev.D.S. Bowen, Messrs. S. Savage, Thomas Grounds and L. Rosenberg. The Chairman gave particulars of the Ann Orred Charity as reported in connection with the meeting at Weston. The Rev. D. S. Bowen moved, Mr. Rosenberg seconded, and it was unanimously decided that the attention of the earish Council be called to South-road and Post Office- road at Weflon Point.

div.head: HALTON.
div.p: HALTON.

TOWNSHIP MEETING.-Ou Monday evening the annual parish meeting was held in the Girls' schiyolroom,Halten. The chair was occupied by the Rev. G. D. Wray, and there were also present :—Messrs. T. Wright, J. McCul- lock,J. Looker, J.Hancock, J.Faulkner, W. H. Bradbury, and Woodier (clerk).—The Chairman read the annual statement of the charities, which were not ecclesiastical. The receipts for St. Thomas' Charity amounted to £25 Bs. 4d., and the expenditure £24 16s. 2J., leaving a ba- lance in hand of 103. 2J. The Eaton Charity receipts amounted to £6 14s. 5d., and this amount was equally divided between St. Thomas' Charity aud Halton Gram- mar School. The Bolton's Charity realised £lB is., and this sum eqlally distributed between St. Thomas' Charity, the Vicar, and the Grammar School. The Hal- ton Grammar School Charity income was £44 6s.,which was paid to the school managers. The Chairman said arrangements were being made for the transfer of the trusteeship of the St. Thomas' Charity, which stood in the name of Sir Richard Brooke, to the official trustees, and it would ultimately be banded over to the Parish Councq who would be asked to distribute it and keep the accounts in future.—Mr. Wright thought the statement of the overseers should be made public, and he would, therefore, give a few particulars of the :recounts. fi)e year coinmenced with a balance in hand of £lB 14s. id., and the Is. 3d. rate each half year had realised £713. The expenses included precept from the Guardians for poor rate, £399 ; highway rate, £186; Sanitary rate, £47 6. 6d. ; Burial board rate, £2O ; School Attendance, £7 ;Assistant Overseer's salary,£4o; and amount allowed by revising barrister for voter's list, £B. He thought they would not have a large balance in band this year. He would take that opportunity of say- ing to the chairman of thelParish Councillthat it would be very advisable for them to make a precept upon the overseers at the commencement of the year, so that the overseers might then be in a position to know what amount they required. The proceedings then ter- minated.
