div.head: GRAND GYMNASTIC 'DISPLAY AT WARRINGTOW.
div.p: GRAND GYMNASTIC 'DISPLAY AT WARRINGTOW.
INTERESTING PERFORMANCES.

On Tuesday evening the third gymnastic display of the present season was given in the Gymnasium, Palmyra-square, Warrington, before a large number of spectators composed of both sexes. Mr.F.Monks, J.P., C.C., officiated as chairman. The programme was commenced by an admirable exposition of the dumb-bell exercise given by the members of the boys' and girls classes, who all gave evidence of careful training. For the rings there appeared Messes. Bamber, Fletcher, G. Vernon, J. Podmore, A. Vernon, Mottram, with Mr. Kinsley, the director. Fletcher led off with a limb-stretching exhibition, and he was quickly followed by the other members who each earned for himself a round of well- merited applause. The last one wit! T. Podmore,who as about the best all-round athlete in the gym. certainly exceeded on this occasion himself and the exploits of his brother gymnasts. As a grand finale Messrs. Fletcher, A. Vernon, Mottram, and Bamber mounted on the ropes until all were sus- pended with their instructor at the top. A diver- sion was then created by the filing in of the ladies' class, who rapidly arranged themselves in order for barbell drill. Their rythmical regularity of motion made a very pleasing sight, and they were fully : deserving of the hearty applause which was ' awarded them.

The next item was of a novel character and one not before introduced into a Warrington gymnastic display, and to it was therefore attached special interest. The item in question was bayonet drill by a squad of 1.2 soldiers from Orford Barracks, under the direction of Sergeant Stamford, who put them through a complicated exercise which all per- formed with great precision and attention to orders. Much amusement was caused by the warlike atti- tudes of our brave defenders, under such peaceful circumstances, while the grounding of bayonets and the stamping of feet made an accompaniment which did away with the necessity of "martial blare." A repetition was loudly called for, but as time went apace this was granted only in the unfising of the bayonets and the orderly march out. ' To a Warrington public boxing is an indispensable adjunct to anything pertaining to strength or skill, and in recognition of this the Gymnasium Commit- tee had thoughtfully arranged or two displays of the noble art, and there was considerable scanning , of programmes by many of the spectators ere the time tor the first " do" come round. The appear- ance of T. Hackett (Warrington) and R. Francis ("Dummy" Manchester) created an appreciable stir, but before the commencement of " hostilities " the ' Chairman announced that he was requested to state that Mr. Francis was both deaf and dumb. Not- withstanding that he was short of two senses the " Dummy "was clearly in strong possession of all other faculties and the first ot the three rounds was initiated with fine sparring, from which Francis got in the first blow. Hackett as rapidly returned and the game became fast and furious. At the end of the round the balance appeared to be in favour of the Warringtonian,though the " Dummy ' displayed superior activity in avoiding the blows by dancing round his opponent and touching the tender spots. In the second round Francis's lightness stood him in good stead and not infrequently he took Hackett off his guard. Still the latter was able to land a neat facer or two. The taller of the two (Francis) led off with his right on Hackett's face in the final round, but the latter returned with interest. Both men then got to close quarters where the nimble- ness of Francis was transferred to his head, that part of his anatomy being continually in the wrong place when Hackett aimed at it. Some neat blows were exchanged on both sides near the end and on the call of time both men were well warmed up, while the spectators cheered loudly. High jumping by the ladies' and girls' classes was then begun at the height of 4ft. 6in. each person jump- ing from the spring board. Successively 41t. 9in., 41t. 51t., sft. 2in., 51t. 4in., sft. 6in.,sft. Bin. and sft. 10in. -vere put up. At sft. 4io. Miss Allen, Miss Whittle, Miss Brierly,and Miss Brundrit bad all jumped splendidly but it was left for the latter lady to run the others out which she did at sft. 10in. in which was the limit of her powers and was accordingly awarded a per- fect ovation of applause. The parallel bars were then run into the room and the boys aud girls went through the elementary stage of the gymnasium drill upon them With well grounded facility. One movement by the boys somewhat resembled an aerial football match and elicited roars of laughter from the spectators. On the conclusion of this, also, a Ryramiti was termed by the boys with Mr. Binslcy as centrepiece. An advanced edition of the same exhibition was then given by Messrs. G. Vernon, A. 'Vernon Ben- nion, Fletcher, Mottram, Bamber, Curbett, J. Padinore, and J. Vernon. Mr. Kinsley commenced with an ex- ample which was found bard to beat, though all made a brave show. Those worthy of especial mention were Fletcher and Podmore,who both made very effective and skilful displays of physical strength and agility. Met. tram, though the youngest of the troup, showed careful training and adaptability, and gave promise of consum- mate skill. Another figure was formed by Messrs Kins- ley, J. Vernon, G. Vernon, Fletcher Mottram, and Pod- more, who came back to the boards by successively walking on their hands along the bars and landing on their feet in somersault style. Hardly was this com- pleted when another " pile "was run up by G. Vernon, Fetcher, J. Vernon, and two of the boys' class. After this the ladies' had again their turn, this time with the clubs which they whirled about with praiseworthy dex- terity. They acted really in the capacity of living time- keeper's to the musical accompaniment, and the two columns in which they were formed were led by Miss Allen and Miss Brundrit respectively. Both these ladies formed an exselleet example of the perfection which drill can be brought to under careful supervision. Boxing came next and on this occasion the manipula- tors of the gloves were T. Allen of Warrington and J. Davies of Manchester. As in the first display there were , three rounds in which the men were fairly matched, though Allen was perhaps tho heaviest of the two, and in the final round the Warrington favourite be a side blow brought Davies to the ground. The hitter was coon to the fore again and retaliated with some severe body blows. In the whole display both men showed themselves to be scientific wielders of nature's weapons, while their activity was about on a par with their skill. Taken all round this was about the best display of the evening. A very large amount of local interest was centred in the tug of war betweeen six of the police force and the same number of soldiers from Orford Barracks. After preliminary arrangements the teams filed in and presented an appearance which augured a tough tussle. Their respective weights were: police,77st. Sibs.: soldiers,77st. The difference in weight was there- fore very slight,but not so the strength,for all the muscle appeared to be on the side of the "nobbles," who with- out the slightest difficulty hauled the soldiers over the line at a run, twice in succession. This was a very poor do for the spectators' who all the same cheered the winners, and laughed at the crestfallen defeated. Miss F. Jones and Miss W. Jones followed with a club duet in musical time, in which they each earned a meritorious name for the first-class exhibition they gave,each move- ment of one being duplicated by the other. Double horizontal bars were put up and the team before enu- merated, under the leadership of their skilful instructor, went through a series of feats of the most difficult nature with commendatory skill. J. Vernon in this set displayed great muscular strength and dexterity, the merits of which were not lost sight of by the spectators. On the proposition of Mr. T. MORRIS, F.G.S., a very hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Monks for hav- ing so kindle taken the chair.

ln reply Mr. MONKS thanked the gymnasts for haying given him such a good object lesson of physical train- ing. He hoped that the :Imo was not far distant when the Corporation would take over the Gymnasium as they had other institutions in the town. (Elear, hear.) That would relieve the Committee of all responsibility at once. He looked forward to the time when every elementary school would have a gymnasium. He thought anyone who had studied the question at all would see the advantages. Be further expressed a hope that in time every boy would be subjected to military training which tended to plotnote discipline. Mr. Monks then threw out as a suggestion that if the Com- mittee found any difficulty in making the two ends meet, they should hand over the building to the Corporation and then physical training would be promoted at the expense of the town.

The vaulting horse was next brought into requisition, and the youngsters of both sexes kept up a continual run of leaping over that animal of doubtful pedigree. Miss Stirrup, throughout the evening, provided very suitable musical accompaniments to the E x ercises . and on her playing the National Anthem, the evening's en- tertainment was concluded. This was by far the best display of the seasontand the committee, Mr. Kinsley, and all who took part are en- titled to much praise for the manner in which they car- ried it to a successful issue. AN IMPUDENT 'MOT. At the Warrington , Borough Police Court, I od Saturday last week, before Alderman Harrison and other magistrates, Thomas Hart, Scotland-road was charged with stealing from Church-street on 'A ednesday the 27th inst. a quantity of timber, value 10s., the property of Mr. Bowers.—Detec- tive-Sergeant Monaghan stated that on Wednesday morning, defeti...ant, was employed bv Mr. Bowers to make up a it. .e at the slaughter house, off Church-St., and comp :..1 s.• ' was to be paid a sovereign cor the job. Defendan three men to drag up she wood. On Thursday, complainant went to look hoc . i.e work was going on and found that the timber was missing. He reported the matter to witness, who afterwards found ' that the timber had been sold cheap at the houses of 15 or 16 i....,21e and that defendant had procured drink with the proceeds.—James Glynn, GeocAe Hwrop, and John Macdonald deposed to being employed by defend- ant to knock down the timber and break it. When this was done he sold the wood to wcmen in pieces for 2d. and 3d.—Defendant was sentenced to one month's hard

labour. ALLEGED STRIKING A [Riesz WITH A CLEAVER. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor and other magistrates, William Allen, Lythgoe's-lane,was charged with having on the 14th March ill-treated,beaten,and tortured a horse.—William Broadhurst and Arthur Ashley deposed that cm the day stated they saw the defendant pass a place where they were working in Manchester road leading a horse, and when about 30 yards away the horse fell, and they saw it get up from the floor and defendant struck it two or three times with something they could not swear to, on the body.—lnspector Luff, R.S.P.C.A., stated that he saw the horse on the 18th of March and it then had a straight cut on the near side over the 11th rib. The cut was about five inches long and had been stitched up. Witness, in consequence of what he heard saw the de- fendant on March 20th, and the latter in answer to in- quiries, said he was bringing the horse home with the cleaver under his left arm when the animal plunged and caught her side against the blade of the cleaver. Witness added that the defendant had told a veterinary surgeon that the horse had shied and caught herself with a hook on a 'bus. Defendant had told him that the cleaver was the only thing he had with him, and the witnesses affirmed that he struck the horse with something. It was also impossible for the horse to have caught itself against the cleaver as the defendant had her on the op- posite side to that article.—P.C. Turner also thought it was unlikely that the horse could have hurt itself in the manner described.--Defendant who strongly denied striking the horse W 37 fined 55. including coats. ANOTHER ROBBERY FROM TUB PERSON. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. R. Garnett and Mr. E. J. Guest, Catherine Carney and Bridget Lally, both women of immoral char- acter, were charged with stealing from the person of James Berry, on Monday afternoon, the sum of 13s. his maney.—The Chief Constable stated that the complain- ant Berry was a forgeman from Dallam and resided 83 Winwick-r, 'ad, and Carney had only been a short time out of the Workhouse hospital, while Lally was only "tea days out from three months." On Monday after- noon the complainant saw a man named Hinds, 8, Bill- et., and at his request went in the house at that number and treated the occupants. among whom were the de- fendants. Carney went away and a moment after com- plainant found that out of 17s. ld. he bad with him, 13s. were gone. He then informed P.C. Hollingworth who in turn told P.C. Barnett, giving him a description of the prisoners. While near the market the latter officer met the prisoners each eating an orange, and ordered them to walk before him to the Police Station. He watched them and saw Carney hand something to Lally whereupon the officer reached forward and found in Lally's hand 3 florins is. Id. When at the Police Station they were searched but only 4d. more found.—James Berry and P.C. Barnett corroborated, and prisoners were sent to gaol for one month's bard labour each.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH COURT. PElDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Dr. Gornall,Alderman Wright,and Councillor H. Roberts. ALLEGED LAMP THROWING. —Sarah Davies was charged with having on the 28th March unlawfully damaged a lamp and a chair, the property of Sarah Briars.—The complainant said she went to the house of her mother in Golden Grove-St., where defendant came in for her husband (who was there), and threw the lamp at com- plainant's mother, bruising her head. Defendant then knocked her husband over complainant's chair, and broke it while the lamp (which was unlit) was also broken. She assessed the damage at 10s. 61 Evidenee was given by complainant's mother and Annie Good- well, and defendant was fined 10s. including costs. Mormar.—Before the Mayor (chairman), Alderman Hairis,m, Messrs. F. Menke, and J. W. Hayward. ASSAULTING THI3 POLICE: SMART SBNTENCIL—TROMBI Baguley, 35, Town Hill, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Golden Grove-street, on Saturday night ; defendant was further charged with assaulting P.C. Clough at the same time and place.—P.C. Clough stated that on Saturday evening he was in Lyme-street and saw the prisoner hawking, oranges and acting in a disorderly manner. Witness ordered defendant to move on but.he replied insultingly and witness then attempted to take him into cu,tody and they had a struggle in which the officer was struck twice. P.C. Corbett then came to his assistance and defendant was taken t, the police station.—P.C. Corlett corroborated, an I stated that he saw the defendant strike dough in the face.— The magistrates were then reminded that the defendant was the man who was let off leniently a short time ago on his promising not to come again and at the same time giving the bench permission to "make it a stiff no" if he came again. The bench this time took him at his word and sent defendant to gaol for three months hard labour. Dacha AND DI9OIIDERt2.—Vor being drunk and dis- orderly on divers d des the following persons were fined: Robert Brown. 29, Crossley-street, drunk on 23rd March, ss. ; Bridget Mannion, 16, Old-road, 26th March,' Z. 61. BRRACH oy THB PEACE.—William Cunningham and I Thomas Baguley were fined the costs for fighting in the Market Place on the 23rd March. STRBRT OBSTRUCTION.—Francia Riley, Sankey-at., was charged with obstructing Golborne-st., by leaving a handcart there an unreasonable time on the 22nd March. P.C. Cooper proved the case and defendant was fined 53.

and Costs. _ DUO-OWNERS ScMMoNED.—JOh9 Hould i ng, 137, Dallam-lane, was dismissed after being charged with keeping a dog without a license on the 16th March ; Owen Hudson. 3, Warburton-St., for the same offence was likewise dealt with; Job Wardle. 62, Sharp-street, same offence on the 19th March, fined the costs ; Frank Berry, 11, Brick-St., dog at large in Bridge-St., fined 53. and costs. TUNSDLY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett, and Mr. E. J. Guest. AN UNRULY PRIsONRR.—JameS Higharn was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Monday afternoon in Rose and Crown-street ; he was further charged with assaulting P.Q. Lewis at tlisame time and place.—P.C.. Lewis stated that there were a couple of men fighting in '

Rose and Crown-street on the above date,and in separat- ing them he pushed the prisoner away. The latter then became pugnacious, and they had several rounds to- gether until P.C. Beecham came and assisted witness to remove the prisoner to the police station.—P.C.Beecham proved the assault, and prisoner was sent to gaol for one month's hard labour. kYNDNESCIAT,—Before Mr. John Fairclough (in the chair) and Messrs. Fleming and Geddes. NON-A2PEARAIOE TO a SIIIIMONS.—James Floyd was charged on warrant, he not having appeared tothe sum- mons served upon him in October, 1891, with hawing committed an assault on one William Cowell.—Prosecu- tor said he wished to Withdraw the summons, as he and prisoner had been friendly since the assault.—The case was dismissed on Floyd paying the cost of the warrant, 6s. 6d.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. W. H. Sleekly (in the chair) and Major Pickmere. CRUELTY TO A Honsz.—John Thomas Harrison was charged with ill-treating a horse, on the 21st March, in the township of Poulton, by causing it to be travelled in an unfit state. Jcseph Knox, a boy, was also charged with travelling the same. Sergeant Barnes stated that on the day in question he saw the defendant Knox in charge of the mare on the highway at Poulton. . It was suffering from strained tendons and excessive blistering. —Harrison said the horse was being brought to Warring- lag to be slaughtered, and this was done the following morning.—lnspector Luff.of the National So6iety for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, said these cases were taken to stop the horses being travelled to the slaughter yards. The owners of the horses got a shilling or two more when this was done.—The magistrates considered that the horse ought to have been slaughtered at the field, and Harrison was fined 2s. 6cl. and coats. Knox was discharged.

NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS. Sartmer.—Before Mr. T. J. Gillespie (chairman), Mr. T. H. Pearson,COl. J. L.Wood, Mr. R. Stone, Mr. C. B. F. Boma. DOGS AT LARGE.—For allowing their dogs to be at large John Smith, Francis Holleran, Newton ; John Baines, and Robert Duckworth, Golborne, fined 33. BJ. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence Samuel Ryder, New- ton ; John Moroan,Golborne ; William Quinn,Golborne ; Patrick Lyons, Haydock, and James Harrison, Haydock, were fined ss. and costs ; Francis Kelly,James Corcoran, Thomas Walsh, Patrick Connor, Thomas Hickey, and Frank Kelly, of Golborne ; James King, Elaydock, were fined 2s. Bd. and costs ; and Samuel Grundy, Haydock, was fi nedlOs CHARGE or W IFE ASSAIILT.—Josph Hazelden, 1, Stan- ley-St., Earlestown, was charged with assaulting and beating his wife,. Alice Amelia Haze!den, on March 15th. A judicial separation was also applied for. Mr. Garner, of St. Helens, who appeared on behalf of the complain- ant, said that the parties were married in September, 1893. They had 0,1-r been married three months when the husband communed to neglect his wife. He went to dances, and he rmve her very little money. About six months after when they were living at Hirst, she re- ceived a thrashing from her husband. The defendant afterwards got employment at the Woodpit, Haydock, and his wife came to live with him in Earlestown. On March 15th, the defendant came home from his work, , early in the morning. His wife was in bed. An alterca- tion place in the bedroom, and the defendant deal his wife some severe blows across the mouth, cutting her lips and also bursting her nose. She went into the kit- chen and he followed her and twisted her arm so much that it was useless for nearly a week. He afterwards renewed the assault. Not content with this cce put a notice- in a local paper, what was known as "crying notchell," saying that he would not be responsible for debts his wife might contract. This implied that she contracted debts, but there was absolutely no foundation for this, as she never got things on trust.—The complainant gave evidence in support of her solicitor's statement—P.C. Burns also gave evidence.—Mr. Stuart who represented the defen- dant said that all the trouble arose owing to the com- plainant grumbling about not having enough money. His client denied the assault, and said that his wife had treated him with marked neglect—Mary Ann Hazleden, mother of defendant, was then called, and denied the assault.—Further evidence was given by Robert Hazle• den, and the magistrates decided to fine the husband ss. and costs, but refused to grant a separation ordc r. CHIMNEY ON Fiaa.—Thomas Berry, Newton, was fined is. for allowing his chimney to be on fire on February

19th. OBSTRUCTION OF ras ROAD.—Paill Caldwell was lined Si. for allowing his cart to stop an unreasonable time in the strat in Golborne, on March 20th. TRESPASSING IN PURSUIT 07/ GAms.—Francis Holleran, and Charles Moore were charged with trespassing in a field in Burtonwsod on March 16th, in search of game. Mr. Longton, who appeared on behalf of Mr. Heaton, tho plaintiff, said that his client saw the defendants enter a field and beat it, and afterwards go into another. Heaton then went towards them, but they ran away. He however ascertained their names and addresses, and reported them.—The magistrates fined the defendants ss. aad costs each.—John Finegan was charged with committing a similar offence on the sanit date. Mr. Longton again prosecuted. Alexander Skean said that he saw the defendant and another man enter the field in Burtonwood with a couple of dogs. They started a hare, but witness prevented them from catching it. The prisoners then bolted, but witness got their names, and summoned them. The other man had not appeared in answer to his summons.—The magistrates inflicted a fine of 103. and costs upon Finegan, and ordered a war- rant te be issued for the apprehension of the other man.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. A. Thomas and T. Rigby. OBSTRUCTING THE FOOTPATIC—k number of youths named Frederick Watson, William Lawton, Thomas Fletcher, William Harding, Joseph Prescrtt, and Francis Smitham were summoned for obstructing the footpath in Egerton-street on the 21st ult.—P.C. Gregory proved the case, and said the boys were a Bourse of annoyance to pedestrians.—Superiatendent Atherton stated that ,he had received many complaints with respect to the misbehaviour of lads in the streets by jostling against people, etc. Defendants were each fined the costs. IRREGULAR Scuoot. ATTEDTDANCE. —The following were fined for neglecting to send their children regularly to school i—Thomas Boyers, York-street ; Thomas Fletcher,Briscoe-street ; William Ellis, Heath-road ; and John Preston, Gas-street. Mr. T.Bowyer, school visitor prosecuted. INDECENCY.—Mary White,who stated that she belonged to Over, was fined 103. and 6s. 4d. costs for indecency in Waterloo-road; and a Norwegian sailor named Martin Nilsen was ordered to pay 10s. and 103. 6d. costs for a like offence. Dausa AND DISORDIRLEY.—JOhn Henry Johnson was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for being drunk and disorderley ia High-street on the 31st March. TRANSFER OF LICENSES.—Edward Orme asked for permission to sell at the Camden Hotel, Surrey-street, recently occupi,d by John Fleming; William Baker made a similar application to sell at the Grapes Inn, Halton-road, lately occupied by James Ditchfield •, and Emma Field applied for a temporary transfer of tab beerhouse license of the Bird-in-hand, Halton-road at , present held by William Baker, all the applications were granted.

A MARRIAGE PRESENTATION. The memners of che Mothers' Meeting, the choir, and the clergy of St. Peter's Church, assembled in the John-street schoolroom to carry out their inten- tion of making Mrs. Gandy , on the occasion of her marriage, a sub7tantial recognition of her services in the past, especially as a member of the choir and a helper at the Mothers' Meeting. There was a large attendance; which included a few friends. Some choice songs were given by Mrs. Yeomans, Mrs. Bailey, Mr. Pearson, Mr. Knight, and by the St. Peters' minstrels, under the superintendence of Mr. Newell. Misses M. and E. Brookes contributed a few duets on the violin and piano, which were well appreciated. Mr. Bailey evoked roars of laughter by his Yorkshire sketch, "The Insurance Agent," as also Master R. Sumner, one of the minstrels, by his stump speech, " Women's Rights." The Vicar said they had come to present a tribute of respect and gratitude to their tried and valued friend, late Miss Edgar, now Mrs. Gandy, whom they all admired and loved. They wished to make her a presentation, not because she was 1 eying them, nor y t because they wished to keep her, but simply to show their gratitude for her constant services in the past and the kind feelings they cherished towards her. lie then presented to Mrs. Gandy, on behalf of the choir and clergy, a hand- some electro-plateci biscuit jar,and on bahalf of the Mothers' Meeting a beautiful electro-plated cruet. The presents, which were much admired, were the product of Messrs. E. and A. Eustance, Sankey-st. Mrs. Gandy, who was received with applause, thanked the Vicar and those present in suitable terms, as did also Mr. Gandy. Mr. J. Roberts (churchwarden) and the Rev. J. A. Coon (curate) bore testimony to the genuine character of Mrs. Gandy and the good work she had done in the
parish. A BADGER /N THE VIADUCT WOHZe,

_ EARLESTOWN, On Friday night between 7 and 8 o'clock, one of the watchmen on duty in the Viaduct Works at Earlestowu, when going his rounds saw a strange animal in the timber shed. He did not like the looks of the beast, and being afraid to go through the shed, he sent for Mr. Harwood, the chief fore- man, who on seeing it, said it was a badger, full grown. As there were no means of removieg it, and the animal did not seem disposed to go away, of its own accord, Mr. Harwood procued his gun, and shot it. It was a fine specimen, and weighed about 30 pounds. flow it had got into the works,it is imposstble to say.

ROOM. 1 WARRINGTON v. TYLDESLEY. 1 The Tyldesley club this year is probably the strongest 1 in Lancashire with the possible exception of Oldham, and, as they have a good lead already over the latter. it ' is very probable that the "Eagles," or the "Bungere," as they are usually known, will head the Lancashire Rugby League this season. When Warrington met them at Wilderspool some time ago; the result was a well-earned victory for the visitors, and consequently the return match was considered to be, a good thing for them. Warrington have, however, returned to form lately, as witness the fright they gave Oldham on the previous Monday,and a good game was looked forward to against Tyldesley. But these hopes were dimmed when it was discovered that Barber, Moores, Jolley and Dakin were not playing, and it was generally voted an easy victory for the home team. A re-arrangement of the Warring- ton team became necessary owing to these absentees,and Callaghan was put three-quarter, the ether vacancy in that department being filled by Cross, late of Stockton Heath. The places vacant in the front rank were filled by Bailey. Holmes and Saunders. A special excursion was run from Warrington to Tyldesley on Saturday, and about 300 enthusiasts accompanied the local team. The weather although cold was fine, and the Tyldesley ground was in good condition. A "gate" of about 3,000 assembled to witness the match which was very pleas- antly contested from beginning to end. Mr. Beswick, of Swinton acted as referee and the following were the teams pitted against each other: Warrington: B meow, full back ; Burton, Heesom, Cross and Callaghan, three-quarters ; John T. Bate and ' James T. Bate, half-backs ; Turner, Taylor. Berry, Bai- ley, Therniley, Houghton, Saunders and Holmes,

foil/ads. - Tyldesley: Bancroft,full back ;Lawten.Cooper,Rvans, and Shaw, thme-quartera ; J. Berry and W. Berry, half- backs Wood ward, Smith, Shepherd, Worthington, Roberts,Harris, R. Berry and Banks, forwards. Turner won the toss, and decided to take the advant- age of a stiffish wind,which blew from one corner to the other. Shaw kicked off and from Burton's return,Cooper was too eagerly tackled by Saunders, and a scrimmage was ordered near the line. From this scrimmage, J. Berry was almost over during the first minute of the match, Warrington now recovered slightly, but play settled down in their quarters with very brief visits to the neutral territory. Buff Berry again made a grand run, but found Boscow too safe. ..After sboett five minutes play, Lawton took a long pasx.fehneauffßerry anti trick- ing Callaghan he made a fine lin* and got over. The position was very difficult lei rgoal to be placed, but Shaw nevertheless landed a fine goal. Turner restarted from the centre, and he made such a ponderous kick that the ball went past the goal pests and over the line, a minor being conceded by Bancroft. Shaw again re- started, and Burton taking a pass from" Smack "Bate, he gained considerable . ground, and Warring- ton attacked strongly. The " Eagles " made desperate efforts to get away but Holmes by dropping on the ball, prevented them. From the ensuing scrimmage, the Warrington men dribbled the hall down, and when a score seemed almost a certainty, Bancroft saved in fine style. An injudicious kick by Cross was the means of Tyldesley conceding a second minor, Following the drop out. Turner was almost over but found himself called back for some informality. Tyldesley at length raised the siege and got to the centre when Cross made a good run and gained considerable lost ground, but unfortunately kicked too strongly and another minor was conceded to Warrington. Tyldesley followed the drop out well, and Lawton securing made a brilliant run, but was run into touch by ildkow, near the line. This let off was however only temporary, for Buff Berry got over immediately afterwards from a pass from his brother William. Shaw failed tosplace a goal this time. Re-starting with eight points to the bad, War- rington played up pluckily, and Burton was prominent by a determined wriggle, through his opponents, and some smart passing between Smack Bate, Heesom, and Burton was witnessed,but immediately afterwards, Buff Berry made a dash over the line, and Tyldesloy were three points further. ahead. Shaw failed to improve. This was followed by a free kick from a rush which was in a favourable position, but Shaw again failed to send the ball over the bar. A general melee now took place, and a confident appeal was made for a try by Harria, but a five yards' scrimmage was ordered instead. Shaw took a pass from W. Berry very poorly, other- wise another try would have almost certainly resulted, Burton preventing him from getting away. Holmes, Saunders' Taylor, and Thorniley now were prominent in a dribble down the field.and Callaghan making his mark followed his kick as well that Cooper was tackled before' be could return, and play remained for a time in the home quarters. Tyldesley again attacked and a brilliant bout ot passing between Evans, Cooper, and Lawton made things look bad for Warrington, Boseow however relieved their apprehensions. Houghton now made his mark and relieved the pressure, and play was pretty even up to halftime, when the score ran, Tyldesley one goal, two tries, (11 points), Warrington nil. Turner restarted the second moiety, and th 3 wire- pullers very soon were on the offensive. A grand dribble in which Thorniley, Holmes, and Saunders were promi- nent,was the means of sending the ball near the line,and the finishing touch was put on by "Smack" Bate. Bur- ton failed to increase the value of the score. This reverse spurred on the Tyldesley players, and a fierce attack was made on the Warrington stronghold ; and on one occasion Callaghan by falling on the hall over the line just robbed them of a try. Berry, Bailey, and Turner kept their opponents at bay for a short time, but Buff Berry by a sadden dash got over, and secured his third try, Callaghan vainly endeavouring to stop him. Shaw for the third time failed at the goal. Tyldesley still at- tacked, and the Warrington defenders found plenty of work to do, but they gradually worked the ball out of danger, and a bit of passing between Bate, Cross, and Taylor *as applauded. Houghton sent the ball past half way from a line out,and a moment later Cross made his mark which was paced for Burton, but the kick was charged down. Warrington still kept up a strong pressure,. and Burton was tackled near the line. The attack canoe to an end by a minor being conceded. A little later Burton had extremely hard sines, for •in rounding his opponents, he put one foot in touch, other- wise he would have had practically a free field before him, and would probably have repeated his perform- ance of the previous fdonday against Oldham. This was the last chance for Warrington, and during the remain- ing portion of the game, Tyldesley were the aggressors, and but for the fine defensive play of Heeson, Burton and Boscow, they would have scored several times. About two minutes before time, the Tyldesley forwards had got the ball over the line, when Callaghan made an almost miraculous lave, falling on the ball at their feet. When the whistle blew for no side, Tyldesley had won by a goal and three tries (14 points) to Warrington one try (three points). The game was a very interest- ing and pleasantly fought game, ,',ere being a total absence of ill-temper on either side. Tyldesley were un- doubtedly the better team. WARRINGTON v. ST. HELENS.

.. This return fixture was played in the Wilderepreil ! ground on Monday, before between 4,000 and 5,000 ' spectators, 400 of whom travelled by special train from St. Helens. The weather was favourable albeit the , ground was a trifle heavy. The loeal captain set the ball in motien. Ashcroft was in readiness to receive it and made considerable progress. Heesom stepped in, but dallying too long the St. Helens forwards were en him and made things early look risky for Warrington. Boscow however proved in grand trim and saved nicely. This early attack and corresponding fine defence by Boscow presaged much of what was to follow, for tak- ing full advantage of the breeze behind them St. Helens pressed almost incessantly during the first half. Time after time they would have scored had it not been for tbe rare saves brought off by &scow. One particularly smart save was when he dashed in front of Rimmer, as the latter was about to ground under the cross- bar. Smack Bate and Burton were amongst the first to effect anything like a clearance; rurner also forced his way through, but he was ill supported, and the pressure was renewed all the keener. From one ot the several scrimmages on the home lines the St. Helens forwards crossed the line all in a heap and Fitzgerald gained the try. Allen made a good but futile attempt at a goal. The pressure was resumed tted continued until close on half-time when Allen was entrusted with the kick from a fine catch by Ashcroft and landed a goal from a difficult place. Half time score : St. Helens 1-1-0 ; Warrington, 0-0-0 In the second half the pres3ure was mainly carried on by Warrington, but their ill-luck at the finishing touches ' stuck to them and they were unable to reduce the heave lead against them. Twice Berry and Barber were bowled into touch in goal when on the point of scoring. St. Helens in the one or two breaksaway which they had made better use of their chances and Doherty dropped a neat goal almost as the whistle sounded leaving the visitors for a second time this season substantial winners. Final result, St. Helens, 2-1-0 ; Warrington, nil. WARRINGTON A. AI. ITLDESLEY A.—Only a poor num- ber of spectators witnessed the return encounter be- tween the above clubs on Saturday at the Wilderspool enclosure. Tyldesley kicked off, Warrington returning smartly when one of the hotnesters secured and placed the leather between the visitors' posts. rue attempt to improve the score was futile. Play was slow for some time, Warrington were' pressing but unable to get over. At length Hughes by a bit of smart play succeeded in scoring the second try for Warrington. The hall travelled rapidly from one goal to the other but neither side was able to score. The half-time whistle sounded, and Warrington were leading by two tries to nil. On re-starting, the visitors made many vigorous ateempts to outwit their opposing team but all their attempts were in vain. Ths play was now and up to the finish of an even character, neither side scoring. Warrington A two tries, Tyldesley A nil.

WARRINGTON ST. MART'S V. WARRINGTON RANGRRS.— Played on Saturday on the St. Mary's ground. W. Dut- ton commenced hostilities for the Saints, and the visi- tors were gradually forced back to centre, where play was evenly conte-ted for the first fifteen minutes. ,A short run and kick by F. Hampson and. a rush by the forwards made a severe attack on the Rangers' defence, Higgiribottom throwing a good chance away by passing on the line. Continuing there was a lot of scrimmaging at halfway. Roughley was twice called upon, and re- sponded with huge kicks. Both sides were pressing strongly, Higginbottom and F. Hatnpson being in flue form. Dicchange kicking by the respective backs took place, and play still hovering near St. Mary's lines Roughley kicked in touch at the centre flag. Resuming, F. Hatnpson got possession and with a neat run trans- ferred play to the Rangers' 25 flag. Halftime score, nil. Oa changing ends the Saints at once began to press the Rangers on their lines, and a neat forward rush by the homesters resulted in Rutter scoring a try, T. Bennett being responsible for a grand goal. Continuing, the. visitors lacked combination, and the Saints got danger- ously near the line. Siddle relieved with a good kick to centre, and a round of passing by T. Bennett,and taken part in by Higginbottom, O'Brien, and Warburton, took play to the Rangers' lines,but they could not score any- thing substantial, a minor accruing. The Saints expe- rienced hard lines, having the best .of the game all through, and administered defeat for the second time this season by one goal five minors to one minor. . STOCKTON EIRATIS V. RIINCORN RICB.BATION.—These teams played their return match on the ground of the former on Saturday. Both teams were short of several of their usual players. Thu early stages of the game were of a desultory character, neither side playing up to their usual standard, and Up to half-time nothing had been scored. On tinning round the game was of a bet- ter description. The visitors' backs di i some splendid passing, and gave the horne side a 1--,t of trouble to keep their linesantact. However, after a piece of good play on the part of Brereton, who got away from the scrimmage nicely; the ball tvas passed out to Paton, who ran in near the corner, Whitney supplementing with a good goal. Thu Recs. continued to have the best of matters, and Houghton had hard lines in not scoring. Th home men now transferred play to the other end, and just on the call of time one of the forwards dashed over the line, the kick at goal tailing. The game ter- minated in a win for the visitors. Score : Ruianc-rn Recreation, one goal, two minors ; Stockton Heath ,one

. _ try, three minors. WARRINGTON JUNIOR CO? COMPETITIOS.-IST Rotre4). —CASTLE RI:GORR WORKS V. WARRINGTON RECREATION. This match took place on Tuesday night, on the Wtr- rington ground. The ;Recs. started, and pla 7 was evenly contested at eentre. Towards the end of the first half, Lally scored an unconverted try. Both sides pressed barque the second half, the Recs.; if anything, having the best of the game. Lally scored again from a scrim- mage on he line, no. goal resulting. Soon after, the whistle sounded tie and the Castle Rubber Works were returned winneraty twcsttiee to nil. RUNCORN y. NOY &Ammer. —Played on the New Brighton ground: on Settirday. There was a fair art"- dance. Owing to the home team being photographed a start was not made until fully half an hour after the ad- vertised time. 'Runcorn Started and immediately began to press. On account of the greasy nature of the ball several malle took placein the passing of the backs, and from a free kick, taken! by Cannel', the Liscard team obtained their first minor. Runcorn immediately com- menced to attack, and Abrafias initiated several rounds of smart passing, the effects of 'which were nullified by the sure tackling of the opposing banks. After several smart bouts of passinge,A.brams received from Fa:lather at half,and (saltily ran Over near the posts, Ward- r con- verting ;finely. On re-starting Jonee put his si 'ln .a good position by a tremendous punt; and afterviar s, in conjunction with Drinkwater,indulged in amaitpaslsing; but Houghton relieved finely and frustrated all the attacks of the New Brighton men. Half-time w,Selcalled Runcern leading by a goal. Hoppe re-itarted. Med Ab- rams attempted to rush through,but Walkeeeeplted with I a fine dribble, unfortunately kicking t hard, at a , critical time. A good deal of rough play 'es indulged o in, and ascidenta of • minor nature we of frequent i occurrence. Houghton was compelled retire for a short time, Warder taking his place, but fie afterwards resumed. The forwards - had most of the game at this period, the play being a very deseltory 9haracter, but a smart pass from Abrams to Faulkner almost ended in another try, and another equally good bit of play ended in leurthavand crossing the line, but he lost the ball. Houghton then tried to. score on his own account, but Fletcher intercepted finely. After several desperate scrimmegea , near the line Dunbavand scored at the corner, the same player landing a beautiful goal. Time . was then called with the score :—Runcorn, 2 goals; New Brighton, nil. RENCORN V. New Benasieon "A" Tsaars.—The re- turned match between these teams should have taken place at Runcorn; an Saturday, but. much disappoint- ment was felt when at three o'clock a telegram was received/saying they could not raise a team. No doubt they wifi be called upon to explain _the fact before the , CounWAutliority. ASSOCIATION. „f is Aneteneme v. WARRINGTON ST. ELPRIN'S.—This match was played on the Arpley Cricket ground on Sat- urday in threatening weather. Mather took the place of Connor; who had an injured leg. The teams lined up, as follows —Warrington:i Goal, Webster; full backs,,i Evans and .1. Mather; half-backs' • Linaker, Williamson (captain), and Phillips;. forwards, T. Mather, Wilsoil, Smithson, Jewkes, and Gorton. St. Elphin's : Goilii Robson ; full backs, Marshall and Taylor ; half-backeie Phoenix, Forbes (captain), and Colley ; forwards, Re*-, ford, Eligginhotto a, Duckworth, Dendy, and Battonli referee Mr. Cattrall, Barnton. There was a large ntirnt her of spectators present when Smithson kicked off feet: Warrington. The Saints took the ball to the Warrington goal, where Hatton shot, but Webster saved splendidly,. and play raged at centre for a few moments. Smithson' had the best of his oponents,and after a fine bout of path- me, in which• Smithson. Jewkes, and Gorton took part,a corner came to Warrington, but nothing resulted, and the ball was sent back to mid-field. Both teams tried hard to score, each goalkeeper playing remarkably well, while the Saints' forwards did all they could, and half- time arrived with nothing scored. The Saints COM- menced hostilities in the second half, and J. Mather, by I a huge kick, took the ball back again. Soon afterwards Warrington, were awarded a free kick, but nothing re- , suited from Linaker's place, Warrington again having bard lines in notscoring,Smithson shooting over the bar. Warrington had the best of the olay, T. Mather sending in a shot from the left which Robson saved at. the ex- pense ot a corner. Shortly afterwards the Saints took up the attack, and after a few exchange kicks Hatton Scored an unmistakable goal. Warrington tried hard to score, Robson being kept busy with shots' one particularly hot (me coming in from the foot of 1. Mather, Robson ' just fisting out in time. J. Mather and Hatton were re- peachy racing down the field after the ball, the last- named almost scoring on many occasions. Each side ' tried hard to score, but could not, owing to the strong defence of the respectiv6 goalkeepers, the final score being—Warrington St. Elphin's one goal, Warrington nil. PENEETR. BOYS' COMPETITION.—PENVITE FRIENDS' SCHOOL Boys v. PRIMATE " BULLIES ."—The final tie in the above cannpetitton was played off on Saturday at Penketh School. The School started with the wind and hill in their favour, and were soon pressing, but wild shots and hard passes threw away chance after chance and it was not till ten minutes t.efore half-tima that the Selsoel m imaged to score, R. Andrew passing from the left wing, W. Charnock and R. Lowe rushing the ball through. Almost immediately after the kick-off, C. Harlow shot and R. Baluley scored from the rebound. At half-thine it seemed like a hard game for the School, but they roused themselves up and kept the " Bullies " at bay, and while the forwards, taking advantage of the more open garne,developed some very good combination, Charnock, liarlow, and Baguley especially doing some very uthful work, the School added two more to the score, Lo we, and Charnrick putting, the finishing touch. Their forwards never seemed to get away, S. Marsden, and R. Houghton being always where they were needed. The result of four goals to nil leaves the School the chempiotte of the" ass's' Competition" for which they get a very good ball offered by Mr. James Woodward, of Penketh. ~ . , . .

-er RIJN CO ILN .SCROOL BOARD. A meeting orthis f3eiard was held in the Board room, on Tuesday :evening. Idr.J.Prirchdrd occupied the chair, and there were aISD present- : Rev. Canon Wood, Messrs. T, Handley J. P., S. Taylor, J.P., CO., E. Imison J.P., Dr. McDorigall and G. Moss (cierk).—At a meeting of the school attendance committee held on the 26th ult, 25 parents appeared for contravention of the Education Act, Proceedings were ordered to be taken against four parents. The visitors' report for the month ending Mitch , 22nd shnwed that the total number on the rolls was 3443, a slight increase on the numbers for three or four glooths past,, but a decrease of 100 as compared with the cor- responding month of last year. The average attendance was 2845, being a decrease of 177 as against last year. During the month 65 parents were summoned before the School Attendance Commit- tee. Warning n*tices were issued in respect of 295 children. Seven parents were proceeded against, and the usual fines were inflicted. The minutes were con- firmed on the motion of Mr. Handley', seconded by Mr. Taylor.—The Chairman moved that a precept be served on the overseers'for the sum of £7OO, divided into two instalments of £350 each.—Mr. Handley seconded, and the motion was earried.—The Clerk stated that Mr. John Ashton, returning officer, had received the following letter from the education department, which he for- warded to the Board. The letter stated that their Lords could not alter the day of the triennial retirement of members of the Runcorn School Board fixed by paragraph 3 of the general order, regulating the triennial election. But they would give, under paragraph 3 of the order, their sanction to the day of election being not more than 50 clear days before the day fixed for retirement. —The Chairman said the letter was not quite satisfactory inso- much as ip did not state whether it would be permanent. —The Clerk stated that Mr. Ashton, had written to the education department in order to be quite certain as to the permanency of the alteration. The matter then dropped.—This was all the business.

div.head: EXTENSION OF THE BOROUGH. LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INQUIRY.
div.p: EXTENSION OF THE BOROUGH. LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INQUIRY.

A public inquiry was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday by Colonel Ducat, Local Government Board Inspector, into the memorial of the Warring- ton Corporation for an extension of the borough boundary, so as to include the township of Little Sankey, and also portions of the townships of Latchford Without, Appleton, Walton inferior, and Poulton-with-Fearnhead. Tbee was a large at-

tendance. , The Corporation were represented by Mr. E. Sutton, barrister, and Mr. Bradbury, barrister; the London and North-Western Railway Company by Mr. Rickards, barrister (instructed by Mr. Mason); the Runcorn Board of Guardians, and Rural Dis- trict Council, by Mr. S. Moss (Chester); the Lan- cashire Co'anty Council, by Mr. F. C. Hulton ; the Cheshire County Council, by Mr. C. Hibbert ; Lord ; Lilford, by Mr. A. G. Steel, barrister (instructed by Mr. E, A. White); the Warrington High way Board, by Mr. Preston (instructed by Mr. H. B. White and I Sons); Ship Canal Company, by Mr. Astbury; Poul- ton-with-Fearnhead, by Mr. T. H. Granger. Among those present were the Mayor (Councillor James Fairclough) Aldermen Hutchinson, Sutton, Wright, Harrison, Bolton, Francomb ; Councillors Bennett, Evans, Heatun, Plumpton, Wilkinson, Woods, Smethurst, Lee, Monks, Garner, Shaw,Muir, Shillcock, Hill, Hepherd, Roberts, Pierpoint, Shaw Green, members ot the Warrington Corporation; Messrs W. THE CRI,TECT OF THE EXTENSION. - Mr. SueTosAnicl .thei with the consent of the other gentlitepn agesent, he would take the memorial of the Warrington. Corporation as :read. The houndiries of the borough did not in any way ollow natural boodaries. That had always been o, but since the making of the Manchester Ship C anal, it had beercgreatly accentuated. The great o bject of the Corporation had in view was to make the boundary follow upon such a permanent water- way as the Manchester Ship Canal. In addition to this. all,the townabips, parts of which they pro- posed to take, were -upplied with gas and water from the Corporation. 'they had a differential rate of 6d. per 1,000 feet per mile.' There was alsoA matter of niost Atel importance to all the large towns dB the north of England, and was probably of exceptional importance now that the Ship Canal had been. Made. 'That was the question of sewage. Warrhigton ssi. Present had no adequate sewerage system,laut'they had undertaken as soon as the municipel authorities higher up the river had car- ried out their echemes, with the' consent of the Local Government Beard to deal With their sewage' ontfall. 4 was, therefore, desirable that the town ships aroland should be.includecl in .the schem , There wen also not sufficient police provision in t , tawnShiPs and it was extremely desirable .thai they, should bp ,under the jurisdiction of Wafring- ton. lie was glad to be able to say that except,for 1 the one serious opposition of the London and North I Western Railway, and the opposition of Lord Lil-1 fOrd would, he hoped, when the case had been I heard, which not be persisted in, all the persona in- terested if they did not absolutely support' the' Corporation did not oppose them. He believed that the majority were active supporters of the scheme. Arrangements had been made whereby the Warring-! and Runcorn Unions should be separated by the 'Ship Canal. At the present time, a road had been constructed across Arpley meadows which was the main thoroughfare between the counties of Lan- catlike and Cheshire. It was desirable that this road should be under the control of Warrington Corporation. The Warrington Rural District Coun- cil and Runcorn Rural District Council had agreed ph the extension. In Little Sankey the parish coun- All had agreed to the extension, and a public meet- 4ng of the ratepayers had ratified the agreement. 41r.ilonks had also agreed to it, and also Mr. B. tbrinashasv, who was a tenant of Lord Lilford. This township was practically an urban district. In .Walton Inferior it was necessary in order to give it :a sufficient supply of water that it should be in the . borough, as there was not at present an ample sup- :ply. The Corporation had agreed to make an ex- tension of gas and Water mains. The chief rate- payers and inhabitantaef Appleton had all agreed to,the scheme,including Manchester Ship Canal,and Messrs. Greenall,Whitley and Co.,M essrs. Francomb and Bolton. He waB also glad to say that the Parish Council had agreed that morning. The township of Appleton 'formerly drained into the River Mersey by what, was called the Stockton Heath outfall. Owing to the changes made by the Ship Canal, the sewage was now emptied into a cul-de-sac. This caused a great nuisance owing to the sewage being deposited on the banks. This would continue to be a nuisance ant an increasing nuisance. . It was therefore absolutely necessary that something should be done. In Latchford Without, the Ship Canal Company were largely interested. He was very pleased that the Company had approached them and they had been enabled to come to an agreement. The Pariah Council and also the parish meeting had agreed to it. There was no doubt that the portion of Poulton which was applied for was at present rural, and Messrs. Hutchins were the only inhabitants. The Corporation had made advant- ageous arrangements with tegard to the roads, to keep them in repair. There was running through that district a brook called Padget° brook, which formerly flooded the fields round about. At the last extension of the borough, the boundary was extended to one bank of the brook, and they had acoured their side of it and greatly improved it. They were, however, unable to scour the other side owing to the property owners interested. lie con- tended that the opposition of the London and North-Western Railway was a purely selfish one, and was merely a question .Of paying rates. They objected to paying rates .as" everyene else did. The Corporation had been unO,ble to come to any final agreement with the Compkny 'in the matter as they wished to be charged at one quarter as though they were owners of agricultural land, which the Cor- poration could not accept as it would not be fair to the other ratepayers. The Corporation were also anxious to provide various buildings which were necessary for the public health. A hospital for small pox, recreation grounds, and open bathing places were needed, and it *as therefore desired to have some places of rural character. ' THE SHIT CANAL COMPANY APPROTES. Mr. Aststua said that the Ship Canal Company had decided to support cordially, the schernd of the Corpora- tion. The Company owned in the district proposed to be incorporated about 205 or 210 acres, and they ex- pected that shortly that land would he covered with valuable buildings and works. Terms had been agreed With the Corporation which were mutually advan- ;tageous. There had been sotne small matters which had been altered from the original proposals. The proposal was that the boundary should go along the centre of the Oka', but at the Company for several reasons did not decire.one half 'Of the oral in one county, and t,he other ha' another county it had been ttecided to sidops the rairtb batik at the lower water level as the boundary,and that no portion of the canal proper should be assessed by the borough rate. The area to be included in the boundary had been arranged for 'under a differential rate upon a 15 years' principle ; and the Corporation would take aiiresponsibeity for Arpley-road from the date of incorporation. In conclusion, he again cordially sup- ported the application of the Warrinton Corporation. Mr. F. C. They had also agreed with Cheshire and the Corparation as to the adjustment of the various matters of difference between these three bodies. WEDNESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

The first witness called on Wednesday was Mr. F. MONKS, I P., C.C., who said that he carried on business as an iron manufacturer at Atherton's Quay, Wigan, and also in Warrington. He was chairman of the Parish Council of Walton Inferier, which had decided not to oppose the incorporation of a portion of the township, but that had still to be confirmed by the parish meeting. The terms offered by the .Corporation had been accepted unanimously by the Council. There had been a dearth of water In Walton Inferior and it would be to the advantage of the township that the mains of the Corporation should be taken to it. His works at Little Sankey outside the borough were rated at £740. The rates would be increased by taking it into the borough by £95 lie. Bd. at the end of 15 years. The firm did not oppose the extension. Cross-examined: The works in Little Sankey were built in 1874. Ilis iron was chiefly obtained from Lin- colnshire and Barrow-in-Fgrness. It came partly by rail, and partly by water. His coal was obtained from Haydock,by rail. He thought that the Corporation had a good claim for the extension. Mr. Josern MCP:INFIELD, builder, residing in Walton Inferior, and clerk to the parish council, also gave evi- dence in favour of the extension. He thought it right for the good government of the district that it should go into the borough. There was a large quantity of land suitable for building purposes in the township, and was I lying idle for want of water. The water supply was dependent upon a well. The cross-examination of Mr. J. LYON WHITTLE (town 'clerk) by Mr. Rickards, was then proceeded with. Be Said that the average rates levied during the last four sears on land including Latchford in the borough was 35. zid. In Little Sankey they had been 2s. ed. The average rates in municipal Latchford for the railways during the last four years was 3s. eid. The railways had in addition to that ith of the Improvement and Sewers rates. In Latchford rural it had been 2-5 3-8. It was not however fair to take an average of the last four years, as great expense had been incurred owing to the small-pox epidemic. The average improvement rate for the last 20 years was 2s. lid. 4-5.

div.head: ALLEGED LIBEL ON A WARRINGTON INBURANCE AGENT.
div.p: ALLEGED LIBEL ON A WARRINGTON INBURANCE AGENT.
TRIAL AT THE ASSIZES.

At the Crown Court, of the Liverpool Assizes, on Wed- nesday, last week before the Lord Chief Justice (Lord Russell of Killowen), 'and a special jury, an action was heard,in which John Martin Dale,l.Friars Gate,Warring- ton, insurance agent, sued the London, Edinburgh, and Glasgow. Assurance Company, and James Seddon, their local superintendent,residing in Liverpool-road,Warring- ton, for £5OO damages for slander which was alleged to be contained in certain letters sent by Seddon to Mr. Hewitson, Burton-on-Trent, and Mrs. Major, Cholmon- deston, and also in a notice issued, with reference tb the dismissal of Dale from the defendant Company. The let- ters complained of were as follows: "Industrial Branch Department, from J. Seddon, of 131 Liverpool-road, Warrington, agent industrial branch to the Lcndon, Edinburgh, and Glasgow Assurance Co pany, Limited, to M.. Hewitson. 28 Needwood-st., urton-on-Trent, November 14th, 1894, re John M. Dale. Dear sir,—l quite agree with you asking any question respecting the deficiencies of this man (Dale) but questions apart from him and which will not assist you, I must respectfully decline to answer. Mr. Dale has been dismissed from our Company's service for dishonesty, and as we have a bond, we shall take the usual course in dealing with that, unless the money is forthcoming from that source, and I have written the bond to that effect. You know Mr. Dale is applying to another office for appointment, and is giving you as a reference as to character, Stc. Can you give him one with these facts before you ? I say that whatever you may do or say respecting him is very important considering your position, and feel perfectly sure a guarded pen is required, and moreover, he is placing his bond in another unpleasant position,by call- ing upon our pokey holders with a view to persuading them to enter with him into another company, and ac- cording to his agreement and according to our bond certificate we are secured against any loss which we may suffer in consequence thereof. I trust he may know sufficient to,see the risk he is incurring." It was alleged that by this,it was meant that the plaintiff had em- bezzled and misappropriated the monies of his employers the defendant company, and was a dishonest person,and had committed an indictable offence. The letter to Mrs. Major ran as follows :—" Dear Madam,— I am much pained to have to write you respecting the deficiencies of Mr. John M. Dale, for whom your late husband stood bond. He has been coming to my office short of cash collected for some months, and at present has run up the amount to over £lO. I have kept finding him money every week "so as to hide it from the com- pany in the hope he would soon redeem himself, and also upon a promise he would get the money either from you or his brothers, but last week he came 19s. sd.short of cash again,and desired me to let it go to London office short. He has also come in short again this weelc-(Nov. 3rd, 1894), to the amount of 293., and has by this act placed himself under the penalty of the law, but before I recommend the company *hat course to pursue, I would like to hear from you relative to the matter." It was further stated on November 27, 1894, the defendant company through their authorised actuary, Wilfred A. Bowser, acting within the scope of his employment falsely and maliciously wrote and published of the plain tiff in the form of a letter addressed to George Harding, 138, Birchall-st., Warrington, the following :—" I beg ,to infor,n you that Mr. J. M. Dale is no longer an I agent of the company, he having been dismissed for dishonesty, and that Mr. S. Wright, J.P., of Mersey- st., Warrington, has been appointed in his stead." The plaintiff was represented by Mr. J. 'Addison, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. Collingwood Hope, barrister (instructed by Mr. F. S. Foley, solicitor, Bolton) ; the defendant Company were represented by Mr. Shee' Q.C., and Mr. J. W. Hamilton barrister (instructed by Messrs. Wynne, Baxter and Keeble, solicitors, London) ; and the defend- ant Seddon was represented by Mr. G. Rhodes, barrister (instructed by Mr. Percy Marsh, of the firm of Messrs. Richardson and Marsh, solicitors, Bolton). Mr. Collingwood Hope, in opening the case, said that the action was brought to recover damages by Dale against the Company and Seddon, for libels in which they alleged that the plaintiff .had been dismissed for dis- honesty, being written by the authority of the defend- ant Seddon. The defendant said that the letters were written without malice' that they were privileged, and that the words did not have the meaning put upon them by the plaintiff. Mr. Addison Q.C., M.P., then addressed the Court. He said that Dale lived in Warrington, and in Septem- ber, 1893, he was appointed collector for the London, Edinburgh and Glasgow Assurance Company. The superintendent of the Company was Seddon. When appointed, Dale had, what was called a cleanisheet. He had to make a new book entirely. The insurances were effected upon people who paid weekly sums of 2d. per week. The plaintiff commenced his duties in 1893, and at the end of twelve months had got together a book— after all the difficulties and troubles which arose from the getting of it together—amounting to the weekly re- ceipts of £4. The terms on which he was engaged were that he should receiVe 4s. in the £, or 20 per cent., and in addition to this,there was an arrangement which was called special salary, whereby the collector was entitled to receive six weeks' premiums for any new assurance, he at the same time guaranteeing the Company the first eight weeks' premiums. The defendant was obliged to give his whole ,time and attention to the business. When he had had the book for over twelve months, if he were not discharged for dis- honesty, he was entitled to dispose of the book to anyone. The book of Dale was valued at about £3O. In October, 1894, Dale brought hie nooks and papers to Seadou, las iwuredi.sto superior, and gave notice of re- signing his post saying that there were so many failures and times were so bad that the policy holders could not pay their premiums. He was then short of money which he could not collect. Seddon said that he would rather explain the whole thing to the Company. He paid Seddon one guinea, but 193. 3d. lie could not pay owing to so many lapses. On October 31st, Seddon went round with the book along with Dale to collect the cash, and some money was Collected short again, Dale there- upon arranged with Seddon to !fell the book, and an advertisement was put in a Warrington paper advertis- izg it. Se far all had gone on smoothly,but on November Ist. Dale got aletter from the manager of the Company discharging him from their employ. It was about this time that the correspondence which is detailed above, which contained the alleged libel, took place. Mr. Addison here read the whole of correspondence. The notice which was sent by Mr. Bowser was sent because the people would not pay to the new man, Mr. Wright. He held that the Company were within the scope of the authority of the court, as by issuing that circular, they became responsible. His Lordship thought the statements in the letters were privileged. Mr. Hamilton said that so far as the company were concerned they made no imputation against Mr. Dale. They knew nothing about the letters until some time ago. John W. Dale was then called. He said that he was appointed agent for the company in September 1893, at the terms and conditions stated by Mr. klelison,and Mr. Hewitson was his bondsman at the time of his discharge. In 1894 he was unable to collect all the premiums he was liable to nay, and Seddon advanced certain neoney te him. On October 23rd, trade was so bad that he Was 19s. 31. short, and Seddon then said that he must write to the head office to explain matters. He had sent in his resignation before he was discharged. By the agreement be entered with the company he was not to canvas the company's members for six months after leaving their employ. He had since got another situatien. Mr. Rhodes said that judgment for £52 had been: obtained against Dale for canvassing members. Mr. Addison: They should not have called him dis- honest after getting £5O against him. (Laughter.) Mr. Shee having made a few observations, His Lordship said that he thought the letters were privileged. Mr. Shea said that his clients did not charge Dale with dishonesty, and he contended that they were not respon- sible for the alleged libel. His Lordship said that if the case went on, he would certainly non suit the plaintiff, He considered that the Cnnpany should pay Dale ten guineas, and not press the county court judgment, except the 1.0.15. of Seddon's, and also withdraw all imputations of dishonesty. Each side must pay their own costs. The case was then settled on these terms.

div.head: BURNING TH A "WITCH."
div.p: THE BURNING TH A "WITCH."
FURTHER EXTRAORDINARY EVIDENCE:,

The hearing of the charges against ten persons alleged to have been concerned in burning the woman Bridget Cleary was resumed at Clonmel on Tuesday. Mrs. Mary Simpson corrobarated the evidence given on Monday by her husband as to the placing of Mrs.Cleary on the 'fire. Those present at the scene cried "Away she goes ; away she goes," as if they were driving something out of the house. They thought the person in the bed was not Mrs. Cleary, but a witch. Mrs. May Simpson said that when the prisoners forced the herbs into the deceased's mouth she screamed ter- ribly, and when she did not answer the question but to her satisfactorily they carried her in her nightdress to the fire, placing her upon the bars. The deceased's father then said to her, "In the name of God,are you my daughter ?" When they were placing her upou the fire she said to them, "Are you going to make a burning of me ?" It appeared to witness that the accused did not believe it was Mrs. Cleary who was -lying in bed, and that they wanted to drive away what was in the bed, supposing it to be a witch. 'Witness saw herbs adminis- tered to the woman by the accused Michael Cleary, who exclaimed, " Take this in the name of God." She was then carried to the fire by four men, who held her there for about five minutes, none of those present seeking to prevent this brutal treatment. She was subsequently taken back to her bed in a raving condition. Thomas Smith, a farmer, deposed that he had known deceased for twenty-six years. There was nothing wrong with her mentally, and she was always healthy and strong. District nspector Wansboro gave evidence as to the , finding of the body of the deceased. The lower parts of the trunk and abdomen were completely charred and the internal organs visible. The further hearing was adjourned.
