THE W.C.C. AND THE W.F.C. Sir,—We notice in your football notes of Saturday last a paragraph with re.:erence to the difference at present existing between the Football and Cycling Clubs. The writer is mistaken in assuming that our griev- ance is becanse of the increased price which the W.F.C. wish to charge for the hire of their grounds. We are quite prepared to admit that the price at which the field has been let to us in the past has been reisonable. At the same time we cannot let the statement go by that 4. the W.F.C. have really been out of pocket by allowing the field at these prices, as a certain amount of work has had to be done to prepare the track." Apart from the price which we paid for the hire of the field, the care- taker received remuneration for the preparation of the track, from our Committee. What we protest against is this. Lastyear weheld our annual athletic festival in June and netted a considerable profit from same. The W.F.C. have been aware that we intended to apply for the field for the same time this year. However, when we did so, I we were informed that they (W.F.C.) could not allow us to use the field for a meeting until after August Bank Holiday,the obvious reason for this being that the W.F.C. intend to hold two sports, one on or about the date we established in June, and the other in August. Thus it will be seen that we were only allowed the choice of about three Saturdays in August, as the football season commences in September. We have no wish to widen the breach between the W.F.C. and ourselves, and are truly sorry that any difference has arisen, as we think that the same will cer- tainly have a detrimental effect upon the success of sports in Warriogton.—Yours truly, ARTHUR BOOTH 1 Hon. Secs. GEORGE H. SMITH I W.C.C. Warrington 28th March 1894. --- ABSTENTION FROM POLITICS. old friend Whitham won't let sleeping dogs lie. In his letter to the" Examiner " of the 16th inst. he evidently alludes to me in the following passage. " I 'was for years intimately acquainted in the dear old town with a good Socialist, who always refused to work or vote with the Liberal party, saying it was a waste of time. He seemed quite oblivious to the fact that he was wasting time with a vengeance by enabling a Tory to get the seat." Now as I was the only Socialist in Warrington for many years, he evidently hurls his shaft at my devoted head. For some years I have retired from active service either on the platform or in , the newspapers so far as Socialism is concerned, my nervous energy not being equal to the excitement required. However lam like the old war horse when he hears the bugle and clash of arms, and experience a desire to again join in the fray. And as my abstinence from taking part in politics is of a public nature,' feel it necessary to state reasons. First let me tell my old friend, Lain as staunch as ever in abstinence from poli- tics as lam from intoxicating beverages. As an Anar- chist my sins are crimson, for I hate laws and law makers—so, I say a plague to both your parties. Ido not love the Tories, but I like Liberals less. In the former we have an open enemy, but in the latter a false friend. Tney remind me of chemists. They deal in political compound pills, (very compounded) plasters, bandages, poultice materials, quack medicines in great variety, crutches, splinters, and other political nostrums too numerous to narrate. This is the party 11. W.," fac. ing both ways," would try and convert, which in my opinion is as hopeless a task as Ei .W. would find in try- ing to convert the Heathen Chinee. We dont want law makers we want law breakers. In plain words, we want men who are prepared to quash the laws that protect nomopolies in land, and in capital, and thus prepare the way for the co-operative common wealth. This the Liberals as well as the Tories are not going to do. "Not for Joseph if they know it." No, "great is" commerce of the monopolists. No, friend VV., cease your trying to serve two masters, and keep clear of the great habylon of politics. Touch not the unclean thing. A time of reckoning is at hand, and the country you have adopted as your home will lead the vabir., the revolution at hand. Certain European coun- tries will have to fAlow. Then woe to monopoly. My hope is, England will steer clear of the horrors that will then take place. 'That will depend upon the education of the masses in commonwealth ideas. Liverpool, March 27. W. H. CHAPMAN. WHICH IS THE TRUE CHURCH.? Sir,—l venture humbly and deferentially to submit ; that, because " lona's " obliquity of vision does not per- mit him to identify the Church of Rome with the Church ' of Christ, it does not follow, as a matter of inevitable necessity, that the Church of Rome is not the Church of Christ. Nor do I think the Roman Church must be characterised as" a pompous and inflated institution," simply because such is " boa's" conception of it. To many a greater intellect than his it has presented an al- together different aspect, its beauty and its grandeur winning both admiration and allegiance. " Who is she that cometh forth as the morning rising, fair as the moon, bright as the sun, terrible as an army in battle array " (Song of songs). Surely " lona. will not pretend that his " spiritual " church answers to this prophetic description from the pen of an inspired writer? On the other hand, how admirably illustrative the pas- sage is of that marvellous organisation which has its centre in Rome and its ramifications in all parts of the World ! Nothing can be more evident than the fact that the Roman Communion is a concrete, tangible church, hav- ing one Lord, one Faith, and one Baptism. If some of its members are not conspicuous for their observance of the Divine command to love one another,this is no proof that the Church of Rome is not the Church of Christ. Rather is it a fulfilment of prophecy. "The kingdom Of heaven," says our Lord, is like unto a net that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind : which when it was filled, they drew up on the beach, and they Sat down and gathered the good into vessels, and the bad they cast away." (Matt. xiii., 47, 48.) As the net was cast into the sea, so the Church of Rome is cast into the world ; and as the net did not gather all the fish that were in the sea, so neither does the Church of Rome con- tain all the human beings that are in the world. Within the net were fish of every kind, both good and bad. In like manner the Chnrcii of Rome comprises men of every nationality and in every walk of life, some of whom are good, and others evil. Finally, the fish outside the net were also of every kind, both good and had; and simi- larly, outside the Roman Chureh are to be found righte- ous men, as well as those of abandoned lives and evil principles. If " lona " can prove that " the Church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth" (I Tim. iii. 15) that rock-based Church, against which the gates of hell cannot prevail (Matt. xvi. 17), that Church which has been Divinely commissioned to disciple all nations (Matt. xxviii. 18-201 to preach the gospel to the whole creation (Mark xvi, 18)—if" Iona" can prove this Church to be the intangible, undiscoverable thing he would have us believe it is, by all meaus let him do so. One other re- quest I beg leave to eirefer ; it is that he will make some attempt to justify' his assertion that the Church of Rome places the teirm-,ial interests IJ f its followers unreservedly in the hand& of an Italian Pepe.— Obediently voure. /WO. J. nu,..-ToN. 31, Arthur-road, North Brixton, London, S.W.,March 5, 1895.

SOCIALISM AND—SOCIALISM.' Sir,—lu the name of reason I would ask" When is Socialism to be associated with common sense ? When will it cease to te that a Socialist with the cork out efforvesces so much that at least one half of what he utters is froth ? I am afraid that these good folk are damaging what is, after all has been said, a very good cause, by intemperance and exaggeration. I, for one, am no believer in this present, being the best system under which we are living in England. I hold,v&h the Socialists, that the land and the wealth of England are in ton few hands. With them again I would make strenuous war upon sweating and all other forms of labour evils, and exterminate their perpetrators as ver- min. Here, indeed, is an evil in want of a remedy. But robbery is no right remedy for this, or indeed for any other, evil. of Now, land nationalization And the nationaliz•dion savings' bank deposits,as advocated by ronh-sncialiets is robb.ery, pure and simple. And this is so altkoozh "Hector" has never beard or read of its being sn.• Ore hero, indeed appears to have been very discriminating in his choice of authorities—so ae t 9 get them all on one side of the question. This is an excellent plan where

firm and unwavering opinions are wished for it is the course adopted by the magistrate who had made up his mind as to the merits of the case and was not going to have that mind disturbed by hearing evidence on the other side. Hence, Hector has never heard the taking of another man's property described socialistically—as robbery. There is One Misapprehension of our Hectoring friend's which I should like to correct. Men of " Tony Lump- kin's stamp " do not think the evils of individualism " cannot be altered" ; but certainly they do think that to add another evil to that already existing is a bad way of mending matters. It is a thousand pities that these highly moral mob-Socialists should be so much belied ; for assuredly the common opinion about them is that their motto and sole creed is " Divide," So much is this so, that the anecdote told of the novice who carried the flag is always received as illustrating their practice and preaching exactly. The newly-caught one had been the bannerman in one of the processions to the place of meeting. On arrival there the candidate for admission into the socialistic brotherhood said :—" Well now, Pre been lugging this bloomin' rag about all this while, and now I should like to know what it's all about ?","Why," said the elders of the movement, " we are going to divide all the money in England." "And what met my share come to ?" queried the novice. " Oh, about sixteen pounds," replied they. "Then I'm havin' none," ejaculated he, " I've thirty pounds i'th' bank" ! And from that day to this socialistic circles knew him not. A noteworthy feature of lower-grade Socialism is the high moral toner assumed on:occasion, of its advocates. For instance, they lift up their hands in holy horror at the way in which the land was " stolen "in the bad old times. But, alas ! this sweet concord is marred by a passing note of inconsistency, when they make this first theft a pl.a for stealing it from those who had honestly bought and paid for it! Property thus acquired in full belief of the bona _fides of the nation, cannot, without , gross injustice, be nationalised without compensation.. But, as I think I have hinted before, all the laws of morality are under Socialistic revision and must give , way if they stand opposed to "the cause." Not only so, but the laws of nature itself must be thus abrogated. Nature says distinctly that " over population means starvation." So much land so many months—so many and no more. "Oh ! no," says the Socialistic," " We can mend all that—when the Socialistic rrillenium arrives." Indeed ! Let him step over to Ireland and see how over- population and patrimonial partition has worked there and wrought misery and degradation. The crime of bringing two children into the world when you can barely keep one is at the root of many of the evils of modern civilisation—mob-Socialism among the rest. One should have more faith in Socialism as a regener- ative agent morally, physically and socially:; if its advo- cates would but take it to some far land away from the degrading influence of InWvidualistic communities, and there make it a success as their converts. But alas! Socialism is a plant that cannot grow by itself, but de- pends for its very existence upon Individualism, while it flourishes most whilst abusing its foster parents. Finally, no amount of Socialism will enable two people to live where one only can exist. And none of the Uto- pian schemes at present afloat, will succeed, unless pro- vision is made to prevent this evil. I fully believe that the preventative restriction of over-population is better than any Socialistic cure. After this whoso wants my opinion on these matters must " See back numbers.— Truly yours,
TONY LUMPKIN.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF OUARDIANS
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF OUARDIANS

At Dutton W.irkhouse on Tuesday afternoon, a meet- ing of this Board was held. Mr. Knowles occupied the chsir, and in addition tone members of the Rural Coun- cil being present there were :—Rev. Canon Wood ,Messrs. T. Handley, J.A., T. Lea, and S. Yarwood. THE ASSISTANT MATRONSHIP. Mr. Handley stated that there had been two applica- tions for the positien of assistant matron. The commit- tee would make a recommendation at the next meeting of the Board. He moved that the advertisement be re- peated in the newspapers. —Mr. Baxter seconded the motion.—A rather heated discussion afterwards took place, and ultimately the motion was defeated by 13 votes to 9.—Mr. Priestner gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the original motion as to the appointment of assistant matron be rescinded.—The Deputy Clerk stated that this would not be in order as tbe advertisement ,had already appeared. The Chair- man informed Mr. Priestner that he could take action on the recommendation of the committee.

- THE CHAIRMAN. Mr. J. Mclntyre, J.P., chairman of the Council, acknowledged the vote of sympathy of the members as follows : "Dear Mr. Ashton,--orry to say I cannot be with you to-morrow, although I am improving nicely. I should like you to tell the Board how greatly we appre- ciate the expression of its sympathy with us in our affliction."

THE TREA.TDIENT OP VAGRANTS. Mr. Potts, clerk to Cheshire County Council, intim- ated that the sub-committee appointed by the Public Health Committee of the Council to confer with the Chairman and Clerk of each Board of Guardians and the Master of each Union Workhouse in the county, with a view of securing information of treatment of vagrants in the county, would hold a meeting at Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, on the 10th April. The meeting appointed the Chairman to attend, and in the event of his being unable to do so, the vice-Chairman should. THE PROPOSED ADDITIONAL NURSE. The Deputy Clerk stated that there had been no appli- cation for the position of night nurse, at the salary of £5O. It was decided to leave the matter over for some time.
WESTON SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICER. . Mr. Cooper, ot Weston, having resigned the position of school attendance officer through ill-hNdth, it was decided to advertise for another in his stead.

FINANCE. Mr. Heywood submitted the statement of the Finance Committee. The amount paid in relief at Runcorn was £95 ; Frodsharn, £33 ; and Budworth, £2O. He stated that the amount was rather heavy for Runcorn, but he understood that steps had been taken to reduce the amount at a meetibg held the previous day of the Relief supervision Committee. Accounts amounting to £l.OOO 154. 8,1. were recommended for payment, which would leave a balance in hand of £1,804 Bs. Id.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: PARIS, H MEETINGS. LITTLE SANKEY.
div.p: PARIS, H MEETINGS. LITTLE SANKEY.

--- - A parish meeting for the township of Little Sankey was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Li verpool-roa.d,on Monday, for the purpose of discussing the affairs of the township and passing such resolutions thereon as may be deemed advisable." Mr. R. B. Matthews, chair- man of the Parish Council presided, and amongst those present were Messrs. Williamson, Jackson, Brough, Grimvhaw. Corradine, members of the Parish Council ; Mr J. L. Tunstall (clerk to the Council),Messrs. Harper, Roughlev, Wilkinson, s;•:.—Thr. Chairman said this was the annual meeting, am 4 it was simply held for the pm, pore of giving the parochial electors an opportunity of attending a meeting and saying what they had to say or bringing forward any grievances or making any sugges- tion they wished to the Parish Council.—Mr. John Bos- ! tock asked would the Corporation wish property owners to pay again or find new paile,because that was a ques- tion that arose four years ago when tho Corporation i took over Wellfield-street and Percy-street. The ques- tion of the tubs was not then mentioned, hut they got a bill in for tubs. The Corporation charged 103. 61. per house,whlch he considered unfair to proporty owners.— After some discussion ,the Chairman promised to see what he could do in thematter previous to Tuesday's Inquiry. —Mr. Bostock f•arther asked if the Corporation would carry out their agreement with regard to watering and sweeping the streets.—The Chairman : Oh, yes.—Mr. Wilkinson mentioned a nuisance arising from the manure wharf and asked who should see to its abatement—The Chairman promised to bring the o- atter before the Parish Council.—This concluded the business. GRAPPENHALL.

The annual meeting of the ratepayers of the Parish of Granpenhall was held on Friday evening in the school room, -Grappenhall, Mr. W. Long presiding. There was a very small attendance of ratepayers. More the minutes of the last meeting were read, Mr. Jenkins said he should like to know if the requirements of the Act had been complied with in callin 7 that meeting ?—The Chairman said they had given notice of the meeting in the manner which had always bean customary in Grap- penhall, and he had no doubt most parishioners were a- ware of the meeting.—Mr.Jenkins thought that not one- third of the parishioners knew there was to be a meet- ing, and he held that sufficient publicity had not been given.—The Chairman said he thought the notice given was sufficient,and he should rule that the business must goon—Mr. Jenkins asked the Chairman to take note of his ohjection.—The Chairman ; And please take notice that this is a Parish Councillor, who, when it was pro- posed to put public notice boards up, opposed them on the ground that they would be broken.—The Assist- ant Overseer read the statement of accounts, which showed that the year commenced with a balance in hand of £lO3 2+. 81 and finished with a balance of £llO 14 10id. Trio whole of the rates, amounting to over £9OO had been collected,with the exception of £lO, which was irrecoverable, owing to empty property. Ile explained that the sum of £2 lie, had been spent in burying an unknown man found la the Olio Canal, but most of that amount would be refunded by the District Council.—The following report of the work of the Parlsh Council was read :—" Considering tiro short time the Council have been appointed, it is pleasing to know that the progress has been of a very satisfactory charac- ter. The expenses in connection with the Council have been kept down, and up to the present the expenditure has been about £4 for books, stationery, and the use of the room. Documents of value have been found in con- nection with the parish.someof them dating as far hack as the year 1628.0 r 267 years ago, It is the wish of the Council that all who know or who have heard anything of the parish in remote days will make it known, either ' to the Clerk or any of the councillors, so that it may be brought forward and looked into."—There was no other business, and the meeting was brought to a conclu- sloe.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATUIWAY, APRIL 6 1895
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATUIWAY, APRIL 6 1895
TiE INDEPENDENT__ LABOUR PARTY.-LECTIME
AT EARLESTOWN.

Under the auspices of the local branch of the I L.P. a lecture on " Labour politics ; the need for an 1.L.P.," was delivered in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on :,:aturday night, by Miss Caroline E. D. Martyn, of Sowerby Bridge. Mr. S. Schofield presided, and he was accompanied on the platform by Messrs. J. Miller, W. Roughley, and C. Wright. At the close Miss Martyn in the course of her lecture said with regard to the members of the 1.L.P., that there were people who believed in the religion of humanity, they were people who en- dorsed the opinion of that great social reformer. Several questions were handed up and satisfac- torily answered._

div.head: EA.RLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON.
div.p: EA.RLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON.
DRUNKENNESS.

At the Town Hall, Newton, on Wednesday morn- ing, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, Thomas Sullivan was charged with being drunk at Newton on Tuesday night, and was tined 2s. 6d. and costs. Margaret Maguire of Lime-street, ilaydock, was charged with being drunk, and with indecent behaviour on New- ton Common, on Tuesday afternoon, and was sent to gaol for seven days without the option of a fine.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS.

The anniversary services in aid of the above schools were held on Sunday in St. John's Church. There were large congregations at each service, the pulpit being occupied by the Rev. J. Grant Bird, vicar of Christ Church, Stalybridge. At the morn- ing service the choir sang the anthem " Doth not wisdom cry," and in the evening "1 was glad." In the afternoon the service of sacred song " Samuel," was given by the choir, the connective readings being undertaken by the Rev. J. G. Bird. The col- lections during the day amounted to .Cl 2 55., this amount being subsequently made up to .E. 21 14s. 81 with the collections from the boxes.

div.head: SAD fIEtOWNING CASE AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: SAD fIEtOWNING CASE AT EARLESTOWN.

A drowning case of an unfortunate nature oc- curred in what is known as " Thompson's pit," Wargrave-road, on Monday morning,the victim be- ing Frank Spotttiswood, 1 year and 8 months old, son of Mr. Charles Spottiswood, of Wargrave-road. About 11.30 on Monday morning,Mrs. Spottiswood was taking the ashes from the kitchen fire to the back, the child following her out into the yard. She went back into the kitchen, leaving the child out- side. When she went out a second time to look for the child it hal disappeared, and after searching round she saw it in the water. She gave an alarm, and a young man named William Rhodes recovered the child from the water. P.C. Schofield carried it into its home, and Pr. 11,n-old Watkins WAS soon on the scene, and tc.gether they endeavoured to restore animation, but although they persisted in their efforts for one hour and ten minutes, they were not suc-;e:sful. It is not known how the deceased got into the water. EARLESTOWN CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

_ On Friday evening the last of the series of smok- ing concerts instituted in connection with the above club, was given in the large billiard room, before a very good company. Mr. C. B. F. Borron, C.C., presided,and an excellent programme of songs and instrumental pieces was submitted and much enjoyed. The Earlestown brass band contributed in an efficient manner " The Village Blacksmith," the euphonium solo being creditably given by Mr. G. Jackson. The other items were, song, "The Reefer," Mr. G. Wright ; song, "The Rolling Deep," Mr. W. H. Kay ; humorous song, " Agricultural Show," Mr. T. Glover; song, "Anchored,' Mr. C. H. Lea ; clarionette solo, " The last rose of summer," Mr. T. 3 ukes ; song," Trusty as steel,' Mr. S. Swann; song," Goodwin sands," Mr. W. H. Kay; song, "our Guard," Mr. C. H. Lea; song, "Jack's Yarn," Mr. S. Swann ; song. " A soldier's song," Mr. J. Wright. The accompanists were Messrs. E. Leyland and T. Jukes.
.NiERgET MISSION TO SRAMEN.-RTINCORN BRANCH.

On Saturday evening an-entertainment was given in the St. John's Mission Hall, Earlestown, by mem- bers of tha drum and Fife band connected with the above. There was only a small attendance of the public, owing, no doubt, to other attractions in the town. In the absence of the Rev. T. It Matthews, who was indisposed, Mr. W. Shaw presided. The performers were attired in uniform, several young ladies being among the number, attired in jackets of the nautical type. Songs, readings. recitations and selections by the band were given, and the various choruses were very nicely sung. The task of accompanying was shared by Miss M. Boyer, and Mr J. Foulkes. The band was in the charge of Mr. Close. The following took part in the programme: Messrs. J. Shaw, T. Shallcross, W. II ulse, W. Cooper, W Marsh, P. Green, J. Gleave, T. Shaw, Byfield, Messrs. RandallsoiShallcross and Tickles. At an interval in the programme, the Chairman gave a short account of mission work, and explained that his work was specially among seamen, flatmen, boatmen and their families at Runcorn, where he had been about 20 years. He thought they had had a fife and drum band connected with the mission about 17 or 18 years They were going on very well, and the audience had heard a specimen of their playing that evening. Sailors, like other people wanted recreation. Their object in coming to ' Earlestown was to increase the funds being raised to pay for a plot of ground, and a monument they had erected in Runcorn Cemetery, for the special purpose of burying sailors who might die away from their homes. They had come there to try and help the cause forward, but he was afraid they would not get very much from their visit. He was very much obliged to the Vicar for his kindness in allowing them the use of the room. He proposed that their best thanks be given the Vicar for lending them the room, which was heartily

accorded. NEWTON DIVISION CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION. The annual meeting of the Earlestown Polling district of the Newton Division Conservative As- sociation was held in the Conservative Club,on Tues day evening. Mr. C. B. F. Borron presided,"and he was supported by Mr. W. H. Owen (Rainhill), and Mr. J. W. D. Barron, of the National Union of Con- servatives. There was a good number present. On the motion of Mr. W. 11. Owen, seconded by Mr. James Smith,Mr. Barron was elected chairman. Dr. llandyside was re-elected vice-chairman. Mr. Mos- crop was re-appointed secretary. Messrs. Haselden, Jones,and James Smith were appointed delegates to the Council. The old committee was re-elected, power to add to their number.—Mr. Catterall moved and Mr. Bailey seconded the following' resolution : —"That this meeting is of opinion that the domes- tic policy of the present Government,is of the most revolutionary character, and fraught with danger to the best interests of the British Empire,and begs ' to enter a solemn protest against the Welsh disPs- tablishment and disendowment Bill now before the loose of Commons.—Mr. J. W. D. Barron spoke at some length in support of the resolution, directing his remarks solely to the Welsh Church question. The resolution was put to the meeting and unanim- ously passel!. A vote of thanks to the speaker and chairman terminated the meeting. 1.0.G.T. ( FBENEZER 140DGE). - - - •

The usual weekly session of the Eeriest Own Ebenezer Lodge was held in the C ,perative Hall on Tuesday. The Gleam of Sunshine juveniles paid the adult lodge a visit, and their officers occu- pied the chairs. There were about 140 juveniles present, and a good number of visitors from the Hope of Farlestown Lodge. The juveniles were responsible for the programme, the following tak- ing part :—Recitation, Mr. Henry Lewis; reading, Miss Alice Lee; recitation, Mr. James Clarey ; song, Miss L. Clarey : recitation, Miss Daisy Clarey ; reading, Miss Sarah Chew ; recitation, Miss S. Naylor; reading, Mr. Eli Baostien ; reading, Miss Lily Sheridan ; song, Mr. John Taylor. Afterwards the adult lodge tendered to the juveniles a hearty vote of thanks fortheir excellent programme,which as !both instructive and interesting and was heartily enjoyed by all. The juveniles were then dismissed, and the adult lodge was opened by Bro. J. Taylor, CT., who presided. There was a good attendance of members and friends. The usual business was then gone through, two candidates being admitted to membership. Three representa- tives were appointed to meet on the United Picnic Committee, the following being appointed :—Bros. J. Taylor, S Wharton, and J. Taylor.
DEATH OF MRS. STELFOX, EAULESTOWN,
Another of Earlestown's old 'residents has been called away by the hand of death. Mrs. l annah Stelfox, wife of Mr. John W. Stelfox. 3 Princes-

street, died on Thursday at the age of 72 years. She had been in a weak state of health for some years, but until a week before her death she was able to perform her ordinary duties. An acute attack of bronchitis and Bright's disease brought about the end, although she was assiduously attended by Dr. Valentine. Coming from Manchester about 35 years 'ago her husband opened a clogger's shop in Bridge. street, and here they remained until about 11 years ago, when they retired from business. The deceased has been a member of the Congregation Church, Newton, for about 20 years, and a member of Mrs. Evans' Mothers' meetine since its commencement, she and Mrs. Lomas, whose death we recorded a few weeks ago, being the two oldest members of the class, She was a very ipeful member of the church,h eying done some good work in an unosten- tations way. The funeral took place on Tuesday afternoon at the Congregational Church, a short service being previously hell at the house by the Re v.James Allatt. The members of the mothers' meeting attended the funeral as a last mark of res- pect. ALL Hotrsanotn LINER hemmed and marked, free of charips --;1. and W Durrow.Sankev-st.. Warrington,— Sr.wrass Mammas Handl £2 18s 6d. Treadle £4 4s.with handsom, walnut cover.—J. and W. DUTTON, 16 and 18 Sankev-at.. Warrington.—Advt. WRINGING MACHINES.—atuLams, Ironmonger, Warr- agton.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARY.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARY.

The usual weekly session of the Hope of Earles- town Lodge of Good Tempters was held in the Co- operative Hall, on Monday evening. Bro. J. Warburton presided. Previous to the opening of the lodge an entertainment was given by the members of the Pride of EarlestownJuvenile Temple, under the presidency of Bro. E. Newman, a number of songs, recitations, &c., being given by the children and adults. The adult lodge was after- wards formally opened and four candidates were initiated, several others being proposed for mem- bership. Arrangements were made for holding the No.l Convention on Saturday. Sister R.Warburton was responsible for the after programme, which consisted of songs, recitations, readings, and piano selections, a very enjoyable evening bei:•:g spent.

div.head: NEWTON ITR,I3A.N DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: NEWTON ITR,I3A.N DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the above Council was held at the Earlest&wu Town Hall on Monday evening. Mr. C. B. F. Borron presided, and there were also present : Rev. E. W. Whittenbury Kaye, Messrs. Simpson, Beatty, Gilmore, MacMahon, Ormand, Smith, Wood, Eonmett, W. Thompson, jun.- R. Stone; J. E. Worsley (law clerk), R. Brierley (clerk and surveyor), Dr. Watkins (medical officer).

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. Watkins in presenting his quarterly report said that the births registered were males 72, females 52, total 124 ; deaths, males 25, females 26, total 51 ; excess of births over deaths, 73. The birth rates was 354 per thousand, and the death rate, 14-3 per thousand. 'The infantile death rate equalled 13.5 per cent, of the total death rate. The deaths included, membraneous croup, 1; erysipelas, 1; measles, 2 ; phthisis, 7 ; other pulmon- ary diseases, 10; heart disease 5 ; injuries, 2 ; all other diseases, 26. Ten cases of infectious disease included scarlatina, 1; diphtheria, 5; enteric fever, 1 ; erysipelas, 3. There had been no cases of searletina reported from December 19, 1894, to March 9, 1895, and the case which Ihappened on that date had been promptly attended to. Influenza had primarily caused four deaths.—Mr. Smith thought that the medical officer's report should be given to the Sanitary Commit- tee and then printed upon the minutes, as the members ought to have time to consider it, and have an oppor- tunity of making any remarks upon it. He proposed that that course be taken.—Mr. MacMahon seconded.— The Chairman said that that motion would give greater publicity, and cause much more careful consideration of the report, and he supported the motion.—Ttie motion was carried unanimously.—On the motion of the Chair- man, seconded by Mr. Thompson, the medical officer's report was then adopted. STREET IMPROVEMENTS. _ . .

Mr. Wood, referring to the minutes of the Highways &c. Committee with reference to the street making, m ,ved that the minute be referred back to the committee for further consideration. Among the property owners of Mersey-street and Nelson-st., there was much differ- ence of opinion whether the streets should he paved or macadamised.—Mr. Emmett seconded the motion which was carried.—Mr. Gilmour rose to make some further remarks about the minute, but the Chairman ruled him out of order.—Mr. Gilmour protested against the ruling of the Chairman.—Mr. Emmett said that lie did not think Mr. Gilmour was out of order. It was hardly fair to put any member of the Board down when he (the chairman) had asked each member to speak, and who could speak as long as he liked if he were in order. He did not see how Mr. Gilmour was out of order.—The Chairman : The resolution was passed, and we have closed the matter.—Mr. Gilmour thought that he had put a very proper question,and he was sorry the chair- man had so far forgotten himself as to call him to order. (Shame). Mr. Smith might call " shame," but he (Mr. Gilmour) would give the chairman no more respect than he gave him. TOLLS 1:720N SELLERS IN THE STREETS. . . . .

Mr. Gilt-n-o-u-r asked whether the Inspector had a right to impose the new tolls upon hawkers and sellers in the streets before the minutes of the Highways &c.Commit- tee had heen confirmed by the Board.—Mr.Ormand also asked the same question.—The Chairman said that the inspector had been premature in doing so.— Mr. Ormand then moved that the tolls here- tofore collected from hawkers and sellers in the streets, be abolished. He considered it a hardship to people to impose such a toll upon them and he therefore thought that they should be freed from it.—Mr. MacMalion seconded the resolution, and said that he had advocated this for some time.—The Chairman then read a letter from the Co-operative Society protesting against the impost on the ground that they were not hawkers, and also that they were very heavily assessed. They therefore prayed that this unfair toll should be taken off them.—The Rev. E. W. W. Kaye said that he was in favour of the abolition of the toll for residents, but he considered that non-residents ought to pay a double or at any rate an extra toll.—Mr. Smith strongly supported Mr. Ormand's motion. He said that he had never before heard of such a toll as was put on coal sellers, &c. It was quite unique to him.—Mr. Gilmour was pleased to find so many converts. He was certain that the motion would give satisfaction to everybody in Earlestown and Newton.—Mr. Emmett was pleased Le find that Mr. S:nith was waking up to his duties. He had been a member of the Commissioners far twelve months and done very little.—The Chairman: Mr. Smith alapears to be the scapegoat of the Commissioners. (Laughter.)— Mr. Gilmour: I thought I was the scapegoat. There must be two of us.—The resolution was passed unani- mously, Mr. MacMahon saying that he was glad tney were all converted.

div.head: NEWTON LAKE WATER,
div.p: NEWTON LAKE WATER,

Mr. Smith asked whether a, sample of the water had been taken from Newton Lake.—Mr. Brierley said that none had been taken yet as there had been so much " fresh "in the lake. His foreman had been instructed to get a sample.—Mr.Woods thought that some one more responsible should cet the sansple, and he proposed that the Chairman, the Medical Officer, and Mr. Brierlev be appointed.—Mr. Thompson seconded, and the motion was carried unanimously. Mr. Woods promised to go also.

div.head: GAS AND WATER COMMITTER.
div.p: GAS AND WATER COMMITTER.

The ChairmX-n;Wed.;:n-d- iii7M—C-M-a.hon seconded the adoption of thiscommittee's minutes which appeared in our last issue.—Mr. Gilmour called attention to the long hours which the men worked at the gas works. Some of them worked 18 hours at a stretch, and he con- tended that that ought not to be allowed. Work ought to be found for other men.—The Chairman said that no complaint had been made by the men.—Mr. Gilmour said that probably there was not, as they were paid for the extra hours, but they ought not to be allowed to work se long.—Mr. Smith : That would be interferring with the liberties of the subject.—After some further discussion, the minutes were passed unanimously.
FINANCE AND SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. The minutes lf these committees which appeared in our last issue, wPre passed unanimously without dis- sussion.
APPOINTMENT OF OYERSEERS.

The Chairman announced that he had a memorial signed by several ratepayers,recommending the appoint- ment of William Mill., Cross-lane as one of the two over- seers required for the township.—Mr. Gilmour said that a ratepayers' meeting had been held at which Messrs. Sankey and Flarrison were recommendee as overseers. The meeting was well attended and the nominations were unanimpusly passed. ELe thought that that meet- ing which was a public one, ought to have more weight than a memorial signed by a few persons.—Mr. Smith moved that Mr. Mills be appointed in conjunction with Mr. Sankey, the old overseer. No memorial had been sent from the ratepayers to the Counql, and he there- fore thought that they should consider the only memorial which had been sent.—Mr. Ormand seconded the nomi- nation of Messrs. Sankey and Harrison. A large num- ber of ratepayers had been at the meeting which nomin- ated them, and their opinion ought to receive some con- sideration.—Mr. Woods seconded Mr. Smith's motion. A long and rather acrimonious discussion ensued upon the subject, and upon he names being put to the Council, there voted for Messrs. Sankey and Mills,Messrs. Smith, Thompson, Stone, Woods, Simpson, and the Rev. F. W. W. Kaye, 6 ; and for Messrs. Sankey and Harrison, Messrs. Beatty, Ormand, Emmett, Machahon, and Gilmour, 5. Messrs. Sankey and Mills were con- sequently elected.

THE: L. Si. N.-W. RAILWAY CO., AND THE WATER SUPPLY. A letter was read from Mr. F. W. Webbe, of Crewe, asking for information with regard to what the New- ton Council were ening, to do with their water supply,as he had heard incidentally that there were going else- where for their water supply.—Tne Company were con- templating going to some expense with the water sup- ply, but if the Newton Council went elsewhere, that ex- pense would be unnecessary. An early reply was asked for. Surprise was expressed as to how Mr. Webbe had got his information.—The Chairman said that it was from the addresses of the candidates at the recent Oen- tions.—The Rev. E. W. W. Kaye said that he had advo- cated a better water supply from the district, and pro- bably Mr. Webbe had seen his address--ft was eventu- ally decided on the motion of Mr. Smith. seconded by Mr. Beatty to refer the letter to the Gas and Water Com- mittee.
ANIMAL MEETING. It was decided to hold the annual mcetilsg on the Thursday in Easter week. This was all the business.

div.head: NEWTON DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: NEWTON DISTRICT COUNCIL.
IN THE COUNCIL CHAMBER.
(BY A LOOKER ON).

The monthly meeting of the Newton District Council was on Monday evening noticeable for the quiet, and with a couple of exceptions, orderly manner in which the business was transacted. There were three absentees, Messrs. Collingwood, Evans, and Slee, the latter of whom is indisposed. The Rev. E. W. Kaye took his seat filling the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. Ratcliffe, Dr. Watkins, the medical officer of health was also pre- sent, and submitted to the Council his report for the first quarter of 1895. The report disclosed a rather serious state of affairs in relation to infectious die- eyes, it being stated that half the cases were of diphtheria and those had occurred within the last three days. He advised the Council to have the sewers freely flushed in order to guard against possible causes of disease. Five cases oh diphtheria in three days is a most serious condition of things, and the Council recognised the urgency of prompt action.

Mr. Smith, full of business, suggested that the Medical Officer's report should be submitted in future to the Standing Committee, and that it be printed along with the ordinary minutes for distri- bution at the Council. Mr. Gilmour got a little mixed over this, but a little consideration would have shown him that the resolution was very pro- perly drawn. There was a passage at arms between him and the Cliaircrla, and although Mr. Gilmour protested,the resolution was very properly adopted. It certainly is very trying to follow the reading of a report which is full or technicalities, and then be expected to discuss it. Mr. Smith's proposition was both wise and beneficial.

Mr. Smith was again to the front while the Law Clerk was busy reading aloud the printed minutes, a copy of which each member had before him. He graciously suggested that it would save time if they took them as read. This appeared to meet with the general approval of the Council, but Mr. Emmett, with his usual cautiousness, wanted to make sure that the minutes would not be passed before the Council had an opportunity of discussing them seriatim, and on being assured by the Chairman " that they could discuss them ds long as they liked," Mr. Emmett acquiesced in the motion of Mr. Smith. It is, no doubt a needless waste of time to wade through a lot of minutes of which each member has a copy before him.

There was a breeze over the street making ques- tion. It appears the sub-committee have surveyed the streets, but owing to the absence of the chair- man, the question was referred back. Mr. Gilmour wanted to know if they were to meet again to sur- vey the streets. He was ruled out of order, but with the dogged persistence which is natural to him, he refused to be put down. He said he was'nt out of order—" he had a right to speak, and he was going to speak." Mr. Emmett supported him, but the chairman would not give way, and Mr. Gilmour said be was sorry the chairman so far forgot himself, a remark which brought forth a cry of"Orcler" frora Mr. Smith. " Order yourself," said Mr. Gilmour, " I have a right to defena myself and I shall do so," " Yes, Mr. Gilmour," said Mr. Emmett," "but in a proper manner." "Well, I treat him with as much respect as he treats me," says Mr. Gilmour, and so the squabble ended, and the question was referred back.

The Council for once were unanimous, and agreed to abolish the imposition of tolls upon resident tradesmen. It was previously proposed to reduce them 50 per cent., but the injustice of levying a toll upon a tradesman resident in the town, simply because he calls at a house, and delivers a loaf of bread, was plainly seen, and very sensibly the Council removed a ridiculous tax from the statute books of the Board. The force of public opinion was certainly an important factor in bringing about this result.

So overjoyed was the Council at having per- petrated a generous act, that they suite forgot where they were, and before they recovered them- selves the Gas and Water Committee's minutes had been passed. Next came the finance minutes, when Mr. Kaye wanted to ask something about the previ- ous minutes, but the Chairman said he was too late —the minutes had been passed. This was a sur- prise, and immediately there was a hubbub. There was no help for it then, but to formally move that they turn back. Accordingly they went back, but nobody really knew why they had retraced their steps, anC the miats having been cleared from their eyes. they immediately re-p....wi the minutes.

Tim next question was the appointment of over- seers. The Chairman read a memorial which he had received signed by a few Conservative house- holders recommending Mr. W. Mills to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. Ratcliffe, and to act with Mr. Sankey of Newton. A public rate- payers meeting, it was pointed out, had nominated Mr. Sankey and Mr. B. Harrison, but the Chairman said in the absence of any memorial from that meeting, he must ignore it, and he did. Accord- ingly Mr. Smith moved the appointment of Mr. Mills and notwithstanding the vehement protest of Mr. Gilmour, all the Conservatives, including the Rev. Mr. Kaye, voted for Mr. Mills, who received the appointment by six votes to five.

The water question was brought up,a letter hav- ing been received from Mr. Webb, of the London and North-Western Company, asking the intentions of the Council,before he proceeded with the laying of new mains fram Parkside, saying that he had some scheme for getting their water elsewhere. Air. Simpson said Mr. Webb had received information from somebody which was not true. Mr. Woods wanted a sub-committee to meet Mr. Webb, but Mr. Smith said it should go before the Water Committee first. Mr. Kaye tried to take to himself the reputa- tion of having issued an election address, in which he referred to the water,and said it must have been from that address that Mr. Webb got his informa- tion—general titter as all the other members with perhaps one or two exceptions, had issued similar addresses and also referred to the water. Mr. Or- mend staggered the Council by asking what the sub-committee was going to see Mr. Webb about, as they had no instructions from the Council. This opened their eyes,and Mr. Woods withdrew his pro- position.

div.head: NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS AND DISTRICT HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY.
div.p: NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS AND DISTRICT HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY.

The annual meeting of the above Society was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Thursday evening. There was only a small attendance, mostly composed of the, commilee. Mr. J. Randall presided. The minutes oi the last meeting were read and confirmed. Mr. T. Wil- kinson, secretary, presented the statement of accounts, which showed that the year commenced with a balance of £l5 45., and the total receipts, including that balance amounted to £B2 194. lid., £39 is. being subscriptions. The expenditure 10,4 s £B2 154. 6d., leaving a balance in hand of Is. Si. £43 19s. was given away in prize money. The Chairman said he was very sorry that the Society seemed to be going down, he was sure that meeting did not encourage him. He felt that the time had almost come for letting the thing drop altogether. They had some exhibitors who came to show, and some who took a great interest in showing, but they let it stop there ; they did not assist the committee in any way, and did , not even show their faces at a general meeting. Mr. W. Liptrott propesed that the balance sheet be ' passed, which was seconded by Mr. Sephton and adopted. The Secretary intimated that at a committee meeting it was resolved to recommend to the gexeral meeting, that the show he held another year, with two classes, and that there should be some kind of sports, which would be an attraction on the date of the show. Mr. Williamson could speak from experience that the Society had been going down at a rapid rate. Three vearsfago they had £5O in hand, and now they had only Is. sd. If that was to boa fair sample, he did not know how they could carry on. If they started again it would be without money. Mr. A. Smith was bound to re-echo the setitiments of Mr. Williamson, and it seemed to him when he looked round the room, that only those taking an interest in the furtherance of the Society,were members of the commit- tee. It was useless for them to attempt,simnly with the committee only being active supporters. Mr. W. Spphton moved that the show be held as usual, with the same schedule, and that they have it at Earles- town one year, and Newton the year following, and that the amount of the prize money he reduced, the amateur class to be done away with, and the details to be left with the committee. Mr. Williamson seconded. Mr. Schofield moved an amendment that there be no show.- Mr. Beesten seconded. The motion was carried. Mr. T. Williamson was afterwards appointed secretary and Mr. W. Gorse, assistant secretary. Mr. Arthur Smith was appointed treasurer. A committee was appointed, with Mr. Randall as chairman.

div.head: SALE OF WORK AT NEWTON.
div.p: SALE OF WORK AT NEWTON.

On Thursday afternoon a three days sale of work was inaugurated in the Congregational schoolroom, in aid of the expense incurred in repairing and renovating the organ and chapel. Preparations for the sale have been in progress for some months, and a vast amount of labour has been expended. The arduous task of secre- tary was undertaken by Mr. J. Owen. The amount required is £2OO, and it is expected that at the close (1 the sale, this sum will be realised. The sale of Thurs- day was opened by Mr. K. Macrale,of Crewe, and ttere were present the Rev. J. Allatt, Rev. J. Camm, Mr. J. Evans,sen.,Mr.T.Molyneux,and a large number of ladies. After the singing of a hymn, the Rev. James Allatt said they accounted themselves more than usually happy in having their friend Mr. Macrae with them on that their opening day. Mr. Macrae's connection with that place dated back a good many years, and represented one of the oldest friends it was possible to have with them to take that part in the opening. Before calling upon him to declare the sale open,he ought perhaps to give one or two particulars for te , information of some who had not been present with them of late. In November last they found it was absolutely necessary to make extensive re- pairs in the outward structure of their church, and a very thorough work of renovation in the interior. That involved them in an outlay of some £2OO, and when the work was completed it gave such general satisfaction to everyone, that they said" now we will set to work and pay off the debt." There was no debt whatever upon those premises,and they did not wish that that compara- tively trifling amount should exist. They had only to look round in that room to see how steadfastly that idea had been kept before them. Every stall in that room represented the devoted personal labour of friends connected with that place ; where that was not so, the stalls were loaded with gifts, the offerings of friends and neighbours. The household stall in the corner was a con- spicuous object, and the abundance of soap there re- minded them that cleanliness was next to godliness. They had called that a sale of work, because it more exactly described what they had in view,than any other word could possibly do.

. - - Mr. K. Macrae said it was a real pleasure to him to be there on an occasion of that sort to renew his acquaint- anceship with old friends, particularly as they were all described as being in excellent spirits. Those who had drawn up the programme, had described them as "merry, merry men," and he hoped there would be more merry men before the day was out, and where tr-li-re were merry men, there must be merry women. It was not often that they found people free ot debt, for he remembered that years ago, when he was coming and going among them, they had a perfect horror of debt. The merry makinr, of to-day would consist in money making, and he bad no doubt they had come there to keep up tin fun, and the result would be that their friends would be able to discharge the obligations upon them before long. Whatever people might say about bazaars, they had become a very popular method of raising the means for decorating churches, and other estimable objects. He had never understood why so many of the goods on the stalls shotild be the product of ladies' hands, but he was glad now to see an announce- ment in the programme that the young men had come , forward and realised the fact that they were the people ' to do something when there was really something to be done. He then declared the sale open. There wersleight stalls and a fish pond which were ar- ranged round the room in such a manner as to give the place the appearance of a fancy fair. They were arranged in alphabetical order, Stall, A, was in charge of Mrs. .Dobson, Kidd, Hayes:J. H. Birks, Misses Arnold, Tasker and Brown, and was devoted to the sale chiefly of under- clothing. Stall B. was laden with clothing for children and adults, antimacassars, photo frames, and useful and *fancy articles. It was presided over by Mesdames Dun- calf, Galloway, Latchford, Misses Wood, Cooper, Turton and Rodgers. Stall C. was similarly laden to the pre- vious stall, and was in charge of Mesdames Tait,Bodrner Misses Tait, Jones, Mather and Hall. Stall D. contained all kinds of fancy articles with a springling, of clothing, . and was presided over by Mesdames Campbell, S. Birks, Syme, Pritchard, Crawford, Misses Carleston arid Wil- liamson. Stall "B" should Wave been called the stall of cleanliness for it contained principally soap and requi- sites for household management, and was in charge of Messrs. H. Owen, K. Hughes, Temple Edwards, Kidd and Jesse Bryce. The fruit and flower stalls contained some choice plants and flowers, and was attended to by Mrs. J. Owen, Misses Crawford, D. Mather, Pollock, Randall, Jessie Roberts' Thompson,and Urquhart. The young men's stall was laden with almost all kinds of useful articles, such as clothes horses, step ladders,knife loxes, wheelbarrows, fretwork frames, &c. and was at- tended to by Messs. Birkenhead,Latchford:Owen,Craw-

ford, Freeman, Hall, Howard, 'Johnston, R. Owen, H. Pennington, W. Randall, J. Rodgers, and W. Rylance. The refreshment stall was in charge of a number of ladies, and good business was done there. There were a number ot side shows and entertain- ments of various kinds, all of which were well patro- nised and a good business appeared to be done at the stalls. The sale will be continued to-day (Friday), and will be opened by Mr. B. B. Glover.

div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT (Continued from page 3.) THURSDAY.

In the House of Commons on Thursday evening, Mr. G. W. RUSSELL informed Mr. CROSFIELD that the report of the Opium Commission would be ready by April 11. In reply to Mr. DARLING, Sir E. GREY said no news had yet been received at the Foreigh Office as to the ex- 34.REZ BALFOUR. Mr. BRYCE, replykli 4"o Mr. J. A. BRIGHT, said he was anxiously hoping for an early Ol or ;nr,r—a•-..- ing the Light Railway Bill. Mr. ASQUITH brought iii a Bill to amend he Coal Mines Regulation Act, particularly in regard to the use af explosives, and it was read the first time. The debate on the motion of the second reading of the Irish Land Bill was resumed by Mr. T. W. RussEtt,who said he was glad that the leader of the Unioni.it party had resolved not to challenge a division on the second reading,for the Bill was pre-eminently one for discussion in committee. The debate was again adjourned.
Jo th,s House of Lords, Lord Rear read a telegram containing particulars of the fighting in Chitral. It is stated Oat the enemy lost at least 500, and that our casualities were reported as 50.

div.head: LIBERATOR COLLAPSE.
div.p: THE LIBERATOR COLLAPSE.
BALFOUR'S EXPECTED EXTRADITION.

The difficulties in the way of the extradition of Jabez Spencer Balfour are endless. On Wednesday it was stated, apparently with authority, that the fugitive had:been given up to the British agent at Salta. We now learn, however, from Buenos Ayres that the legal diffi- culties, which the Argentine authorities seem only too willing to raise, are' not yet overcome. Falfour's counsel has demanded that as a condition of extradition the Argentine Government should require of the British Government that the punishment be imposed ip this country for the offences which are imputed to Balfour should not exceed that which could be inflicted under the Argentine Code. This would mean, it is said, that the maximum penalty would be imprisonment for two years. The Federal authorities have resolved to defer the surrender of Balfour until this fresh point has been discussed. The five directors of the "Balfour group " of com- panies, against whom various charges of fraud and conspiracy have been brought, were on Thursday com- mitted for trial at the Central Criminal Court. Bail in heavy amounts was allowed. WESI ON.

PARISH Mnornsd.—ln the Church schoolroom on Fri- day evening the annual parish meeting was held. The Rev. Canon Wood presided, and there were also present —Messrs. T. Sill, J. Tudor, J. Vase, James Price, and J. 1 Collier (clerk). The Chairman said the gathering was to take place of the old vestry. Strictly speaking,there had been no vestry for the township of Weston. An ac- count of the charities, not ecclesiastical, should be laid before those in attendance, and accordingly be would present these of the Ann Orred Charity, which he believed originally consisted of £l,OOO left by a lady of that nante about twenty years ago. As it had net been in existence 40 years, it did not come within the province of the Parish Council to add to the trustees. The amount was invested in consols, and now stood, he believed, at £1,044 10s., bearing interest at 2t per cent. ' It was in the name of official trustees, who paid the in- come quarterly to the working trustees. The year com- menced with a balance of £7 4s. 11d., and the interest made the total receipts into £35 os.3d. From the charity during 1894, 24 different beneficiaries had received money to the amount of £2B 7s. 9d., leaving in hand a balance of £6 12s. 6d. The income. it would thus be seen, had been slightly exceeded, but as there was a balance in hand he did not see why this should not be done. He had a complete list of the beneficiaries,and he would lay the document on the table.—On the motion of Mr. Sill, seconded by Mr. Tudor,a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman.

NEWTON CRICKET, BOWLING AND TENNIS CLUB. This club wilt open its cricketing, bowling, &c., season on Saturday next. A good list of fixtures has been arranged, andit is expected that the sea- son will be a successful one. The tennis players have also several engagements on hand, and, given respectable weather, they anticipate an enjoyable time. ST. PETER'S CHURCH, NEWTON.

• In aid of the Newton Parochial Funds, a concert was given in the Town Hall, Newton, on Saturday evening, by the choir of above church. There was a very fair audience, and an excellent programme of vocal and instrumental music was submitted by the Earleetown Orchestral Society, Miss Rothwell, Miss Ada Airey, Mr. W. Turner, Mr. Devereux, and a glee party. Messrs. E. traireleugla and Wykes officiated as conductors.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be held at the COURT HOUSE, NETHER KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the Bth day of April next, at half- past eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Rucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials af all prisoners com- mitted from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Knots- ford District must be.in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the 4pening of the Court on MONDAY, the Bth day of .April next, at half-past olsven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will be Adjourned to the Castle of Chester, on THURSDAY, the 11th day of April next, at eleven &clock in the Forenoon. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District,and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-men- tioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Spssions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on THURSDAY, the 11th day of April next, at eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester. 18th March, 1895.

LAD/F8 AND GENTLEMEN, Having succeeded to the business so long. and suc- cessfully carried on by my late father I beg to appeal to the public for a share of their patronage and support. SHIP CANAL. ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. The steamer Egret belonging to the Cork Company met with an accident at Runcorn on Sunday, whilst pro- ceeding on her outward journey. After passing under Runcorn Bridge the top-masts of the vessel were raised. with the result that they struck a wire guage which Stretches across the canal, a short distance from the bridge. The wire was cut; the fore-topmast was smashed; and one of the poles upon which the wire guage was suspended was snapped in two. Other damage was also done, but fortunately no one was injured.

Among the deaths announced is that of Mr. William Steenstrand, well-known in connection with the Liver- pool cotton "corner "of 1890. In the Queen's Bench Division on Tuesday, Miss Eva Fraud was awarded £l,OOO damages against S idney Herbert Snell, a London doctor,for breach of promise of marriage. Mr. Such adinitted the promise,but said that he had been induced to make it by a representation that no near relative of the lady had died of consumption, whereas this representation was untrue, as the young lady's mother had died of that disease. The match between Mr. Stoddart's English Eleven and a team representing South Australia on Tuesday at A3e- laide ended in an easy victory for the Englishmen. The Colonial Eleven, who were 212 runs behind on the first innings, and who on Monday lost two wickets for 88 runs in their second attempt, were all out for 255. The , Englishmen had thus 44 runs to get to win. They scored them without losing a man, and thus won the match lav ten wickets.
